the next item is the debate on the oral question to the commission on the status of members of the european parliament elected in poland, tabled by mr giuseppe gargani on behalf of the committee on legal affairs (o-0082/2007 b6-0002/2008).
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the subject raised by mr gargani is certainly a relevant one: it is a relevant issue because there are two principles at stake here that i think are both relevant and both important. the first principle is certainly that of article 10 of the protocol on the status and immunities of members of the european parliament, which states that members of the european parliament must be accorded the same status in their home countries as members of the national parliament of that country. but there is another rule at stake - and one which is equally relevant in my view - and that is article 13 of the 1976 european act, which concerns the election of members of parliament. this article states very clearly that when a member state introduces a national rule relating to the very case in question, the loss of qualification status, that is to say the loss of the position of member of the european parliament, the termination of the mandate of a member of the european parliament in that country is subject to national law. in other words, there is an apparent contradiction, because on the one hand the legislation contained in the protocol on privileges, the one cited by president gargani, speaks of equality of prerogatives between members of the polish parliament and members of the european parliament elected in poland, but at the same time the european act of 1976 on the election of members of the european parliament and the loss of the status of member of the european parliament, apparently - i would say explicitly - regulates the loss of the status of european parliamentarian and states that the loss of the status of european parliamentarian is regulated by national law. in my view, there is rather a problem here of a violation of a third framework principle for the european union, which is the principle of equal treatment as established by polish domestic law. what is in the constitutional legislation of all european countries is the principle that similar situations must be treated in a similar way. it is rather this general principle that is at stake, and it is a general principle which does not, however, allow the european commission to determine in what direction the polish legislation should change its legislation, because since the matter is left to national law, if the national law wanted to regulate not the loss of the quality of a member of the european parliament but the loss of the quality of a polish national parliament in a different way, it could do so, the important thing is that it equates the discipline of the one with the discipline of the other. this is my personal view in the sense that the commission cannot today say 'we are going to the court to say that the polish national law must be amended in a certain direction', but i think that a general principle can be derived. the general principle is that the polish legislation must take action to correct this on behalf of the ppe-de group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. president gargani has very accurately portrayed the situation of members of the european parliament in the context of polish law and the unequal treatment in the same context of national members as well as senators. i agree with commissioner frattini that this violates the principle of equal treatment of members before the law. i would like to inform you that the current ruling coalition in poland, the civic platform and the polish people's party, has already started preparations to change this law so that the rights of meps are equal to the rights of national meps and senators. this amendment will be aimed at the same provision as in the european parliament electoral code, so that the same principle applies to national members of parliament and senators. but in this context, because president gargani said that we are starting a sort of discussion here about a problem that is perhaps wider, i wonder whether it would not be worthwhile to consider a common electoral system, at least in general terms, a common electoral system for the european parliament for all the member states of the european union, because today we have a very different situation in all 27 member states. it is difficult not to agree i of course accept all kinds of legal restrictions on members, but it is difficult for me to agree to a situation where you are punished, even with a fine, but in a procedure for a public prosecution for an intentional offence and automatically lose your mandate as a member of the european parliament, and also in a situation where you can be held accountable.
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. today's debate raises the issue of unequal treatment of polish meps and sejm meps in terms of eligibility criteria and loss of mandate. article 9 of the act of 23 january 2004 on the electoral system for the european parliament states that the right to stand for election to the european parliament is granted to a person who has not been convicted of an intentional offence or prosecuted for a public offence, and article 142 states that the loss of a mandate may be caused, inter alia, by the annulment of the election of a member of the european parliament, as a result of which the conviction of a member (as has already been said of the european parliament) by a final judgment for an intentional offence is equivalent to the automatic loss of his mandate, whereas in the case of members of the sejm this is neither an obstacle to participation in elections nor a loss of mandate. as regards the powers of members of the european parliament, rule 5 (1) of the rules of procedure of the european parliament states that 'members of the european parliament shall enjoy the privileges and immunities provided for in the protocol on the privileges and immunities of the european communities', which in its preamble states that it regulates the matters relating to the privileges and immunities necessary for the performance of the tasks of the european communities, and rule 10a states that 'during the session of the assembly, its members shall enjoy in the territory of their state the immunities accorded to members of the parliament of their state', so that members of the sejm and of the european parliament are protected by the same immunity. article 11 of the said protocol provides that 'representatives of member states participating in the work of the institutions of the communities and their advisers and technical experts shall, while exercising their functions and during their travel to and from the place of meeting, enjoy the customary privileges, immunities and facilities'. it is common ground that a member of the european parliament is a representative of a member state participating in the work of the institutions of the communities. since members of the european parliament and the sejm should enjoy the same immunities and privileges, the conditions for their election and forfeiture of their mandate should also be the same. by acceding to the european union, poland accepted the obligation to respect the law in force in the union, in particular that which has direct effects on the internal legal order of a member state. i therefore call for the legislation on the status of members of the sejm and the european parliament in poland to be harmonised as soon as possible, and i fully agree with commissioner frattini on this point.
mr. chairman, please! the proposal that mr zwiefka has put forward to equalise the status of members of the european parliament and of members of the polish sejm is not a solution to the problem. i think the best solution would be, as is written in polish law, that in a situation where someone has been convicted of a crime committed intentionally, the court additionally decides to deprive the person of public rights, which means that the person cannot run for office. this is the case in france, for example. i would like to give a specific example: our colleague, mr onesta, vice-president of the european parliament, was sentenced a few months ago by a french court to a suspended prison sentence for an act for which, under polish law, a polish member of the european parliament would automatically lose his mandate. i think it's absolutely wrong the way things are now. it is better to go in that direction than to accept the solution proposed by mr frattini.
mr. chairman, please! in fact, in addition to the votes with which i largely agree, i think that we should of course harmonize the rules as quickly as possible. to show how necessary this is, i will draw attention to the story of our colleague, the member of the european parliament who is here in this chamber, mr tomczak, who has been in poland for many years now, and who is currently facing a criminal case which is coming to an end and which may affect his fate as an mep. a case that has a low-level of malice in which witnesses deny the event. a case that was once closed, which has now, perhaps, with some political turmoil, returned and today mp tomczak, who has already been democratically elected twice (in 2005 he became an mp, in 2004 an mep, our colleague), today can be questioned his immunity and his mandate. it's an incredible thing, it's harmful, and it should be cut down and removed from this forum as soon as possible.

in writing. - the rapporteur, paolo costa, shows the essence of the abolition of discrimination in transport rates and conditions. indeed, considerable benefits can be achieved in a short time by relatively minor changes to existing legislation. as shadow rapporteur, i note that a common position has been reached between the council, the commission and parliament.
in writing. − the rapporteur, johannes blokland, rightly points out that appropriate regulations should be introduced at international and european level to enhance the protection of the environment and public health. the development of specific infrastructure in less developed countries will strongly oppose the irresponsible use of chemicals that can have harmful effects on the environment, the economy and working conditions.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report by mr blokland on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the export and import of dangerous chemicals. the report raises the issue of allowing transportation without explicit consent. the current situation is economically disadvantageous for european chemical exporters if they are not allowed to import the substances listed in the annex. these regulations make it easy for european exporters, who are subject to severe restrictions in europe, to export chemicals outside the european union. the introduction of a flexible change may result in less developed countries, in particular, having no protection against the introduction of chemicals into their territory. in order to avoid uncontrolled exports of hazardous substances to third countries and to protect countries that have less or no ability to assess hazardous chemicals, the period of tacit consent should be shorter. it is important that the commission proposal addresses the issue of introducing tools to facilitate customs enforcement of the provisions of the regulation. close cooperation between customs offices and designated national authorities is necessary for the effective and proper functioning of the mechanisms proposed by the new regulation. the implementation of the new rules should be preceded by the development of product use guidelines and information documentation and by the provision of training in accordance with community standards, especially for the new member states.
in writing. - recalling the principle of the four fundamental freedoms of european economic integration, i would like to draw attention to the importance of regulation 1408/71, which aims to promote the mobility of workers in the european union. although the report in question deals with strictly technical matters, those matters, in seeking to update the regulation in question in order to take account of developments in the field of social security at national level, have a direct impact on the daily lives of citizens travelling, working or residing in another member state. i also agree with the rapporteur that the social conditions must be clearly defined when the principle of mobility is being implemented in europe. finally, i would like to emphasise how important the proposed changes and the transparency of the rules are for the thousands of polish citizens living and working abroad. this is one of the main reasons why i supported the csaba őra report.
in writing. - mr csaba őry rightly believes that effective coordination between member states in the field of benefits should be ensured at european union level. this regulation, by introducing updates to take account of recent developments in certain member states, has the potential to guarantee in the future the possibility for citizens moving from one member state to another to benefit from social security.
in writing. - ladies and gentlemen! taxation is perhaps one of the most sensitive eu issues. as soon as they are discussed in international forums, thousands of words of criticism are heard, mainly because member states are jealous of their right to establish them. in the discussion of ms kauppi's report on tax losses in border situations, the tax problem was indeed analysed in a substantial way. it highlighted the major problems associated with subsidiaries of companies that benefit from different tax regimes, often within the same company but in different countries. there is no doubt that the european union needs competitive tax rules. that does not mean harmonized in any way, but competitive. such that they do not constitute undue hardship but, on the contrary, provide an incentive for the possible opening of a business. i believe that the european union should not be concerned with the harmonization of corporate taxes at all, but should coordinate taxes at eu level in such a way that they bring real benefits from tax competition. i am glad that the rapporteur shares my views in the report.

madam president, the rapporteur on the black sea regional policy reminds us that the european union supports new energy infrastructure and viable transport corridors, diversifying both suppliers and routes. the prime example of such an undertaking is the nabucco gas pipeline, already recognised as a priority project of european interest. it is, therefore, regrettable that this project is being undermined by an alternative russian-italian pipeline by the name of south stream. as a member from poland, i see many parallels between south stream and the nord stream baltic gas pipeline. both are much more expensive than overland routes. indeed, south stream may prove to be usd 4 billion more expensive than nabucco. both may disturb the fragile ecological balance of sensitive marine environments. furthermore, in both cases, the pipelines may be seen as a political weapon in the hands of russia. nord stream will isolate poland, the baltic states and ukraine; south stream will play the same role with respect to turkey, the south caucasus and, possibly, romania, which may now be bypassed in favour of serbia. south stream goes against the principle of energy security in europe, based on diverse sources and routes. thus, if south stream does go ahead, it should not receive eu funding at any stage. if russia is going to push forward economically unviable and environmentally questionable projects, because they serve its foreign policy aims, then it should not be at our expense.
madam president! in taking part in the debate on the countries of the south caucasus and regional policy in the black sea region, i would like to draw attention to the following points. firstly, it is a huge area of energy production and transmission, which is of great importance for the diversification and security of supply of energy resources to the union. however, support is needed for projects to transport energy resources from this area not only to the south of europe, as is the case so far, but also to the north to ukraine and poland and further west. secondly, only the european union's support for political stability and democratization processes in the region, as well as for the peaceful settlement of conflicts between neighbours, will give these countries a chance to develop rapidly and to reduce significantly the huge unemployment and poverty. third, the strong economic growth in the region as a whole, in some countries exceeding 30% of gdp per year, is based solely on the extraction and export of oil and natural gas. it is therefore necessary to promote alternative sources of income in the area, in particular the development of tourism and related infrastructure.
madam president! the rapporteur is very pleased to present to the european parliament the initiative to strengthen black sea synergy, a proposal put forward by the german presidency and concretised by the european commission. the idea also gained support from the newly integrated southern and eastern baltic countries. their position also reflects their conviction that black sea synergy needs to be closely integrated with the so-called eastern dimension of the european union. local cooperation will thus acquire a more general meaning, a potential for implementation in line with the basic community message. in other words, black sea synergy should simply be expressed in the identification and synthesis of multilateral undertakings, identifying them with the well-understood interest of both the black sea region and the whole of eastern europe as an integrated region. the special geographical, historical and political-economic situation of the black sea is an important factor enhancing its special role. for thousands of years, this region has been a crossroads of european and asian influences. the european union's involvement in the black sea must therefore be free from unnecessary institutionalisation, political influence and restrictions which threaten to weaken the conditions for rational cooperation and even destabilise the region, both in terms of security and the functioning of the transport network, environmental protection, etc. additional favourable conditions should also be created for the black sea to be more closely involved in the process of diversifying energy supply routes, with possible consideration of new sources, especially from the so-called caspian direction. many eu countries are interested in it.
member of the commission. − mr president, the commission warmly welcomes the motion for a resolution on the role of women in industry. i congratulate the rapporteur, ms figueiredo, on addressing this issue of the situation and role of women in industry, which is complex. one of the several reasons is that, as shown in the report, the gender equality challenges in industry are even more acute than in other sectors. in industry, the problems of working conditions, the pay gap and the reconciliation of work and private life tend to be even more pronounced. it is also a complex issue because it goes beyond equality policy to relate to the general situation in industry in europe and the way community policies can support industry and workers – both men and women – in the difficult context of globalisation. as you know, the adoption of the roadmap for gender equality in 2006 underlined the union’s full commitment to do its utmost to make progress towards a situation of real equality between men and women. the six priorities of the roadmap are linked to improving the situation of women on the labour market. the first is economic independence for women and men, the second is reconciliation of private and professional life, the third is equal representation in decision-making and the fourth is the elimination of stereotypes. the commission welcomes the fact that parliament’s motion for a resolution highlights precisely these areas. whilst the progress made in the area of gender equality is unquestionable, major challenges remain. the commission shares the rapporteur’s view that we must continue our efforts and consolidate what has been achieved. as far as women’s participation in industry is concerned, two issues should be tackled. firstly, there are still very few women in industry compared to the services sector. secondly, those women who work in industry tend to be in typically female sectors which are very labour-intensive and characterised by poor working conditions and low wages. the commission is conducting various policies to meet these challenges. combating stereotypes in education will, in the long term, lead to there being more highly skilled women in technical and scientific occupations and will also help to meet the needs of certain industrial sectors for manpower or womanpower. it is also important to support the careers of female engineers via networking, mentoring and measures to balance work and private life. in order to diversify women’s employment in industry, it is vital to provide every opportunity for training and retraining. the european social fund provides essential support in this area. it is also vital to improve the current situation of women working in industry. for example, there is still an unjustifiably large gap between women and men. in industry, this gap is as much as 30%. for this reason, in july 2007 the commission adopted a communication on tackling the pay gap between women and men. the communication examined all the resources that must be mobilised to achieve this aim. the involvement of enterprises is an important way of making progress in the areas of equality between men and women at work, the gender pay gap, training, work-life balance and career development. in addition to the laws on equal treatment, which all enterprises must obey, it is important to encourage them to adopt voluntary measures to promote equality, in particular in the context of corporate social responsibility. finally, the commission will shortly relaunch an awareness-raising campaign for enterprises about gender stereotypes. the report on women in industry underlines the vital role of work-life balance in order to achieve real gender equality and the commission shares this analysis. this point was mentioned during the adoption by parliament of the kauppi report in september 2007. the commission will report in 2008 on progress towards the barcelona objectives in the area of childcare. the second phase of the consultation of social partners on work-life balance concluded in july. the commission takes the view that this issue should be tackled using a combination of different instruments, including the amendment of current community legislation in order to better take account of new challenges. as i stressed, the issue of women in industry also reflects the general situation of industry in europe. the commission will continue to pursue all the necessary policies to face up to globalisation, ensure a future for industry in the member states and help workers of both sexes when the companies for which they work are restructured. european laws on employee information and consultation, social dialogue and the european social fund are all instruments designed to achieve this. the european globalisation adjustment fund, launched in 2007, will provide assistance of up to eur 500 million per year and its rules provide specifically for gender equality to be taken into account. the commission is, therefore, responding to all the challenges identified by the report on the role of women in industry by taking measures of various kinds: improving equality, working conditions and the role of women in industry, combating stereotypes, creating better conditions for reconciling work and family life and providing general support for companies and workers in industrial sectors in difficulty. i should like to make a personal statement: i sincerely support this way of tackling the difficulties in this specific area.

in writing. – today’s debate creates a new favourable environment to encourage a wider social debate on the role nuclear energy will play in europe in the future. nuclear generation is a proven and efficient way of producing electrical energy free of greenhouse gas emissions. i suspect that the average european citizen is probably totally unaware of this fact. the public debate focuses almost exclusively on renewables and limiting the impact of burning fossil fuels. we should be honest and admit that there is a limit to how much energy we can generate from renewable sources and still maintain competitive energy prices. renewables are important, but we cannot mislead citizens by saying that renewables alone will solve the problem. while ccs schemes will reduce greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels, the technologies are still to be implemented on an industrial scale. furthermore, they will have a substantial price tag. a responsible approach to tackling the challenge of climate change requires a balance – a mix of economically viable renewable technologies, ccs systems and modern nuclear technologies. it is our responsibility to ensure that all options are explored, none to the exclusion of others.

on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. parliamentary immunity is primarily intended to protect parliament itself as a democratically elected representative institution. it protects the collective independence of the institution from outside pressure and guarantees members freedom of speech and action in the performance of their parliamentary duties. the legal basis for the immunity of members of the european parliament is laid down in the 1965 protocol on the privileges and immunities of the european communities. article 9 of the protocol states that members may not be subject to investigation, prosecution or detention in the performance of their duties on account of their opinions or voting positions. article 10 also states that, during a sitting of parliament, members shall enjoy in the territory of their own state the immunities accorded to members of their own state and in the territory of another member state the immunities against arrest and immunity from jurisdiction. immunity shall also protect members when travelling to and from the place where parliament is sitting. in the light of the foregoing, it must be concluded that the charge against mr witold tomczak does not relate to the opinion or position he took in voting while in the performance of his duties, since he was not a member of the european parliament at the time of the incident. there is therefore no legal basis in this context for granting a member the right to exercise immunity. however, the witold tomczak case also showed the inconsistency of the electoral system for the sejm and the european parliament in poland with regard to the eligibility of polish members of parliament and their loss of their mandate. we discussed this issue at a special meeting and, by joining the european union, poland accepted the obligation to respect the law in force in the union, especially that which has direct effects on the internal legal environment of a member state, and i call on this occasion for the swift unification of legislation relating to the status of members of the sejm and the european parliament, since the same act may result in the automatic loss of the mandate of a member of the european parliament, whereas a polish member of parliament is not punished in this way for such an act.

the next item is the report by mr ignasia guardans cambó, drawn up on behalf of the committee on international trade, on the eu strategy to provide european businesses with better access to external markets (2007/2185 (ini)) (a6-0002/2008).
mr. chairman, please! mr guardansa's report covers all the areas of strengthening partnerships to facilitate access to third country markets for european exporters. this access is often restricted by protectionist practices, unfair competition and the creation of bureaucratic barriers. the most affected are small and medium-sized enterprises, which are the largest employers in europe. they have limited opportunities due to the lack of resources for research, new technologies, entry into these markets and adaptation of products and services to the target market. the report rightly emphasises the need for substantial assistance to be provided to them by the european and national administrations and diplomatic services. the european union should increase increase logistical activities and provide appropriate support to facilitate these businesses in third markets.
mr. chairman, please! we want to draw attention to three points in this debate. first, the european union must take a clear and firm position on any case where the export interests of any member state are affected by unfair practices by third countries. in this situation, the european union's position on the blockade of polish meat and vegetable products on the russian market deserves recognition. unfortunately, it was presented to russia after more than a year of restrictions on polish exports, when poland blocked the preparation of the eu-russia agreement by law. second, the opening of the union market to goods and services from third countries should be done on a reciprocal basis, with the union ensuring that third country exporters include in their manufacturing costs the costs of complying with environmental standards and social security for workers in their own countries. without these costs, european goods will be uncompetitive on world markets. thirdly, the union market should be opened very carefully to agricultural products from third countries. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's agricultural policy is not undermined by the introduction of the single market.
mr. chairman, please! open economies, open markets are the hallmarks of the modern market economy, the economy of the 21st century, the new quality in the world economy. not all economic operators are able to cope with competition, especially competition that is not always fair, competition dominated by the big and powerful. if large and small firms can import, then large firms have a better chance of exporting. because entering new markets requires a lot of investment in promoting and building the entire logistics system. it therefore seems appropriate that smes organise joint ventures to develop exports, and in particular to promote them. some aid, state support for companies in the field of export promotion, mainly in the area of know-how, should be allowed. finally, at wto level, facilitations should be created for the development of trade by small and medium-sized enterprises. the availability of information from global market participants is of particular importance. in the area of trade, a new quality should be created, first of all, equal opportunities in market access.
i'm closing the debate. the vote will take place on tuesday 19 february 2008. the competent authority shall inform the applicant of the reasons for the refusal of the application.

mr. chairman, please! the volume of trade is a measure of the level of economic development. developed economies are characterized by high exports, but usually the road is two-way, and imports should flow in the other direction. if this movement is predominantly one-way, then there is an imbalance, a lack of partnership, a deepening of the differences in development. so we need to create some kind of rules that will set the appropriate standards and quality standards that create stability and partnership in trade. we have too often seen that we talk about solidarity and equality, when in reality we are looking after our own interests, not the common interests. too often, the promotion of exports and the possibility of investment in countries is presented without considering whether they respect the principles of democracy, human rights, environmental requirements, wages and social protection. market protection instruments must take into account elements of fairness and equal opportunities.

on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the debate on the safety label has a long tradition. it is the duty of the state to protect its citizens from products that threaten their health and life. thus, certain groups of goods have become subject to certain requirements according to the relevant legislation in different countries. signs and testimonies were associated with these requirements. the relevant state services exercised oversight. in the european union, the ce marking is required for a large group of goods. the ce mark confirms that the product is safe and must be affixed to, for example, a €5 or €50 iron. so adding additional plus or minus symbols to this sign doesn't make much sense. the ce marking procedures are not particularly problematic, but the problem is the introduction of arbitrary changes in products marked by manufacturers, the arbitrary marking of products with the ce mark, the attribution to the certificates received of similar products without certification processes. this is why the european union needs better synchronisation of all the institutions that are supposed to protect consumers, such as sealing the union's borders to prevent products without certification from entering the market, an efficient information and surveillance system, and a tightened and uniform system of penalties so that it is not worthwhile to circumvent the ce system. due to the high cost of certification, small and medium-sized enterprises in the european union should be supported in obtaining these marks. the uen supports all actions aimed at protecting consumers and improving the european market.

on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. as the rapporteur rightly points out, the demographic situation depends on natural growth, life expectancy and migration flows. i would add a fourth cohesive element to this dynamic, which is human relationships and the political will that influences them. man is a particularly demanding and difficult animal, which not only reproduces when the time comes, but also must be provided with the right conditions. the 20th century, and especially the years following world war ii, did not inspire man with any particular optimism or procreative zeal. as if the world didn't seem interesting enough for people to call their children into existence. today, it is time to understand the reasons for europe's pessimistic demographic future and start to make amends. immigration, the report notes, is not a sufficient solution. first of all, the conditions must be created for europeans to grow naturally. i support virtually all the solutions proposed by the rapporteur, with two being the most important. the family must be given greater care than ever before, especially women who not only devote their time to motherhood but also take care of sick and elderly family members. this work requires a special professional status with a salary. in addition, every child must be provided with a place in a nursery and kindergarten after the mother returns to work. and finally, demography is a political problem among other things, and we are politicians, we are able to reverse the bad state of affairs.

mr president, the word ‘integration’ has been used 24 times in this report. the proposed integration of immigrants out of the national taxpayers’ pocket has not taken into consideration one important aspect, namely religion and civilisation. militant secularists of socialist origin avoid this subject, although the muslim population is shooting up. by 2025, one in three people living in western europe may, or will, be muslim. the archbishop of canterbury has recently suggested that europe should adopt sharia law, which the president and the establishment of this parliament would probably call ‘multiculturalism’. this brings a confused debate to the fore that has been developing over the ways and possibility of integrating and assimilating the new immigrants flooding into the continent. does assimilation mean that immigrants should absorb and be absorbed into european civilisation, or does it mean that they should join the descendants of old european nations to create some sort of new european man? or is the creation of a common civilisation either undesirable or impossible? although europe has always had its full share of varying cultures, it has also had a mainstream christian culture or civilisation, so to speak, in which most of its people, whatever their identities, have shared. for almost 20 centuries, this civilisation has been the central and the lasting component of the european legacy. one has to ask: would europe would be the europe it is today if, in the seventh and eighth centuries, the ashes of ancient rome had been conquered and settled not by christian societies but by muslim and any other? the simple answer is no. it would not be europe. it would be egypt or libya. fortunately, there are people who will not accept cultural rights as a cover for sharia. religion should be protected from the state – the european state, in particular. it is only christianity that can integrate other religions into a shared european project, by acknowledging what secular ideologies cannot. i believe that europe can do that and europeans should recommit themselves to christian culture and the traditions and values of liberty, equality, law and individual rights that, for over 20 centuries, have been embraced by europeans of all nations and that have been the source of prosperity and moral leadership in the world. this report can integrate nobody and nothing. it is a symbol of dead men walking. it might create a continent of zombies, unaware of their national identities.
mr. chairman, please! the report under discussion is proof of the union's impotence even in assessing the situation. we're on the demographic titanic, and no one's even ordered an orchestra yet. and we're holding these crucial debates in the evening hours, when the ratings are lowest. we have a demographic crisis in the union. while the report talks about change, the thesis of paragraph f is in clear contradiction with the thesis of paragraph 1. they talk about female infertility, but what about male infertility? they talk about infertility in couples, as if homosexual couples could be fertile. they talk about infertility, but they don't talk about the fact that the main reason for the decline in the population in europe is abortion. in the last half century, some 75 million abortions have been performed in the 27 member countries. if it weren't for this, the population of the european union would be 15% higher and we wouldn't have the crisis. we in the union talk all the time about rights, but never about obligations, including obligations towards the future. it's not like it's anything other than adult childishness. and hence the crisis: children cannot have offspring, and the elderly cannot have offspring, and without offspring, there is no future.
mr. chairman, please! when i was in primary school, 100 million europeans were under the age of 14, just like me. when i am 87 years old, there will be only 66 million children of that age in europe. one in four europeans is now over 65 and in 40 years' time, one in two will be. and remember, these are not just statistics. this alone will cause a huge increase in public spending and benefits. we have a demographic crisis in europe, including my country. a hundred years ago, one in six or one in seven people on the planet was european, and in 40 years, one in 20 people will be on our continent. what do you do? promote motherhood, create economic incentives, including tax incentives, for having children, support large families, but of course also treat infertility, for example. if we are complaining today about the immigration problem, the root of the problem is the demographic decline of the european nations.
the demographic future of europe is a long-term problem. europe is clearly aging. we are facing a shrinking working age population, a declining competitiveness of the economy and a destabilising funding of social welfare and pension systems. the great enlargement of the european union and the labour migration of people from the new member states to the old member states have alleviated this problem in western europe, but have not solved it. the ageing process in europe continues and strong action is needed, including, inter alia, the protection of human and labour rights, the promotion of family policies, health and social care, and the improvement of human resources management, including that of immigrants. these actions will only be effective if the processes of globalisation do not destroy the individual and the family and if people, not capital, are truly the supreme value.
mr. chairman, please! in taking part in this debate, i would like to draw attention to the following problems, the main causes of low birth rates in europe, namely, first, the difficulties in reconciling family and working life, i.e. the lack of childcare facilities for young children, the lack of socioeconomic support for families and the lack of employment for women. secondly, the uncertainty of young people's employment situation, the volatility of jobs, the late access of young people to employment, and the high cost of housing, which is therefore unaffordable for young people. support for families is needed through tax systems, mainly personal income tax and vat structures, the first best option being the solutions adopted in france, for example the family allowance, which allows for a significant reduction in the tax burden for families raising children. the second is the need for preferential tax rates on children's products. thirdly, it is necessary to maintain the principle of solidarity between generations in social security, i.e. the principle that the working population bears the costs of benefits, pensions and health care paid to the non-working population, i.e. children, young people, the disabled and the elderly.
in writing. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. according to demographic projections, the average age in europe will increase from 39 (as in 2004) to 49 years in 2050, which will affect the population structure and the so-called age pyramid. this will result in, among other things, a decline in the number of young people, a decline in the working-age population, and an increase in life expectancy. these changes increase the costs to society of maintaining a population inactive in employment. they also exacerbate territorial disparities, characterised by an outflow of young people, which accelerates the ageing process, or by a positive balance of migration, which slows down the process. however, immigration is only a short-term and partial solution and member states should therefore engage in actions to ensure respect for gender equality, social and financial support for families and protection of maternity. only societies that put children at the centre of their policies and create a family-friendly environment are able to counter the adverse effects of demographic change. i would like to emphasise that the increase in life expectancy is a positive phenomenon and that measures should therefore be taken to combat the poverty of pensioners, so that they can live out their final years with dignity. member states should request the establishment of affordable care facilities for dependent persons and children. the eu countries should also pay attention to the problem of infertility, which has a major impact on the process of increasing demographic imbalances and on cooperation in overcoming difficulties.

lagging countries such as greece and portugal, but at the same time acknowledge the failure of this policy to bring the level of development between regions closer together. unfortunately, member states allow excessive concentration of investment and other development elements in national capitals. and so do the regions, which also concentrate their investments in the central areas, neglecting the equitable development of the whole. the disparities within and between the regions of the european union are much greater than in the united states or japan. all of this points to the need for a mechanism to stimulate decentralisation within the member states. a sustainable but dynamic regional policy is needed for the next financial perspective. the guellec report balances the need for a skilful combination of the lisbon strategy and cohesion policy, which cannot be a tool of the former alone. cohesion policy, which aims at equitable and sustainable development, is an important objective in itself. it's the cheapest way to counter something that's incredibly expensive, because of the consequences, the conflict, the mass emigration and immigration, the relocation of vice-president of the commission. − madam president, let me begin by saying that, as everyone knows, the common european visa policy has so far brought us tangible results with several third countries, such as, very recently, canada and australia. this has not been the case, unfortunately, with the united states. since 2004, we have been working very hard to achieve the aim of having all member states in the united states’ visa waiver programme. i, together with the presidents-in-office of the council, have constantly pressed the united states administration to make the voices of all eu member states heard in washington. president barroso, as you know, has raised the issue personally with president bush, as well as with the leaders of the us congress on each of his official visits to washington. we have all argued that eu member states already meet the additional security criteria as set out in the reform legislation recently adopted by the united states. we fully understand that the lack of progress with the united states has created a lot of frustration among those not yet participating in the us visa waiver programme. our citizens have a legitimate right not to understand the reasons for such discrimination. we should not allow ourselves, however, to be divided and bullied into going beyond what has recently been agreed and accepting what should be out of the question – for example, providing others with access to schengen migration data and asylum data. all this should be out of the question. we need detailed discussion, negotiation and consideration of reciprocity. we have, after all, achieved a great deal together. most recently, we have celebrated the expansion of the schengen area to most of europe. in turn, it gives us collective responsibility for dealing with all matters relating to the security of the external borders and for ensuring the correctness of the screening and handling of data pertaining to all those who visit our common territory. i do not question the right of eu member states to engage with the united states on issues which are national prerogatives, for example cooperation between intelligence services or air marshal programmes, but we are of the view that what the us is asking from all of us in different visa-related issues raises serious legal and political questions. allow me to underline that, although the sense of urgency may be understandable, we all have to acknowledge that the signing of the memorandum of understanding does not get anyone into the visa waiver programme the next day. the united states still has to set up the electronic travel authorisation and the air exit control. it will undertake extensive on-site evaluation visits in the countries concerned. therefore, there is no need to hurry into something that is legally questionable and leaves each country to its own devices when negotiating with the united states. since all european union member states, both those seeking the waiving of visas and those already in the programme, are concerned by this and are being approached by the united states, coreper – the ambassadors of the european union member states – adopted on 5 march a common baseline: a set of common parameters that will guide the discussions the member states will have individually with the united states. it will be a good basis for our talks with us partners at the eu-us ministerial troika on 13 march 2008. in parallel, i will present tomorrow a mandate for proper eu negotiations with the united states on matters arising from visa policy. by pursuing a common approach based on common parameters, we will reinforce the possibility of reaching, in the short term, an agreement with our american partners on the mandate proposed by the commission. we need to keep in mind that the eu and the united states are close allies. this has been demonstrated on numerous occasions. fighting terrorism is a global challenge, which not only affects us all but which can also only be successfully countered if we work together. the european union is ready to do its part by keeping member states united and respectful of european common legislation and competence. in conclusion, we will be negotiating with the united states. it is simply not possible to abandon, to renounce, not only our european legislation but also our common criteria, on the basis of which we have been negotiating. we will continue to negotiate. no member state will be entitled or allowed to violate or to derogate from european legislation on this.

vice-president of the commission. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for the contributions i have heard. i believe that, since it is a fundamental right of our fellow europeans, the right to freedom of movement which we have recognised by enlarging schengen, it must be said first of all that the european commission and the european institutions must strive for an absolute, not a relative, result. all citizens of all european countries should be allowed to travel to the united states without an individual visa. that is the clear objective and i therefore understand the anxiety, the concern and even the uneasiness of some members who come from member states which have been members of the european union for many, many years, such as greece, or have been members for four years. there is one first element, however, which we must clarify, even if it is for the sake of honesty: it's not true that we haven't achieved anything! we have achieved important results by working at european level rather than at national level, as we have done recently with canada. i was in canada last year when none of the new member states were yet included in the visa waiver program with canada. today, after 12 months, they all are. we have established a system of equal treatment with australia, so that there is no discrimination between old and new between commas member states of the european union. we have not yet done so with the united states, it is true, but i would remind the honourable members who spoke of four years, that is to say the date of accession to the european union, that the united states changed its law in august 2007, less than a year ago. and it was only from that date that, for the first time, the united states said, we are available for the extension of the visa waiver program. and so we are not talking about four years, even with the united states being further behind, but we are talking about less than 12 months of negotiation on the basis of a new law. what we had negotiated earlier, on the basis of a law that has changed today, obviously can no longer be considered. i would therefore say that we must work with the united states to bring all european citizens into an individual visa-free regime, without any member state thinking that it is getting there first. i must say this with great frankness. why would you do that? because it is clear that this gives our interlocutor in the negotiations more power, in this case our american friends, who are friends and allies but who are engaged in negotiating, and from their point of view will continue to do so if they find weaknesses in the european house. we must commit ourselves not to offer these weaknesses: that's the point, and we need to be very clear. you see, when i presented to this parliament the europe-us agreement on pnr, an agreement which was criticised by some and welcomed by others, i said: the european union will be stronger than the united states of america with this european agreement. today i say to myself: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. so we have evidence that this european agreement is a difference between a weakness of the member states who have been asked for additional data - it is true, they have also been asked for access to databases which are our european databases. but thanks to that agreement, which some criticised and others supported, we will today say very clearly to our american friends that we are not going beyond that european pnr agreement. that's a sign of strength, not weakness. we already know what can be done and what cannot be done. it is set out in our rules, in european laws, in the agreements we have signed and that we have signed. and i have to say this: it is not only obvious that europe must speak with one voice when it deals with these matters, but it is also obvious that the logic of divide and rule is the most wrong logic of all from a european point of view and it is a logic which we must oppose and the institutions must of course oppose. but why are we discussing this subject in the chamber today? because despite clear laws, despite precise agreements, there has been, so to speak, the temptation to leap forward. a temptation which is politically understandable for the citizens of those countries who are anxious, but institutionally unacceptable. and that is why we had to react, to react, of course, in the spirit of solidarity with all the member states, including those aspiring to join the visa waiver program. what did we do? we have asked coreper, the ambassadors of the member states, to share a guiding document. we regard this document as a red line: it reaffirms what can be done and what cannot be done. and we have asked the member states that any political negotiations should be guided by this red line, at this key point, reaffirming for example that exchanges of information beyond those already provided for in the european agreements cannot be done, that matters such as the return of overstayers should be negotiated at european level and not at national level. things like that, frankly, wouldn't even have to be stated in a formal mandate. it was necessary to make it clear, to say once and for all that we understand the concerns of the member states that do not yet have the visa waiver programme, but we must respect those concerns even more, the rules of the european union. if we challenge them, even once, this precedent will be followed by many others, each more dangerous than the last. in conclusion, madam president, we will work this week to offer the united states a negotiating mandate proposal which will say very clearly: the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. is there room for individual negotiation? of course, in areas outside the european sphere of competence, that is clear. but for all that, and that is the vast majority, which falls within european competence, the member states will give us a unanimous mandate and i can say that the slovenian presidency is strongly determined to do so. i shall ask the commission tomorrow for a formal mandate to represent to the united states that this is our line and that we cannot make concessions or retreat from this line.

vice-president of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i too believe that the concerns expressed by many of the speakers are shared concerns, in the sense that we do not yet have a satisfactory system of personal data protection when we look at new technologies, when we look at the internet. and it is clear that the same attention we have to the proper protection of personal data during an antiterrorist investigation we should have, if not with even greater concern, when my personal data is exposed not to the attention of a magistrate but to the attention of a private industrial group. so the concerns are serious and obviously, although it is a rather new topic, mr lambrinidis' idea of a kind of world data protection charter is absolutely consistent with the global nature of the internet. you know, as i just mentioned in my introduction, that the existing rules apply with reference to the territory of establishment of a given provider, but the internet does not tolerate this territorial limitation. so i think we must work in that direction, just as i think it is important to link the aspects of competition to the aspects of consumer protection policy, including with regard to their personal data. it is a debate which we are obviously beginning, and as you know the commission is following the development of many areas of data protection which are not covered by european legislation. i am referring to the action of the council of europe, the united nations, the international conference on data protection. but there is clearly a risk that we must consider. that's a question i'm asking myself now: is there not a danger that a world data protection charter might weaken protection by having to apply to an extraordinarily large number of recipients? it is clear, then, that we should regard our european legislation as the example - if i can afford it - to be exported and not accept weaker data protection rules, just because these rules have to be applied in a very wide territorial area. in conclusion, i can inform you that just to start thinking concretely, the so-called 'article 29 committee', which all those involved in the work know, which is a committee that is responsible for coordinating actions on data protection, is working on a reasoned opinion on data protection in relation to search engines and service providers. we are dealing with this, in other words, and a questionnaire has been sent to prepare this reasoned opinion, a questionnaire on data protection policies, and this questionnaire has been sent to a very large number of managers, search engine operators and service providers. i believe that the answers that will be collected and this opinion, which i can tell you will be published in a rather short time, i hope before the summer break, will perhaps for the first time give a coordinated answer as to what the problems are and what the directions to follow.

madam president! the aviation sector needs specific regulatory provisions, but these should be as flexible as possible and at the same time ensure appropriate harmonisation, particularly in the field of flight safety. the document we are discussing today is of this nature. it is a difficult but good compromise, in my view, reached by the conciliation team, whom i thank for their work. the efforts of mr costa and commissioner barrot are particularly noteworthy. because of the shortness of time, i will address only a few points. first, the charges for aviation security should be transparent and should relate only to the costs of aviation security. secondly, the measures must not distort competition between airports and airlines, which is natural for a free market. thirdly, there is a need to standardise the rules on civil aviation safety worldwide. it is therefore good that a provision on cooperation with the international civil aviation organisation (ecao) has been added. fourthly, safety standards must also be respected by carriers from third countries, otherwise our european action will be ineffective. fifthly, we must prepare the procedures and methods for dealing with a crisis that may not have happened but which is possible in the event of a terrorist attack. finally, let us work together to ensure that the passenger, including the disabled, is the subject and not the object of the actions of all those involved in air transport, also with regard to the safety issue, which is a bit cumbersome.
vice-president of the commission. - madam president, i would like to congratulate mr albertini on his excellent report. the need to reduce the environmental and energy impacts of transport must of course be the subject of a broad consensus between parliament, the council and the commission. but at the same time, we must maintain mobility, which is the basis of our competitiveness, of our quality of life. how can this sustainable mobility be achieved? this is a huge challenge, and by 2020, we need to achieve a 20 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, a 20 percent reduction in energy consumption, and a 20 percent increase in renewable energy in our energy consumption. transport is of course expected to make a major contribution to these objectives. first of all, i will try to remind you of the many initiatives we have taken in this field: the development of the transeuropean networks, which we are putting our money into - mr albertini has just mentioned this - the development of rail, which allows a modal shift which, of course, goes in this direction. we have the ten-t project and the marco polo programme to support the motorways of the sea. with the naiades programme, we are supporting water transport. research, of course, must also enable us to develop greener and more efficient technologies. and then i will also mention the recent proposal for a directive on clean vehicles, which the committee on the environment will be starting to work on. to get a clear picture of all these measures, the commission will present an inventory of all the european initiatives. this will be a useful tool for taking stock of all the efforts made and for drawing lessons for the future. i personally hold this inventory very dear. secondly, we are moving towards a strategy of internalising external costs for all modes of transport. the package i will present in june will include a strategy on the internalisation of external costs for all modes of transport. and here we are responding to a strong request from the european parliament. this initiative responds to a need. the external costs are heavy for our economy and our environment - air pollution, noise, congestion - which is also a negative factor for transport mobility. if we want sustainable mobility, we must ensure that the external costs of transport are integrated into what users pay. by proposing in 2006 to include aviation in the european emissions trading system, we took a step towards internalising external costs in the aviation sector. i intend to accompany this strategy of internalisation with a proposal for a revision of the directive on heavy goods vehicle pricing. this revision will allow member states to include not only infrastructure costs in tolls, as is the case today, but also external environmental costs, if they so wish, which is not possible today, except in very limited cases. this revision will make it possible to internalise external costs in another sector, rail. community legislation provides that the internalisation of external costs in rail can only take place if other modes also internalise their external costs. in short, we are moving towards smart tolls, educational tolls, which will make it possible to punish more those lorries which have the worst environmental standards or which use the main routes during periods of congestion and congestion. i would add that we will be taking a number of initiatives during the second half of the year. i will be making a statement on measures to reduce noise in the railway sector. and then, on the roads, gains can be made in terms of reducing congestion through the intelligent transport system. we will aim at interoperability, the one-box. this will facilitate the organisation of logistical clauses at european level. the report by mr albertini also calls for the creation of a genuine single european sky. you're right, mr. albertini, this is the way. in fact, as has been said before, we really must make progress in the cesar project, which must play a vital role in ensuring the technological development necessary for this purpose. initiatives to reduce nitrogen oxide emissions from the aviation sector and noise around airports are planned. we are also working on measures in the maritime sector. urban transport, of course, must also be part of this effort: 40% of co2 emissions and 70% of other pollutant emissions come from vehicles in urban environments. in the european parliament, i am very grateful to mr rack for his work on this subject, and i hope that we will succeed in presenting a toolbox this autumn that cities can use. these are just a few examples of a major project which is, it must be said, one of the main priorities of my mandate: making transport greener, greening of transport, while ensuring transport accessible to all european citizens. mr albertini, you are right, your report is coming in on time. there is a great madam president! mr albertini's report takes account of all the decisive elements of a sustainable transport policy, taking into account environmental protection and energy policy. transport consumes over 30% of energy, and this consumption is expected to increase by 30% in 20 years. the sector consumes 70% of oil and in cities and urban agglomerations generates 40% of co2 and 70% of emissions of other harmful compounds. the rapporteur supports technological innovation and other measures to save energy. the european union needs to act swiftly and efficiently. the most environmentally and economically beneficial energy in the face of the sharp rise in oil prices is electricity, which should play a greater role in transport, including urban transport, for example by building cheap electric city cars. the increase in demand for this energy should be met by the latest generation of nuclear power plants with no harmful emissions.

mr. chairman, please! i want to focus on two issues in this debate. firstly, the percentage of agricultural expenditure in total budget expenditure is falling steadily and will be only 32% in the last year of this financial perspective. these measures represent on average around 30% of the income of farmers in the union. it is essential to maintain this level of support in the future to maintain interest in agricultural activities and, above all, to ensure food security in europe. it should be recalled that many developed countries in the world, through various instruments, support agricultural incomes by more than 50%. these include countries like japan, south korea, norway, and switzerland. secondly, far more rapid alignment of support to farmers in the old and new member states is needed. according to the experts' calculations, the average level of support per hectare of agricultural land in the new member states between 2007 and 2013 will be only 62-64% of what farmers in the old member states receive. without these two basic requirements, it will be difficult to think of developing european agriculture.
mr. chairman, please! the current review of the union's agricultural policy aims to improve it, taking into account the experience gained since the last reform in 2003 and the situation on the world market. however, it should be borne in mind that the changes made must not undermine, firstly, the community nature of this policy we oppose its nationalisation secondly, the european model of agriculture. it is not justified that direct payments should be based on historical production levels and should be so differentiated. the future subsidy model after 2013 should be based on simple principles similar to saps. but we must also allow market intervention in emergency situations, or even subsidies for production, as in the case of tobacco or milk production in mountain areas.
mr. chairman, please! the common agricultural policy and the structural policies supporting it are facing increasingly serious challenges. the general shape of the common agricultural policy for 2007-2013, which was adopted by the european union's agriculture ministers in luxembourg on 26 june 2003, adopts solutions, some of which are beneficial for poland. some of them, however, are more protective of the interests of the old members of the european union. i share the rapporteur's view that the commission should prepare a detailed report on issues such as the additional costs incurred by farmers for complying with community standards on environmental protection, animal welfare and food safety. in response to the report presented to us, i agree that it is necessary to continue the current process of reform and further development of rural areas. the common agricultural policy must evolve to meet new challenges such as climate change, growing energy demand, a growing world population and increased openness to global markets.

on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i congratulate the rapporteur on the important subject of improving the situation of women in rural areas in the european union. we have recently been discussing the demographic future of europe. we've identified a number of factors that may be responsible for her pessimistic outlook. the problem is even more acute in the countryside. all efforts must be made to ensure that rural people, especially women, have the right conditions for living and for economic and personal development. it is likely that social exclusion and poverty are more common among women in rural areas, probably because we need better statistics here. perhaps the key to improving the situation in this respect is that the spouses of self-employed persons, in this case rural women, should have their own independent social and pension rights.

mr. chairman, please! in recent years, there has been much talk and discussion about the role of women, their rights, their social and professional status. today we're debating the plight of the rural woman. and rightly so, because it is rural women, especially in the less developed regions, who work the hardest and enjoy the least of their rights. women in the city have a comfortable home, easy access to technology, education and culture, the right to maternity and parental leave, the opportunity to work and enjoy the benefits of civilization. a rural woman often has a house without plumbing, numerous responsibilities in the family and on the farm. she cannot count on a place for her child in nursery and kindergarten, and her contact with the world and culture often comes down to limited radio and television broadcasting. a woman from a small colonial village living on a family farm is virtually denied any chance of advancement in her career, social, political or cultural life. please note that cultural funding is mainly directed to urban centres. we have almost everything there. in the countryside, there is only amateur activity, and it is often done in one's own home and at one's own expense. in the european union, there is a lot of talk about lifelong learning, and rightly so. but let's make sure there's a woman in these programs. i believe it is high time for a meaningful programme for women, funded from the union budget.
mr. chairman, please! the situation of women in rural areas is markedly different from that of women in urban areas. it's not just about access to health care and education. i would like to draw attention to paragraphs 4 and 10 of the report, which stress the need to ensure equal social and economic rights for women who are selfemployed or employed on family farms. in particular, the right to paid maternity leave and to a pension derived from earnings. in some countries there are even legal prohibitions on formal employment and social security for members of family farms and family businesses. the effects of these provisions are primarily directed at women and should be changed as soon as possible. i congratulate the rapporteur.
mr. chairman, please! in rural areas, women are a particularly vulnerable group. because of the traditional division of roles, the poor infrastructure in many areas, such as childcare, many women never appear in the official labour market and therefore are not even registered as unemployed. women perform work comparable to a profession, but not recognised as such, not protected or paid. member states, together with the european commission, should address as soon as possible the problem of the large number of women working in family farms or small and medium-sized enterprises, which in many member states do not have a fixed legal status. this leads to financial and legal problems for these women in terms of their right to maternity leave, medical leave, pension rights and access to the social security system. for the purpose of harmonious development, member states should ensure the creation of high-quality jobs in rural areas by, inter alia, promoting entrepreneurship among women, upskilling them and ensuring easy access to standard 21st century infrastructure and services in all rural areas. finally, i would like to congratulate mrs klaß on a very well-prepared report.
