the next item is the statements by the council and the commission on the european code of conduct on arms exports.
the chairman of the council. − first of all, on behalf of the council, i would like to express my great satisfaction with the traditionally good relationship and cooperation between the council's coarm working group responsible for conventional arms export controls and the european parliament, more specifically with its sede subcommittee on security and defence. i am confident that this will go well and that excellent cooperation in this area will continue in the future. and that is why i welcome today's debate. allow me to say a few words about the eu code on the export of arms and military equipment. as is well known, the code was adopted in 1998 and at that time it gave the european union a new impetus in the field of the control of arms trade. in accordance with this code, the union has started to prepare annual reports, which are in fact reports on the transfers of arms that have been carried out. we will start this year with the preparation of the tenth annual report. it is also worth noting that these reports have become increasingly informative and transparent over the years. in recent years, the code has led most member states of the european union to publicly publish their annual national reports on arms and military equipment exports. in 2003, the european union also defined its own list of arms and military equipment covered by the code and began to coordinate export policies to individual third countries more seriously. member states shall also exchange information on refused and realised arms exports in accordance with the code. this dynamic has also been transferred to international organisations, especially those in which the member states of the european union play a major role, particularly the wassen arrangement. in 2006 and 2007, the code was further improved, in particular by further updating the user manual. as is well known, the code is not a legally binding document, but member states are politically bound to comply with its provisions. in the past, attempts have been made to build upon the code with a common position, which would be a legally binding document to be followed by member states in relation to arms exports, but there is no consensus on the adoption of such a common position. the slovenian presidency is striving to achieve this during our presidency, i.e. in the first half of this year, or at least to make a significant move in this direction. there is probably no better opportunity for such a move than the preparation of the 10th eu implementation report on the code, but at the moment we really cannot predict whether this will be our wish. this does not, of course, deter us from our determination to try, and we will therefore invite all the member states to communicate their views on this matter and try to encourage them to come together to reach a common position, and if there are no reservations, the slovenian presidency will of course be very happy to complete the adoption process and report back to all the institutions concerned, first and foremost to this parliament. let me say a few words, very briefly, on the other two priority issues: the common position on the mediation of arms and military equipment and the efforts of the member states to adopt an international binding treaty on arms trade. as regards arms brokering, the european union adopted guidelines as early as 2001, followed by a common position in 2003. by adopting this position, member states undertook to transpose its elements into their national legislation and thereby to regulate the field of brokering in the trade in arms and military equipment. at present, the vast majority of member states, 20 in particular, have already incorporated elements of this common position in their national legislation, and seven have yet to complete this process. the presidency will monitor progress in this area and encourage those countries which have not yet completed these procedures to do so as soon as possible. the last point: the international arms trade treaty. this is one of the key projects in the field of disarmament. as you know, the council of the european union recently adopted a decision in support of this international treaty. the general assembly last year also approved the indicative composition of the government expert group to work in this area. the information on the start of the work of this group is encouraging, but much work and effort will still need to be put into this process. we will follow closely the work of this group and support the process leading to an international treaty in the context of our activities.
member of the commission. − mr president, i took a little more time on iraq but i shall be a bit briefer now, so i will try to make good on my time. even if the responsibility for controlling and monitoring the sale of arms rests primarily with member states and thus with the council, the commission also has a clear interest through its contribution to the implementation of the eu small arms and light weapons strategy under the common foreign and security policy. we greatly value the effective control and monitoring of eu arms exports. we remain concerned that european controls should encourage other regions to adopt and apply – at the very least – minimum standards, in order to ensure that legitimate exports are not subsequently diverted, thereby exacerbating armed conflicts and human rights violations. in this connection, the commission continues to engage actively with member states, third countries, international organisations and others in order to deal with the financing of illicit arms trafficking, often linked with illicit trade in other commodities (particularly drugs), for example diamonds. we in the commission took advantage of our chairmanship of the kimberley process last year to push for the development of controls to prevent and deter the use of diamonds to fund arms purchases by rebel groups. further, in close collaboration with the relevant customs authorities, we intend to take forward measures under the new instrument for stability to combat illegal trafficking in arms by air, targeting particularly aircraft travelling to and within africa. we also play a role in the implementation of arms embargoes by prohibiting related technical assistance. within the european union, control of firearms trafficking is crucial in the fight against insecurity and criminality, especially against organised crime. the policy being developed to combat firearms trafficking involves the reinforcement of controls on the legal sale and holding of firearms within the union. this goes on to encompass the proper monitoring of the movement of firearms within the union and the development of cooperation between national administrations in charge. besides these efforts, we can see that a significant quantity of firearms is also in the possession of criminals and available on the black market. the unauthorised transfer of firearms across borders, and the transfer of unmarked firearms, are therefore important sources of these illegal weapons. steps are currently being taken at european level to enhance rules on record keeping and marking, to develop an export/import system for firearms for civilian use, and to improve cooperation between national law enforcement administrations. improving the traceability of firearms is a key objective, and externally – very briefly – we are also taking concrete steps outside the union to handle the problems arising from explosive remnants of war and small arms in crisis regions, again under the stability instruments. for instance, in bosnia we are currently considering supporting a project to deal with unexploded ordnance and other explosive remnants. certainly we will continue to support member states’ efforts to establish a treaty covering the arms trade, as our council president has said, although we might not be under the illusion that this will not take a certain time. but hopefully it will happen very soon.
on behalf of the ppe-de group. – mr president, for nearly 10 years the european council has dragged its feet on transforming the eu code of conduct on arms transfer into a legally binding document. for the last two years there have been no technical barriers to adopting a common position on the code. why do we finally have to get our house in order? firstly, there are currently estimated to be some 400 companies in our member states producing arms. given that research and development costs in this industry are extremely high, companies naturally wish to maximise their profits by ensuring the longest possible production runs, selling licensing agreements and, in short, seeking markets wherever they can. companies from the 20 nations whose governments imposed strict guidelines on arms exports are clearly at an economic disadvantage vis-à-vis competitors whose governments show more leniency. all companies should have a level playing field. secondly, we have documented instances of companies from eu states supplying arms to china, colombia, ethiopia and eritrea. how can we on the one hand applaud all efforts to promote economic development, democracy and human rights while we make the very implementation of this impossible by contributing to violent conflicts? thirdly, we deploy military personnel from our member states on eu and nato peacekeeping missions but, by failing to apply this code of conduct, we risk that they may come under fire from weapons produced within our very states as a result of irresponsible transfer. fourthly, how can we envisage a future europe with a common foreign and security policy when we lack such a fundamental element in the form of a common position? finally, before we stand up in this chamber championing human rights and democracy, let us ensure that we also take action that gives substance to our rhetoric. the ppe-de group congratulates the authors of this motion for a resolution. we trust that the overwhelming support from parliament will help the council in finding a way out of the current political impasse and finally make adherence to the code of conduct a legal requirement for all member states.
the chairman of the council. − i note that there is a thread running through the speeches of the honourable members in this debate which is in favour of making the code legally binding as soon as possible. and let me say that the presidency shares this ambition, and i hope, mr pflüger, that this year we will have more luck and succeed in that intention or at least, as i said in my opening speech, make significant progress in that direction. i would like to thank you for the support you have given to the council reaching a common position, and you can be sure that the slovenian presidency will accordingly step up its efforts in this direction. i would also like to thank the honourable member, mrs gomes, for pointing out that the code is also being implemented with the aim of involving new actors beyond the borders of the european union. the previous presidencies, for example in 2007, already included in these activities mainly the countries of the western balkans, but activities are also under way with regard to other countries and their possible inclusion or participation in the code, countries such as turkey, ukraine and the countries of north africa and other countries in eastern europe. i hope that the next time the european parliament deals with this subject, we will no longer be talking about the code but about the common position. that's my hope.

member of the commission. − mr president, i am very pleased and happy to replace my fellow commissioner, ms viviane reding, in introducing such a very important and very good subject. the ageing of the population throughout europe obviously poses significant challenges to our society and economy. today, for every retired person there are still five people who pay taxes. by 2025 this will drop to three-to-one, and by 2050 to only two-to-one. the cost of care, especially care for the growing group of people over the age of 80, is rising rapidly. we are rightly concerned about ensuring a good quality of life as well as the financial sustainability of health and social care for the elderly. at the same time, i stress that an ageing population is also a great opportunity and a promising market for new products and new services for healthy ageing and independent living. we are all convinced that we can and should mobilise information and communication technologies for ageing well in europe. the ‘ambient assisted living’ joint programme will help to tackle these challenges and exploit the opportunities. it is also an innovative cooperation of member states in market-oriented research and development that merits european support. the compromise amendments that you suggested have certainly helped to strengthen the european dimension of the initiative by clarifying the scope as well as the roles and commitments of the member states. this will be helpful in ensuring the success of this important european endeavour for the benefit of us all.
draft opinion of the committee on women's rights and gender equality. - mr president! - what are you doing? the ageing of europe's population is a challenge for the whole european community. life expectancy is now 80 years and the number of people of retirement age is expected to increase by as much as 40% by 2030. the european union should take a comprehensive approach to this challenge, as demographic trends affect a number of policy areas, including employment, housing, education, social assistance and health care. the overall objective of this research and development programme is to enhance the quality of life of older people and to strengthen the industrial base in europe through the application of information and communication technologies that will help older people to improve their quality of life, maintain good health and be active in work and in the community. the experience and skills of older people are a great asset, especially in a knowledge-based society. it is also worth noting that in an ageing society, the proportion of women is higher than that of men, due to their longer life expectancy. therefore, it is necessary to target and evaluate the programme in terms of gender. finally, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs gill, on a very well-written report.

member of the commission. − mr president, i very much appreciate the support of the committee on economic and monetary affairs to the commission proposal and in particular the efforts of the detrimental to the environment. i should stress that, during the council discussions, a large number of member states have underlined the positive effect of the commission proposal on the environment, on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the commission's proposal to raise the minimum rates of excise duty on motor fuels aims to reduce excessive fuel consumption in transport and thus reduce environmental pollution. the commission also hopes that its proposal will reduce the differences in excise duty rates between member states, thus contributing to a level playing field in the single market. these goals are generally sound and deserve support. however, the commission proposal also contains solutions which may have negative consequences for the economies of the member states. these include: additional fuel price increases and rising inflation, rising costs and weakening competitiveness of european businesses, and suggests that the main burden of adjusting to the new rates will fall on the less developed member states of the union, which raises serious doubts. the amendments proposed in mr schmidt's report are therefore designed to reduce these negative effects, without undermining the main objectives of the commission's proposal. as part of the compromise reached between the main political groups, we propose three main changes to the commission's original draft. first, we propose to reduce the target minimum rate of excise duty on fuel from eur 380 per 1000 litres to eur 359 per 1000 litres. applying the highest rates of excise duty on fuel not to raise them until 2015, in order to facilitate the process of convergence of rates. mr president, commissioner, i would like to stress that on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the president of the european union and the commissioners begin their speeches by declaring their support for economic freedom, free competition and small and medium-sized enterprises. but when we move from declarations to deeds, they take the form of reports similar to those we are debating. the report proposes to impose uniform fuel tax rates on all member states, to standardize prices, all under the pretext that it would be simpler, easier, fairer. in the background we have the thesis, accepted a priori, that the best solution for the countries of the european union is a single tax system, a single monetary system, a system of certification and marketing authorizations, a system of regulations and production limits, etc. the proposal assumes that there are no differences in the cost of obtaining fuels in the union, for example due to distance from sources of supply or labour costs. and none of this is true. so i ask, what is economic freedom, free competition in the european union? shouldn't we be talking about economic violence and coercion instead of economic freedom? is not a single fuel price eliminating all competition the ideal solution for multinational fuel companies to the detriment of consumers, small businesses? does the uniform price of fuel not favour the highly developed countries over the backward ones? finally, by adopting the report, and by standardizing fuel prices under the pretext of freeing the companies and the state, is the union not actually imposing new taxation chains on them, or worse still, is it at the same time taking their shoes off and driving them into poverty? we'll vote against it.
mr. chairman, please! i want to draw attention to three things. first, the price of crude oil seems to have been consistently above $100 a barrel, causing fuel prices to rise steadily. it is only because of the weakness of the us dollar that fuel prices in europe are not rising sharply. and it's not always going to be that the united states wants its currency to be weak. in this situation, the proposal to increase the amount of excise duty in the coming years in the european union seems to be a complete disregard for economic realities. secondly, the new member states, because of their lower gdp per capita and consequently lower personal income than in the old member states, can only equalize the tax burden once personal income levels have been equalised. finally, thirdly, member states should have more freedom to reduce the tax burden on non-european fuels in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity. such solutions would encourage the use of renewable fuels. this would reduce co2 emissions and meet environmental commitments.
mr. chairman, please! it seems that the single market, the free movement of goods and services, is full competition. but this is not entirely the case, because the cost of production, the competitiveness of goods, is significantly affected by the prices of the means of production, including fuel prices. it is true that even in neighbouring member states we now have different taxes on fuel, which gives rise to so-called fuel tourism in border areas. but the scale of this phenomenon is not very large. it seems right that the excise duty should be approximated, but the process of maturation should be slow, spread over many stages. the alignment of the minimum excise duty rates for diesel and unleaded petrol should also be spread over time. the general principle here is that we should try to keep taxes and excise duties on fuel at a lower level, so as not to increase production costs and inflation and increase household expenditure, especially in the new member states where wages are much lower.

member of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs budreikaitė, on this excellent report, which presents a precise analysis of the challenge of development policy for the new member states. your report reminded me of the debates and concerns that have been stirring public opinion and the european political world on the eve of enlargement, with doubts and fears expressed on both sides that enlargement would dilute solidarity with the developing world and would make africa fall out of the european union's priority list. actually, it's not that. what was foretold and the predicted troubles have not proved to be justified. never has european development policy been more ambitious in its objectives, never has it been more unifying in its approach and never has africa been more high on the union's foreign policy agenda. your report confirms that this was possible, not despite, but thanks to the commitment and political will of the new member states to assume their responsibilities fully. let us first consider the question of funding. of course, the new member states still have a long way to go before they reach the targets set for 2010. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. since joining the european union, these countries have doubled or even tripled their aid. in 2007, the aid from these countries reached almost 800 million euros. in addition, these countries have committed to allocating 0.33% of their gdp to official development assistance by 2015. the second is the effectiveness of aid. last year, the european union adopted a code of conduct setting out a number of principles for a better division of labour within the european union. i am very pleased to see that the new member states are doing very well in implementing these principles. the twelve member states all apply the principle of concentrating aid on a limited number of countries, which is obviously a principle that has long been defended in terms of efficiency by best practice. many of these new member states share the implementation of their assistance with other member states through co-financing, thus reducing the burden on the partner country administrations. i am thinking of the support - but of course not limited to it - that slovakia is giving jointly with austria to infrastructure in kenya or to the water aid that the czech republic is giving jointly with luxembourg. these are very moving examples. another example is that the majority of the new member states support developing countries on the basis of their sectoral added value, which is derived from their experience of political and economic transition. i am thinking in particular of assistance in the areas of governance, capacity building of public administrations and economic reforms. these steps, as agreed in the code of conduct on the division of labour, are fundamental to me. in april i will present a first assessment of the implementation of the code, one year after its adoption, with analyses and proposals for increased support and coherence. on this basis, i want to have a serious debate with all the member states on how to proceed. with the accra conference on aid effectiveness only a few months away, the developing world is looking to europe to lead the way and rightly so, because europe - i think it should be said again - is by far the world's leading donor and has the potential and the duty to lead by example. your report highlights another fundamental point, that of raising public awareness in the new member states. it is true that in most of these countries there is not much tradition in development aid, particularly aid to africa. it is therefore also our responsibility to continue to convince public opinion and to show them that this is not just about charity, but also about mutual interest. i think about peace and security, migration, climate change, food security. with this in mind, the european commission launched the third capacity building programme for the new member states in mid-february. through this programme, the commission will provide the expertise needed to develop communication strategies to enable administrations to better report on their activities to the general public, to raise public awareness, especially among the media and students, of development policy issues. ladies and gentlemen, there is no longer the old europe or the new europe. there's no first class, no second class. there are no longer any old or new member states. there is only one europe, a europe of solidarity, openness and political union, which also carries universal values. the development policy evolution since the last enlargement is proof that the european union can expand and deepen at the same time. this is, in fact, an extraordinary lesson in history for the future of development policy and european integration.

member of the commission. − mr president, first and foremost, i wish to express my gratitude to the european parliament, and particularly to the rapporteur, mr gierek, for the interest and support shown regarding the research fund for coal and steel. let me also thank the chairwoman of the committee on industry, research and energy, ms niebler, and the shadow rapporteurs, ms laperrouze and mr březina, for their constructive help. i understand that the request for a debate was made by a number of members of the itre committee. i am therefore more than happy to summarise what is at stake. in 2002, a protocol annexed to the treaty of nice created the research fund for coal and steel, a smart financial design using the interest accrued from the assets made available at the expiry of the european coal and steel treaty. activities under that treaty were funded through a levy paid by the coal and steel industries, 27.2% and 72.8% of the budget being respectively allocated to coal and steel. through a bottom-up approach, this research fund is intended exclusively to fund research projects in the sectors related to the coal and steel industries, two major traditional sectors where research is still needed: firstly, to comply with current eu policies on environmental standards to combat global climate change and, secondly, to maintain energy security of supply by having a fuel mix that meets european demand. the essential principles and proper decision-making procedures related to the management of this fund are defined in the multiannual technical guidelines for the research programme of the research fund for coal and steel. these technical guidelines are to be reviewed or supplemented every five years, the first period ending on 31 december 2007. on 10 july 2007, the commission adopted a proposal for a council decision on the revision of these technical guidelines. this proposed revision looked to further the positive results achieved during the first five years of the research fund for coal and steel research programme, notably in terms of environmental protection. in the commission’s view, no major overhaul was needed, but rather a fine tuning of the existing rules in order to adapt the guidelines to eu enlargement, to the seventh framework programme and to current european regulations, notably in terms of gender balance and financial management policies. this proposal for a council decision was sent to the european parliament for consultation, and this is the reason why we are here today. i would like to express my appreciation of the fact that mr gierek’s report by and large supports the commission’s proposal.
the rapporteur. - mr president! - what are you doing? the commission's decision on the continued operation of the research fund for coal and steel is welcomed. this fund was set up as a bank contribution of 72,8% for the steel industry and of 27,2% for the coal industry after the expiry of the treaty establishing the european coal and steel community. the interest on this fund amounts to some eur 60 million per year, which allows for additional funding for research not covered by the 7th framework programme. this is the research necessary to rationalise both the operation of the iron and coal industry and the research leading to further improvement in the quality of the final products in this sector, namely steel and coal. the need for such research activities is very much relevant to these industries in the new countries of the european union. steel. steel is still the most important structural material today. the technological possibilities for improving the quality of various steel grades and increasing the efficiency of steel production are still far from exhausted, especially in the area of new technologies for the production of intermediate products for further processing. the increase in the reliability of steel structures and the operational efficiency of various machines and equipment requires numerous empirical studies in this field. this is both to further improve the chemical composition and the performance of the various steel grades. efficient and environmentally friendly recovery of scrap, such as steel from the troublesome galvanised automotive scrap, is also of great importance. coal, coal is energy security. the competitiveness of this solid fuel, the definition of which is proposed in this regulation to be extended to include, for practical reasons, bituminous shale also known as oil shale, extracted in estonia, depends on the efficient use of its regional resources. specific mining problems are highly dependent on local geological conditions and require routine exploration. they should precede the construction and operation of e.g. deep-sea methane-coal mines. coal mining also includes unconventional underground gasification technologies. the continued proper functioning of the research fund for coal and steel requires that each advisory group be composed of experts who guarantee an optimal representation of the european union coal and steel industry in terms of location, with particular regard to experts from the new countries of the european union.

the rapporteur. - mr president! - what are you doing? i can only take one view of the matter raised here, namely that the mines should be closed as soon as possible for ecological reasons. i think that energy security in my country, for example, in the czech republic and in many other countries of the union contradicts this view and this view is not generally accepted. on the contrary, given the emerging new technologies, such as clean coal and ccs, we will probably build new mines in the future. coal will remain an important and competitive source of energy in europe for a long time to come. we must also not forget - and here i am addressing those who would like to close all the mines - that coal is not only an important energy resource but also a chemical resource. so, first of all, the research fund for coal and steel is needed. secondly, the fund does not overlap with the seventh framework programme, i.e. it is a completely different area of action. thirdly, an increase in eligible costs from 40% to 50% is appropriate. fourthly, the exclusion of bituminous shale from the programme of the research fund for coal and steel, as proposed by the greens in this amendment, would be detrimental to estonia, whose energy sector is based mainly on this fuel.
in writing. in poland, 95% of electricity comes from coal-fired power plants. poland is therefore particularly interested in new coal technologies that will increase the efficiency of power plants, reduce co2 emissions and enable the conversion of coal into hydrocarbon fuels with reduced co2 emissions. new technologies open up the possibility of using nuclear reactors as emission-free heat sources to achieve the above-mentioned objectives of the coal industry. however, high-temperature reactors (htrs) are needed to achieve a coal-nuclear synergy. in europe, research into high-temperature reactors has been going on for several years. the commission considers that the aid is compatible with the internal market if it is granted in accordance with the rules on state aid. such a centre will strengthen europe's technological capacity, including its coal industry. it can also make a significant contribution to the acceptance of nuclear energy in europe by working directly with the coal industry, seeking to modernise it rather than competing with it. given the importance of coal in the polish energy sector, it seems reasonable that such a european hub should be established in poland. without decisive action, we will lose the technological race in this area with the us, south africa, china and south korea. i urge the commission to take into account the need for such a centre in the multiannual technical guidelines for the research fund for coal and steel research programme.

the rapporteur. - madam president! - what are you doing? with the adoption, the discussion today and the vote tomorrow on the 2009 guidelines, we are taking the first step in a budgetary procedure which, for at least two reasons, is different from the routine of previous years. the first reason is that we are testing a new form of cooperation between parliament's administration and the budget committee we are treating this as a pilot project, but it should be in line with the rules generally applicable to the budgetary procedure after the entry into force of the lisbon treaty. secondly, 2009 brings new challenges that no one is disputing. the likely entry into force of the lisbon treaty, thus the substantial strengthening of the european parliament's codecision powers, paving the way for parliament's activity as a genuine legislative body, is certainly such a challenge. secondly, it is an election year, so it has the costs of the election campaign and some costs - apart from the savings, of course - of the end of the current term of the european parliament. thirdly, the statute for members of the european parliament comes into force, which increases the burden of personnel costs, the burden of our costs on the budget of the european parliament. in many of these cases we already have some quantification, some calculation, because in parallel with the rules we are getting the first forecasts, the first preliminary budget for 2009. however, the most important aspect, the increase in the european parliament's powers following the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, is the work of the working group which will determine the additional costs that may be involved. while recognising the particular challenges ahead in 2009, we cannot at the same time exempt ourselves from the burden of managing european taxpayers' money sparingly, i.e. from certain self-restraints that we will also expect from other european institutions. the increase in the administrative budget in an election year is certainly not the message that the european electorate is waiting for, when we ask them to renew the mandate of the european parliament. the core of the guidelines is also an internal commitment to look for opportunities in the so-called redeployment of existing human resources, not in the augmentation of the staff pool, and to focus on those functions that will shape the future of the european parliament, which we call correctivity, and which are related to legislation. we must also talk today, and we should talk about an issue which has some media significance and which of course also has extra-budgetary dimensions. well, we need three new regulations in parallel. the first is the statute for members of the european parliament, which should be implemented and which has a clear budgetary dimension, the second is the new rules for the pension fund and the third is the rules for the recruitment of assistants, which should be sufficiently transparent to avoid member of the commission. - the mr president, i thank you for the opportunity to refer to the commission's work in progress on the development of the framework we need for adaptation to climate change in europe - but also in the rest of the world - particularly in the very poor countries, which, while not having contributed to the greenhouse effect, will nevertheless be the ones to suffer the most adverse consequences. following the green paper on adaptation to climate change, adopted in june 2007, the commission is preparing, as mr sacconi said, the white paper to be published in autumn 2008. the main objective of the white paper is to provide the european union with an ambitious and effective strategy to limit the effects of unavoidable climate change. a change that has already happened and will happen in the coming years, regardless of the measures to limit carbon dioxide emissions that i hope we will take and for which i hope we will have an agreement in copenhagen in 2009. the european union also has a leading role and will continue to play it in international initiatives on adaptation - initiatives developed under the united nations international treaty. the commission has meanwhile continued its cooperation with the intergovernmental panel on climate change and other scientific bodies active in research in relevant fields in order to find the most appropriate ways for the international community to address the challenges identified in recent reports. the commission welcomes the european parliament's resolution on the green paper and i can tell you that it supports most of it. i will mention in particular the need to derive maximum benefits from the synergy between efforts to reduce emissions and adaptation, the need to strengthen research and further scientific information collection, the protection of ecosystems, the analysis and evaluation of current and future funding mechanisms. the need to strengthen the link between research and policies and to integrate, where necessary, the adaptation parameters into the internal and external policies of the european union, while ensuring the full involvement of all national administrations and civil society in tackling the problem. in drawing up the white paper on adaptation, the commission will of course make full use of the input of the stakeholders in the dialogue, as well as the views of the european parliament, and i thank you for your support to date of the european commission's efforts.

the commission's vice-president - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for asking me these questions in connection with the european visa regime with regard to ukraine and belarus. firstly, ukraine, the agreement on readmission and the agreement on the facilitation of the issuance of visas, which have entered into force since the beginning of this year, represent an important milestone in the relations between the european union and ukraine. on the one hand, they will promote contacts between peoples, which will improve mutual understanding and strengthen relations in all areas, and on the other hand, they will engage both parties, the european union and ukraine, in close cooperation against illegal immigration. the first priority is to ensure a rapid, operational and harmonised implementation of the agreement, aimed at facilitating the issuance of visas for ukrainian citizens. in order to ensure the correct and harmonised application of this agreement, draft guidelines have been drawn up and approved by the member states and the ukrainian authorities. these guidelines should be finalised and adopted in the short term by the joint committee established by the agreement. as stated in the preamble to the agreement between the european commission and ukraine on the facilitation of the issuance of visas, the introduction of visa-free travel for the citizens of ukraine is recognised only as a long-term perspective. the process leading to such a regime is based in particular on the satisfactory implementation of the agreement on readmission and the agreement on the facilitation of the issuance of visas. i would like to stress that the enlargement of the schengen area has had no impact on the control arrangements applied at the borders between ukraine and the member states which joined the schengen area on 21 december 2007. these member states have applied the schengen rules on external border checks at their borders since the date of their accession and since september 2007 they have also been carrying out checks on persons in the framework of the schengen information system 'sis'. but to facilitate the movement of ukrainian citizens living in the border area, agreements on small border traffic have been signed between hungary and ukraine, and between ukraine and poland. the commission has also requested changes to the agreement between ukraine and hungary in relation to the delimitation of the border area so that the agreement is fully in line with community rules; the same was true of the agreement between ukraine and poland. so, here's to those movements of ukrainian citizens who live in the border area. however, the situation is different when it comes to visas. before 21 december 2007, member states which did not fully apply the schengen acquis were not bound by the schengen provisions on visa rights. these member states could therefore exempt all ukrainian citizens from this right. but today, that's not possible. the general visa fee of eur 60 does not apply to ukrainian applicants. as confirmed by the agreement between the european community and ukraine of 1 january 2008, the fee for processing visa applications of ukrainian citizens is still eur 35. in addition, the agreement exempts broad categories of ukrainian visa applicants, which suggests that more than 50%, i repeat, more than 50% of ukrainian nationals travelling to schengen countries today benefit from visa-free travel. i now turn to belarus. in its communication on the strengthening of the european neighbourhood policy of 4 december 2006, the commission underlined the importance of visa facilitation for relations with the countries concerned by the european neighbourhood policy. the commission reaffirmed the eu's willingness to commit to developing action plans with neighbouring countries and to enter into negotiations with them to facilitate the issuance of visas and readmission authorisations. belarus is one of the countries covered by the neighbourhood policy but it must be said that no action plan has yet been developed with this country because of the general political situation. this is why the opening of discussions with belarus on possible visa facilitation and readmission is not envisaged at this stage. however, i would point out that the acquis in force on the issue of short-term visas provides for exemption from visa duties for certain categories: children under the age of 6, students, researchers. in addition, member states may still, within the framework of existing rules, exempt from or reduce visa fees in individual justified cases, for example on humanitarian grounds, to protect cultural interests or in foreign policy matters. in addition, neighbouring member states, notably poland, latvia and lithuania, can still negotiate agreements on small crossborder traffic with belarus. this would be a means of facilitating border crossing and movement of border residents between belarus and neighbouring countries, by promoting contacts between local communities. border residents holding a special permit for small border traffic would be exempted from the visa requirement. negotiations between poland and belarus in this regard have already begun. that is what i wanted to indicate by pointing out the timeliness of the questions you have asked and by giving you the latest information on this problem.

mr. chairman, please! transplantation suffers from a shortage of available organs. the demand is high, and therefore the money involved is high. and where there's a lot of money, there's abuse. as a result, we have a whole new class of crimes. we know of examples of poor donors buying organs and giving kidneys for transplantation for a few pennies. we hear about organ harvesting from death row inmates without asking their consent. we hear about potential donors being kidnapped and killed to get their organs. there have been cases of death being hastened to harvest organs. that's the phenomenon i want to look at. since the advent of transplantation, the definition of death has changed. there's a brain-dead criterion that was originally defined in 1968 in boston, known as the harvard criterion. since then, many other criteria for brain death have been developed, each one less restrictive. the irreversibility of brain function is not an observation, but a prediction. to test it, you disconnect the life support, and that disconnect could be the cause of death. in some cases, anesthesiologists are used to harvest organs from supposedly dead bodies so that the donor's body will not be harmed. what we need is to tighten, not liberalize, the death penalty. taking one life to save another is unacceptable.

member of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, the sharp rise in food prices since the beginning of the year has raised global awareness of the global food challenge. in a few hours a meeting of the main actors in the field of food aid is to begin in london. an international conference on the green revolution in africa will be held in early may. all political actors, operators and specialists in the sector are now involved. for several years now, the world has been facing a steady increase in food prices. since 2000, the dollar price of wheat has tripled, that of rice and maize has doubled, and the beginning of 2008 corresponds to a further increase of 20%, which is reflected in our industrialized countries by concerns about purchasing power and is obviously reflected in developing countries by the risk of famine for entire populations. when you live on less than a dollar a day and spend most of your income on food, such increases are obviously simply unbearable. this is the root cause of the hunger riots that have occurred in recent weeks around the world in haiti, mexico, egypt, morocco, cameroon, senegal, côte d'ivoire, guinea, mauritania, ethiopia, uzbekistan, yemen, the philippines, thailand, indonesia, and more. all analyses indicate that the era of cheap food on the international market is over. food prices will not return to their previous levels and their volatility may increase if action is not taken quickly. the current context of soaring food prices poses a serious threat of political, financial, economic and social destabilisation for many states around the world, and therefore a swift response is necessary. and this goes far beyond the mere capabilities of the european commission, or even the european union. the whole international community must be mobilized. our analysis of the possible solutions leads us to identify two main ways. firstly, the first way, to save lives and respond to the social crises created by the soaring prices and sometimes amplified by tense national political contexts, and then the other way, which is obviously in the medium and long term. i would stress the need for action on both fronts. the biggest mistake, of course, would be to give a structural problem, food security, a humanitarian response in the form of food aid. this would undoubtedly alleviate the guilty conscience of some in the short term, but it is clear that urgent food aid is not enough to solve a short-term problem. in the short term, therefore, it is obviously necessary, in addition to national responses to better control food prices, to meet the food needs of the most vulnerable populations in genuine humanitarian distress. that is why we must mobilise additional emergency humanitarian aid to increase echo's response capacity to provide urgent food aid. but we are not dealing with a classic food crisis. it is a crisis of purchasing power which affects above all the poorest who can no longer afford to buy food. our response must therefore also be based on other forms of food assistance, for example to counter the negative effects of child malnutrition and to support the purchasing power of the most vulnerable households. the rapid growth of local agricultural supply should also be encouraged, allowing farmers access to agricultural inputs, seeds and fertilisers. given the scale of the crisis and its likely persistence, it is absolutely crucial that the european union also commits to a medium-term approach to supporting social protection policies that are being implemented or to be implemented in the most exposed countries, in particular on the african continent. in the medium and long term, the only answer is to do everything possible to ensure that agricultural supplies are adequate. production must increase globally to keep pace with world demand, but this must not be the case only in the major exporting countries. the european union has already taken concrete steps in this direction. the milk quota was increased and customs duties on cereals were abolished. the african continent must play its part with our support and bring about a genuine green revolution that would enable it to reduce its overall dependence on the international market. african agriculture is currently the least productive in the world, but it has enormous potential for development, provided that policies in favour of small family farmers are implemented over time and that priority is given to investment, productivity growth and facilitation of access for farmers to national and regional markets. the commission, for its part, is already giving this approach a high priority. we were the first to emphasize the importance of agriculture in development policies, well ahead of other international actors. we have revised our own programmes in line with those of the african union, proposing to align european assistance in the field of agriculture and rural development with the african union's detailed programme for agricultural development in africa in a communication of june 2007. when the 10th european development fund was being programmed, we made sure that the rural development sector as a whole could benefit from a doubling of the amounts - 650 million euros from the 9th edf, 1,250 billion euros from the 10th edf - but it was not that simple, because you must know, and you know it, that it is up to the developing partners themselves to choose the areas of concentration. that's a big increase, a doubling in absolute numbers, but if you translate that into a percentage, it's not a percentage increase in the share of agriculture and rural development. there is a doubling of the money supply but the percentage in relation to the european development fund remains more or less the same. in this context, we are therefore pleased to note today the renewed general interest of the donor community in the agricultural sector, which has been largely neglected for the last 25 years. the commission as a whole, and i in particular, as the commissioner responsible for development and humanitarian aid, are well aware of the major political significance of the present crisis. i had the opportunity to talk to the un secretary-general about this at the last meeting of the africa mdg steering group in new york last month. i also spoke to the chairman of the african union commission, mr ping. it was in the wake of this meeting that i used the term 'humanitarian tsunami' because i felt it was necessary to create a shock of conscience so that political leaders would finally go beyond speeches and professions of faith. the causes of the crisis are many and complex, although care must be taken not to get lost in too many subtleties. there's a rise in demand, particularly in asia, because of the improvement in the living standards of many people who can afford to eat more and better. there is also the increase in oil prices which directly affects the cost of transport and fertilisers. add to this the supply-side problems caused by the consequences of climate change and we have, in part, the recipe for the current crisis. what is the commission doing? she's working on the long-term, i told you, it's crucial. but the results won't translate into the field for 24 months. increasing agricultural production is not just about opening the tap more, so we're also focusing on the short term and the urgency. last march, it was already decided to mobilise eur 160 million in food aid; it has just been decided to release an additional €57 million, which was budgeted for 2008 but will be made available much earlier in the year. 60 million will be raised in fresh money, either from a redeployment within heading 4 or from a request to you to mobilise the emergency reserve. finally, i would like to point out that the commission will continue to monitor this situation very closely and is prepared, on the basis of changing needs, to consider additional emissions if necessary.
the chairman of the council. - first of all, i want to apologize to all of you, ladies and gentlemen, for being late. i was in a meeting with the conference of committee chairs and i thank you for arranging the debate so that i can now take the floor. the european union is following with great concern the rise in agricultural prices that we are facing not only in the european union but also elsewhere in the world. we are aware of the seriousness and scale of the potential consequences, particularly for the poorest countries in the world. where are the reasons? on the supply side, price increases are mainly due to crop failures, including the effects of climate change, and to reductions in stocks, especially cereals, and to increases in production costs. on the other hand, demand is being strengthened by the growth of the world population and also by the rapid development of some large countries such as china, india and brazil. in these countries, increased purchasing power and higher standards are changing dietary habits. increased demand for meat and dairy products has an indirect impact on the increase in feed grain prices. some, or many, also cite the growing market for biofuels and the associated demand for agricultural products for non-food purposes. this is why, in the council of the european union, we are working within the framework of the working groups set up specifically for this purpose to develop clear sustainability criteria that will allow the sustainable production of biofuels with the least possible impact on factors such as food prices. as the reasons for higher food prices, on both the demand and supply sides, are structural, we can expect that prices and their growth, including in the long term, will remain at higher levels than we have been accustomed to over the past decade. at the global level, the rise in food prices has a particularly negative impact on countries where agricultural products or food represent a significant share of imports. this issue is particularly acute in countries with lower and medium gross domestic product and less competitive structures in food production and trade. to ensure a basic food supply, agricultural production in poorer countries should be encouraged, among other things. wealthy countries should also be encouraged to devote financial resources to development aid to the poorest countries and to become more active in humanitarian organisations. the european union is trying to control food prices in a number of ways. recent reforms of the cap have been aimed at making european agriculture more sustainable and market-oriented. the european union has already adopted the abolition of the compulsory dust requirements for 2008, thus increasing the processing area for food production in the european union. the review of the common agricultural policy also proposed the permanent repeal of this obligation and the abolition of the premiums for energy crops. efforts to promote research to enable the production of second-generation biofuels are also important. these would use as raw materials by-products such as straw, shavings, waste in general. in addition, the european union is prepared to eliminate export incentives by 2013 in the context of the wto negotiations. the question of the instability of agricultural markets is certainly becoming one of the central challenges for agriculture and agricultural policy in the european union. the council of agriculture and fisheries of the european union had already discussed the issue of high prices at its april meeting, given the scale of the potential consequences. it is very likely that it will be discussed at future meetings of the council, and that the issue will be taken up by ministers in other council configurations. international organizations such as the food and agriculture organization (fao), the international fund for agricultural development, the world food programme, and other agencies are also actively working to keep food prices down. the slovenian presidency will participate in the international conference on food security and the challenges of climate change and bioenergy, which will take place in rome in early june under the auspices of the fao. in conclusion, the increase in food prices is a global problem and must be tackled with great deliberation and with intensive action in all the areas affected. our objective is to restore price stability to the markets. (applause) i would like to thank you.
mr. chairman, please! until recently, the european union's main concern was overproduction of food, and our debates were mainly about how to produce less. the decoupling of subsidies from production, the elimination of export premiums, the maintenance of production quotas, all served to limit the potential of european agriculture. reality has verified that policy. the first signs of a food crisis have appeared sooner than expected. food is getting more expensive, we have less and less of our own, and imports are getting more and more expensive and less and less secure. this is largely the result of a policy that has been designed to encourage farmers to produce less. we need to radically change our policy approach to agriculture. we must recognise it as one of the pillars of european security. food security, alongside physical security and energy security, is a fundamental pillar of security, important both for nations and states and for each individual. let's stop playing with agriculture. let us see them as a pillar of our security and, in turn, support them to ensure that europe has food security and that food is available to all.

mr. chairman, please! the posting of workers directive is one of the foundations on which the practical implementation of one of the four fundamental freedoms of the community, the european freedom, which has accompanied the treaties and the european community from the beginning, is based. article 49 of the treaty is one of the most explicit provisions governing the internal affairs of the european union and provides unequivocally that restrictions on the freedom to provide services within the community are prohibited in respect of nationals of member states who have their establishment in a community state other than the state of the recipient of the service. it is therefore surprising that persistent practices in many member states are aimed at administratively restricting this freedom guaranteed by the treaty. since my election to this parliament, i have received complaints from businessmen, mainly from the new member states that joined the union after 2004, about the activities of regional and local administrations which arbitrarily impose on these businessmen additional requirements that are not justified in any of the union's legal acts. i have raised this issue many times in this chamber, calling on the european commission to take a clear stand on the side of eu law and thus on the side of freedom to provide services. i am pleased that my efforts have been so clearly confirmed by the case law of the european court of justice, which we are discussing today. i am convinced that, in the light of the recent judgments of the court, we will succeed - parliament together with the european commission - in developing a formula for the organisation of the internal market in services which, while safeguarding the fundamental rights of workers, will not impose on eu entrepreneurs additional burdens which will restrict their activities and which are, by definition, contrary to european law. the free market in services and the mobility of workers must be promoted, not opposed. these are the challenges of the 21st century.
mr president, commissioner, i have to ask you to stop this. the aim of the posting of workers directive is to ensure freedom to provide services while safeguarding workers' rights. i think that this directive has served the european union well and the criticism i hear here today is largely unjustified. i would point out that in the rüffert case under discussion, the breach of social standards and the setting of a wage at the scandalously low level of 46% was not the result of any shortcomings in the posting of workers directive, but rather of the failure to implement part of the relevant legislation in lower saxony in the manner provided for by the posting of workers directive. so we are dealing with the problem of the implementation of the law in germany, not with the shortcomings of the directive on the posting of workers. the same applies to laval, whereas in sweden we have a situation where the minimum wage is not fixed either by law or by collective agreement in the way that the directive on the posting of workers provides. i therefore believe that the solution to this situation is first and foremost to bring national legislation into line with the current directive, although i agree that there are many areas where the directive can still be improved and i support the commission's position on these issues. i would also like to refer to the concept of social dumping, which has been mentioned many times here. well, i would point out that the concept of social dumping does not exist in either international law or economic theory. it's a purely propaganda term. there is no dumping when posted workers polish in germany or latvian in sweden receive higher wages than in their home country. nor can we speak of social dumping when there are no social and wage standards in europe for all countries, and this is because the level of development of our member states is different, and in addition there are different policies in individual countries.

the chairman of the council. − i would like to briefly inform you about the progress of the visa waiver and esta interviews. first of all, i would like to say that the issue of visa policy is of the utmost importance to the european community and that since the accession of new member states to the european union, both the commission and all the presidencies have made a great effort to ensure that all countries and all citizens have the same conditions for entering the united states of america and that of course everyone is on the visa waiver programme. the abolition of visas would, of course, mean equality for all citizens of the european union. the united states has begun this year with certain procedures, agreements, and opened the door to entry into the visa waiver program. the only bilateral talks that have taken place have been those concerning certain misunderstandings, certain in-depth discussions which we clarified as the presidency together with the commission earlier this year and agreed at a number of meetings on a bilateral system of cooperation in this area. such a system was also confirmed at the eu/usa troika meeting in slovenia on 12 march. the dual system means that the commission is given a mandate to negotiate and agree with the united states on matters of community concern, while at the same time the states can hold bilateral talks on matters within the competence of the member states. at the last home affairs council on 18 april, the council also voted on the mandate for the commission, so that the commission can now start such talks. we want transparency in this two-way cooperation. some member states have already started initial talks at bilateral level on what these agreements would be, but they are not yet in writing and we expect transparency from both the member states and the commission so that we can work at this level. if i may touch on electronic travel authorization, i must say that we have had several conversations in this regard. we are conducting so-called exploratory talks with the commission and the us side. so far, from the information we have so far, it appears that the united states will not require any other information from passengers than what passengers already voluntarily fill in on flights to the united states on the so-called form one to ninety-four, which is white or green for those on the visa system. this is extremely important. in the current discussions, it was also agreed that these checks would be free of charge and that once authorisation has been granted, they would last for two years. in fact, once that system is in place, citizens will send the same data to the united states authorities via the internet and will, of course, then treat it in the same way that the united states treats this data now. there is another area, of course, on which something specifically needs to be said, namely the talks with the united states of america, linked to the high level group on personal data protection. so far, we've managed to talk about 12 principles and we've found that they're the same. there's one principle that's still open. we hope that by the end of june we will be able to reach a point where we can see that it would be possible to continue the talks and give a different mandate to this group, which would begin by preparing the talks for the possible conclusion of a framework agreement with the united states of america in this area. why do we want this framework agreement? firstly, we want to follow the european parliament's resolution of last december, which specifically stated that it would be good to accept such an agreement, and we naturally believe that the possibility of negotiating and agreeing on such an umbrella agreement is only possible in principle and after the adoption of the lisbon treaty, that is, together with parliament, together with the council and together with the commission. only consensus among all three bodies will enable us to achieve common principles and common operating principles. at the same time, of course, once we have such an umbrella agreement, we will still specifically opt for any exchange of data, on a case-by-case basis. it will not be possible for this agreement to cover all subsequent ones. the current situation is such that with every agreement, every arrangement, these principles are reopened and renegotiated again and again. if we had such common principles to base ourselves on, concrete agreements and arrangements would, of course, be in a much better position. mr. president, that's all for now.

on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. preserving biodiversity is a challenge for the modern world, not just for its beauty, but also for the balance of nature and the well-being of humans. for years, we have seen the problem of chemical pollution and other negative effects of civilization, such as environmental degradation, climate change, pollution, deforestation, and habitat destruction. the greenhouse effect has become a hot topic recently. unfortunately, the problem of biological contamination by genetically modified organisms is being underestimated, and we are part of it. we forget that chemical contamination is time-degrading, whereas biological contamination is often irreversible. so we have to make a very clear decision: are we for biodiversity or are we for gmos? are we concerned about people and their environment or about the interests of monsanto and other companies like it that make huge profits from gmos? to save biodiversity, we also need to ensure that the most threatened species in the wild are fully identified, so that conservation objectives can be set and future extinction of species can be prevented. let us remember that it is easy to destroy, but it is often impossible to rebuild.
mr. chairman, please! meeting the growing demand for agricultural products and raw materials produced for non-food purposes leads to an intensification of agricultural production. in particular, this intensification is due to the production of biofuels and biomass. we know that intensive agriculture reduces biodiversity. the question arises: how can biodiversity conservation be reconciled with intensive infrastructure and economic development? modern biodiversity management requires increased monitoring of existing processes and appropriate investment in scientific research. if we are to benefit from economic growth, we must use part of the profits to finance the maintenance of biodiversity, and finally we must be aware that preserving and protecting the environment requires action at both local and global levels, on the part of each of us individually and across the economy. this is a task for all of us.

member of the commission. − madam president, the commission recognises the risk that feed imports may become more difficult and more expensive, due to asynchronous approvals of gmos in exporting countries and in the eu. i am aware of the agriculture and rural development dg study on the issue of feed shortage. i must stress that the effects of a zero tolerance policy for unauthorised gmos on feed imports only become an issue in the event of so-called asynchronous gmo approvals. one of the key factors is the difference in the duration of the gmo approval procedure in third countries and in the eu, in combination with the lack of appropriate segregation mechanisms in exporting countries and the marketing strategies of the seed industry in these countries. the increased use of gmos by your main trading partners in commodities also has an important influence. against this background, the commission is focusing its efforts on addressing these key factors. discussions with the european food safety authority have been initiated with the aim of making efficiency gains in the duration of the authorisation procedure, without compromising on the quality of the efsa scientific assessment. i would like to remind you of the importance in this respect of the cooperation of member states in the standing committee and in the council. last but not least, i would like to note that the commission recently adopted the authorisation of ga 21 maize, which will facilitate imports with the advantageous presence of this gm event from argentina. the commission is also currently in the process of sending to the council a proposal for the authorisation of a gm soya bean, after the standing committee failed to reach a qualified majority. this soya bean authorisation will also enable a number of feed imports and thus contribute to the temporary improvement of the feed shortage problem that the honourable member raises. the eu legislative framework on gm food and feed aims primarily at ensuring the safety of the products placed on the market. this is why gm food and feed products are subject to pre-market approval. the zero tolerance approach for unauthorised gmos currently applied by the eu has been laid down in eu legislation, having been approved by the european parliament and the council as the best way to protect human and animal health and the environment. it is similar to the approach followed by the vast majority of third countries, including major gmo producers. at international level, the commission, in close collaboration with the member states, continues to support the development of codex guidelines on the issue. the commission, however, recognises the possibility of incidents of the type indicated among the reasons behind your question and recognises that such occurrences are becoming easier to detect because of constant improvements in measurement techniques. the commission will examine whether it is appropriate and feasible to come up with an individual solution for this specific problem, in full respect of existing legislation. in the case of the wto complaint brought against the european community in 2003, the corresponding panel report, concluded in 2006, did not call into question the eu legislation, but rather the way it has been implemented in the past. the commission has managed to contain this dispute until now in the context of a regular dialogue on biotech issues with the complainants. we clearly showed the complainants that there is currently no moratorium or undue delay in the ec approval system of biotech products. sixteen products have been approved since the establishment of the wto panel, with only seven in 2007. we cannot rule out that complainants, notably the united states, will take into consideration the trade implications of the issue of advantageous presence in their decision on whether to proceed with further dispute settlement. however, the european community would be in a good position to defend its case, and the present dialogue makes this eventuality unlikely.
on behalf of the uen group. - madam president! - i have to go. there are three areas where gmos can be dangerous. the first area is public health. there are more and more signals about the possible harm of gmos to human health, but these signals are being ignored. hard evidence of gmos' harmfulness could come up at any time. there was a time when there was no evidence that asbestos was harmful, and when it was found, it cost billions to remove. the problem with gmos is that once they're spread, you can't get rid of them. the second area is the environment. many scientists warn that the environmental consequences of gmos could be catastrophic. for this reason, among other things, a huge shelter for traditional seeds has been set up on the ice of the norwegian island of spitsbergen in case they are destroyed by the expansion of gmos. the third risk is economic. the expansion of gmos is a way to make farmers economically dependent on the big biotech companies. farmers will grow gm crops under conditions dictated by powerful corporations with patented seeds. europe is not starving today. food is getting more expensive, but the union's agricultural policy continues to be based on administrative restrictions on agricultural production. europe does not need to look for super-intensive food production technologies. europe should focus on healthy food produced using traditional methods. there is, of course, the problem of competition. i agree with mr stevenson and the other speakers on this point. the ban on gmo crops and the ban on gmo feed should not unilaterally harm our farmers. it should be equivalent to a ban on the import of products containing gmos, both plant and animal. there should be a clear principle the same requirements for producers exporting their products to the european market as for our own producers.
