vice-president of the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. the european union and the united states together account for 60% of world gdp and 40% of world trade. transatlantic trade services and audit flows amount to $3 billion a day. the transatlantic economic relationship creates jobs for 14 million people. that's the scale we're talking about here today. in april 2007, the european union and the united states signed a framework agreement to deepen transatlantic economic integration between the united states of america and the european union. this agreement is based on the recognition that the european union and the united states are not only each other's most important economic partners, but also that we share common interests, common challenges and a wide range of shared values, such as a commitment to free trade and openness to investment, a commitment to free and undistorted competition, respect for property rights, including intellectual property rights, and effective protection of consumers, workers and the environment. the transatlantic agreement is a confirmation of our shared commitment to intensifying economic cooperation and accelerating the removal of transatlantic trade and investment barriers. to make this cooperation work, we have created the transatlantic economic council. the aim of his work is to remove barriers to a truly transatlantic market. but at the same time we are dealing with common challenges in our relations with other countries. the transatlantic economic council has already proved to be a valuable forum for strategic dialogue on our respective approaches to china and to sovereign wealth funds. the safety of imported products and the enforcement of intellectual property rights in third countries are also concrete examples of practical cooperation on specific issues. the biggest obstacle to trade between our advanced economies is the disparity in rules and regulatory approaches. the so-called tariff barriers have been virtually eliminated in eight major rounds of world trade over the last 60 years. non-tariff barriers, such as regulations and administrative procedures which unnecessarily restrict trade, are now the main obstacle. these barriers are often less visible and more complex, and they can be very politically sensitive, as they are very often the result of deliberate domestic policy decisions. the good news for us is that the united states, which in the past has always been very skeptical of regulations that it did not make itself, is now becoming increasingly open to international cooperation, especially with us, on regulatory issues. the decision by the us securities and exchange commission to accept the international accounting standard ifrs was a historic step forward. as the european chairman of the transatlantic economic council, i have already learned an important lesson. transatlantic cooperation is not possible without political leadership. it is one thing to agree that a market without barriers to trade is desirable. but once you start to look at the obstacles in concrete terms, you realise that economic integration requires a lot of hard work, patience, perseverance and political leadership. the same experience we had when it came to the creation of the european single market. i would remind you that our european project for a single market was preceded by 30 years of economic and political integration. changing existing rules and procedures is not always popular. there are always groups that use the status quo to keep their privileges. some group in their own country always feels threatened. if we give in to this pressure and lose sight of the benefits for the european economy as a whole, we will end up isolating ourselves and sticking our heads in the sand. i would also like to point out today that economic integration and the reduction of the regulatory burden are not only hampered by existing rules, but that new legislative initiatives can also undermine the desired objective. an example of this is the us congress act which requires that all cargo leaving our ports for the us be 100% screened beforehand. this is something which will of course be discussed in the context of the transatlantic economic council. we have the next meeting of this transatlantic economic council next tuesday here in brussels. it will be the first meeting on european soil. the american side is coming with a large number of government members. we have a broad agenda that will show progress in many areas. as at the first meeting in washington, we will continue our strategic dialogue. the subjects for discussion are the integration of russia into the world economy, how we are to react to the growing dangers of protectionism and, above all, what consequences we must draw together from the crisis on the financial markets. so you see, it's a very broad spectrum. the whole process involves the parliamentary parties on both sides. i am very grateful to the european parliament for the strong interest it is showing in this process. i am very grateful to the european parliament for the close contacts it has with the congress and i must tell you that you have a very important role to play here as parliamentarians, because much of what we want and can agree on politically must ultimately be formalised by legislation. we need the approval of the congress on the american side and your approval on the european side. this is why the legislative dialogues are part of the whole project. in conclusion, let me point out that the new approach is very different from all previous efforts, which have all failed to a greater or lesser extent, and both sides are convinced that this on behalf of the alde group. i would like to take a moment to reflect on the relationship between human rights and democracy. well, it is widely believed that only in a democracy can these rights be fully respected. democracy, on the other hand, is identified with majority rule, which is exercised through the electoral system. that was greek democracy, the majority decided everything. but in this system, by majority vote, socrates was sentenced to death. the will of the majority does not always have to be the guarantor of civil liberties. and so in the 19th century, there was a fear in political thought, which is not well understood today, of extending the right to vote to a wider group of people, which is associated with the assumption that only an enlightened minority is capable of respecting freedom and human rights. today, we often see elections, even fairly honest ones, that lead to or sustain dictatorial rule. just think of countries like belarus and the hamas government in gaza. it is also worth recalling the famous response of egyptian president mubarak, who, in response to the call for a fair election, said that the result would include radical, fundamentalist muslim groups in the government of egypt. so, of course, elections are incredibly important, and they need to be monitored for that. but who knows, in many countries, the rule of law and a truly independent judiciary may be more important than elections today. otherwise, we could have a democracy that is nothing more than a dictatorship based on electoral mandate. a dictatorship in which there are no independent institutions to create a complex system of checks and balances and safeguards for the citizen against the arbitrariness of the authorities. because democracy must be liberal democracy, not dictatorship by the majority. so we should continue to observe elections, but we cannot limit ourselves to this in the fight to build a true liberal democracy. therefore, more attention should be paid to building a democratic culture and civil society institutions. such actions cannot be supported by autocratic authorities. we must therefore develop better and more flexible aid mechanisms than those in place today, and extend our support to help these brave people who are facing numerous reprisals for their work.

mr. chairman, please! deep-sea fishing, because of the specific nature of the resources and the marine ecosystem, creates a unique microclimate, a micro-world that reveals very clearly both the well-known advantages of fisheries policy and its still visible imperfections. ms. ramos's fascinating report and the discussion it has generated is a significant lesson in insight, another reason to remain humble in the face of the mysteries of the deep. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's fishing fleet is able to compete with the other fleets in the world. listening to the dynamic parliamentary debates, one cannot help feeling that many research centres still use schematic, stereotyped methodological bases. there are three depth zones: up to 400 meters, between 400 and 1,000 meters and above 1,000 meters. there are even advocates of formal, rigid fishing criteria, such as the mythical significance of depths of over 1 000 metres without any convincing justification. i am in favour of continuing to look for more efficient methods of measuring the state of the resources, adapted to the ecosystem of the particular aquarium. the results of such comprehensive surveys, rather than mere estimates, should form the basis for the catch limits for deep-sea fisheries. not just for this fishing. it is precisely the increasingly sophisticated methods of research that can guarantee a more precise system of information exchange and control of this important and delicate fishery.
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i am pleased to be speaking on behalf of the former prime minister of finland and to be debating the report of the present minister of foreign affairs of finland, until recently our colleague, mr alexander stubb. the fate of the european parliament's rapporteurs is, so to speak, uncharted territory. the latest ngo report shows that lobbyists have become a real problem when it comes to influencing the european commission's decision-making process. for example, by filling a significant number of expert posts in the various bodies around the european commission. the five thousand lobbyists who make up the european parliament, out of the fifteen thousand in brussels, must operate according to very clear rules. the proposal to establish a joint register of lobbyists of the european parliament and the european commission is a good one. the sword of sanctions is also good. finally, our voters have a right to know, they should know who the lobbyist is, who is funding him and what lobbyists have tried to influence what reports in various ways. this report is a step in the right direction, a step towards regulating a certain reality that already exists.
mr. chairman, please! lobbying within the eu institutions is a complex issue. on the one hand, access to the institutions' activities is the result of the principle of transparency enshrined in the founding treaties and fills the gap associated with the so-called democratic deficit, since expert organisations provide valuable expertise that has a positive impact on the quality of european legislation. however, on the other hand, lobbying influence on the work of the institutions may allow large multinational corporations to pursue their own interests primarily through specialised firms. the problem of lobbying in parliament is becoming more important as the powers of our institution increase, and the commission's initiative to establish interinstitutional cooperation to define a framework for lobbyists, including the establishment of a common register of lobbyists, should therefore be welcomed. the principle of transparency, which allows lobbyists to gain insight into the work of the institutions, should also apply to them. registration should be a mandatory, not a voluntary, condition for lobbyists to gain access to the eu institutions.
in writing. – the pluralism of interests is an important feature of democracy. it is therefore legitimate that members of society organise and lobby for their interests. however, lobbying does lead to the risk that democratic principles may be corrupted. the power of corporations to influence politicians can lead to unequal access to law- and decision-making processes vis-à-vis the ordinary citizen. very few european countries have regulated lobbying. this parliamentary report on lobbying will be a valuable step in strengthening transparency, accountability and citizens’ participation in the democratic process at the european level. however experience in countries that have implemented lobbying legislation shows that this should only be one part of a broader range of guidelines and measures. from non-transparent lobbying it is only a short step to corruption and the distortion of the market to the detriment of those companies who play by the rules. the involvement of industry representatives in preparing this report is welcome. they should now be urged to take up the initiative and show that responsible corporations have a vital role to play in the process of regulating lobbying.
in writing. i would like to extend my warmest congratulations and appreciation not only to the rapporteur, but also to commissioner kallasa, who has taken the initiative of new regulations on lobbying. this is particularly important in the light of the new powers of the european parliament in the light of the adoption of the treaty of lisbon. however, i have doubts about the effectiveness and fairness of the voluntary registration system for lobbyists. it should be common and binding on all the european institutions. however, the nature of parliament should preserve its autonomy. the mandatory registration should cover the full spectrum of lobbying entities, including regional representations, trade organisations, lawyers acting as lobbyists, research centres. all those who exercise influence for economic or social benefit should be registered. the requirement to provide only financial information is not always reliable and does not allow for a full assessment under the regulation.
in writing. the lobbying regulation is welcome, as it finally provides a chance for parliament to work transparently with interest groups (lobbyists). the idea expressed in the directive of making it compulsory for parliament and the commission to establish a register of all lobbyists interested in representing and defending their interests before the eu institutions should be supported. enrollment in the register will allow interested lobbyists not only access to the ep premises, but also to attend committee meetings and to have contact with members, but without disturbing their work in the offices. however, the effectiveness of civilized - and therefore transparent - lobbying depends to a large extent on the behaviour of lobbyists, and it will therefore be necessary to develop a parallel code of ethical conduct for lobbyists. parliament should also monitor the implementation of this directive, in particular by checking the accuracy of the information contained in the register. a lobbyist who provides insufficient or false information should be subject to proportionate and dissuasive sanctions, ranging from suspension of registration to deletion from the register. the new legislative proposal, which is also drawn up on the european parliament's own initiative, will be of great informative value to the other european institutions and to the national parliaments of those eu member states which have not yet adopted legislation on the subject.

shipping and ports, shipyards are sectors that have been somewhat neglected, but which have considerable growth potential. an appropriate concept for the development of competitive and safe maritime transport, ports and related sectors, guaranteeing a high level of maritime safety, is necessary. sea transport is a much more energy-efficient means of transport than road transport. so let's give the shipyards a chance to develop, including those in gdynia, gdansk and szczecin. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive. europe has been linked to the sea since the beginning of its existence. it can't be otherwise, since our coastline is 70,000 kilometers long, which is three times the length of the coastline of africa. for years, the sea has provided our ancestors with a source of wealth and income. today, it is similar. only an integrated, coordinated approach, with appropriate actions, will allow us to realise the potential of the sea.
, in writing. access to the sea is not shared by all eu member states, but there is a widespread understanding of the importance of exploiting the sea. it is estimated that the marine industry, maritime services and activities located in coastal areas contribute 40% to the cumulative gdp of the community of 27 countries. this is why we are waiting for the next practical steps to be taken to implement the eu's integrated maritime policy, following the european commission's green paper. we note the efforts to make better use of the potential of cabotage and thus to reduce the burden on land routes, in which, unfortunately, my country has little involvement. but it seems to me that economic issues are being pushed into the background by environmental and climate priorities. this is a trend that is characteristic of the whole of eu policies. but it's hard to reconcile the two. the growing dispute over conservation periods in the baltic is just one illustration of the tension between the economic interests of fisheries and the concerns of conservation of natural resources. from the polish perspective, a country with a lot of work to do, finding a balance between economy and ecology is essential. the report is particularly welcome in connection with the first european maritime day. it would be more important, however, to turn the common maritime policy into a financial and legislative instrument, rather than a mere ceremony.
mr. chairman, please! there is a great deal of controversy surrounding the production and consumption of tobacco. we must be aware that the fact that tobacco is grown in the union does not really affect the level of consumption of tobacco products by our citizens. if we reduce or stop tobacco production in europe, it doesn't mean that the number of cigarettes smoked will decrease. imported tobacco will be used. i fully support the development of public awareness campaigns on the harmful effects of smoking, which should be funded by cigarette and tobacco manufacturers.
mr. chairman, please! employment is the key to our growth. however, it is difficult not to note certain shortcomings in the area of social and territorial cohesion. in the union, which is seen as a prosperous area, nearly 80 million people, or 16% of all citizens, still live in or are at risk of poverty. many jobs are of low quality, there are no facilities for young people to be employed, or for many experienced workers to be extended, and there are no jobs for disabled people. it should be borne in mind that it is the regions whose development is lagging behind that are facing the greatest problems. high unemployment, low participation of the elderly, disabled, high proportion of people unemployed for more than 12 months, women's more difficult situation in the labour market than men's are just some of the problems they have to face. in poland, this situation is found in the regions of the so-called eastern wall. the czech republic's situation is commendable, as it has made reducing barriers to the movement of workers one of its priorities for the forthcoming presidency.
mr. chairman, please! respect for human rights is a fundamental task of the european community. unfortunately, the european union is not doing very well. the situation in this area will not change after just two hours of debate. nor do they offer any hope of improvement in the work of the european commission and other authorities. europe and the rest of the world continue to face discrimination on the basis of race, gender, culture and nationality. the trafficking of people, including children, for money, for pleasure, for organs, is increasing every year. violence is on the rise, and victims are increasingly choosing to remain silent because they do not trust the state to help. i have the impression that we in the european parliament work mainly for the benefit of businesses, corporations, regions, and not enough for ordinary people, for whom the most important things are existence and equality of rights. our actions don't produce the desired results, but only appease the conscience that we are doing something. it's time for a radical change. that is why i voted against the report.
mr. chairman, please! i voted for this report for a number of reasons. first, one of the fundamental challenges facing europe is climate change. this also directly concerns marine areas, especially coastal regions threatened by rising sea levels. secondly, the significant exploitation of marine resources, especially through overfishing, as well as climate change, pose a serious threat to the marine environment today. the relationship between the oceans and the climate is seen as an important part of the eu's climate policy. third, nearly 80% of marine pollution comes from land. environmental hazards, such as wrecks and remnants of munitions and chemical weapons on the seabed, are also important. fourth, intensive fishing has led to a disruption of the ecosystem and contributes to the loss of biodiversity. fifth, oceans and seas also play a significant role in europe's energy security strategy. on the one hand, they are a source of oil and gas, and also a source of renewable energy. on the other hand, they are a means and a means of transporting energy and thereby increase energy security. so we need to create a sustainable policy for the seas and oceans.
in writing. − employment growth in the european union is directly related to vocational training and the mutual recognition of qualifications. i supported mr andersson's report because i believe that eu member states should create a common model for the verification of professional qualifications, regardless of where they were acquired. this will encourage staff to continuously improve their skills and students to learn, gain new experiences and improve their foreign languages in different parts of europe. as the representative of lesser poland, the third largest region in poland in terms of the number of students, i would also like to draw attention to the particular importance of the recognition of diplomas for young people. all academic exchanges, opportunities to compare qualifications are extremely important for young people wishing to gain experience abroad.
in writing. - one of the four principles underpinning the european union's common market is the free movement of persons. the free movement of persons gives eu citizens the opportunity to take up employment in another member state. however, different education systems and regulations on vocational qualifications often make it difficult to take up employment in the occupations in which we are qualified. this is why it is so important to be able to compare professional qualifications between different member states. the european commission and the rapporteur consider that decision 85/368/eec, which regulates this issue, has not sufficiently contributed to the comparability of professional qualifications to the benefit of workers seeking employment in another member state. this is why it was decided to replace it with a newer and more effective instrument, in particular the european qualifications framework, which increases transparency, promotes the transfer of qualifications and facilitates the assessment of learning outcomes. i am pleased that this step has received broad support from a wide range of stakeholders: social partners, industry and sectoral organisations, educational institutions and ngos. this guarantees wide acceptance of the changes. i therefore support the repeal of the decision and believe that the eqf as a tool for the comparison of qualifications will allow for easier movement of people and will achieve the objectives not achieved by decision 85/368/eec and thus ensure greater mobility of workers on the european labour market.
in writing. - the vote on the report by mr sergio berlato, while positive, will not solve the problem of smoking and tobacco production. you could say that we've put off deciding these important matters for a few years. so the problem is going to come back to us and it's going to continue as long as people smoke tobacco. it will have to be solved, but not at the expense of the farmers who have become involved in tobacco production and have made the necessary investments. tobacco farming is a livelihood for tens of thousands of families, often without any other alternative source of income, as is the case in regions with poor soils in poland, for example. that is why we need strategic decisions today, made with deliberation, not under the pressure of lobbyists representing the middlemen and traders operating in the international system.
in writing. - i abstained on the report by mrs van lancker on the guidelines for employment policy. unfortunately, this report has not been able to avoid contradictions. on the one hand, it is full of words about 'the knowledge-based society', 'competitiveness', 'technological challenges' and on the other hand 'the need to ensure job security', 'stability', etc. the first one emphasizes intention, the second emphasizes persistence. there can be no progress without a disruption in the employment structure. it's never worked in history. so instead of talking about job security, which is the preservation of the job and the nature of the job, we should be talking about something else, namely the provision of access to work. for this work that is now, at this historic moment. this should be our common concern.
in writing. - in the report on the employment policies of the member states, i find many contradictions. the rapporteur writes that the renewed lisbon strategy has produced results, including the growth of eu gdp in recent years and a decline in unemployment, and that the employment guidelines do not require a complete revision, but only changes to a number of specific points. the rapporteur also notes that in recent years as many as 6 million young people aged 18-24 have left school early and interrupted their education, and that 40% of total unemployment in the eu is young people, with the figure being twice as high among migrants. 78 million people live in poverty, that's twice the population of poland. it also notes the increase in the number of jobs obtained at the expense of their lower quality, the increase in the proportion of people employed on a part-time and fixed-term basis, often under a contract concluded under duress. reality speaks for itself, but we don't always want to listen to it. and the problem is that society is not integrating, it's dividing. poverty is not decreasing, but it is increasing every year. discrimination against women, older workers and migrants in the labour market is not diminishing, and stereotypes in thinking and acting are not disappearing.
in writing. - i support the above report and the position of the honourable member that the common social objectives of the member states should be better reflected in the lisbon agenda. i also support the transformation of the current lisbon strategy for growth and jobs into a strategy based on growth, jobs and inclusion. i believe it is essential to promote common social standards at eu level. it is necessary to create quality jobs and to reinforce the value of the european social model. i believe that one of the key tasks of the eu's sustainable development strategy is to create an inclusive society in which operational goals and aspirations are at the forefront in order to reduce the number of people at risk of poverty and social exclusion, significantly increase the participation of women, older workers and migrants in the labour market and promote the employment of young people.
in writing. − 2009 will be a year of many challenges for the european parliament, in particular the entry into force of the lisbon treaty, the elections to the european parliament, the new statute for members and the change of term of office. the overall level of the 2009 budget will have to meet challenges, even though it will be lower than the traditional voluntary limitation of parliament's contribution to 20% of administrative expenditure. it is worth noting that this year's procedure has introduced a pilot process for early and closer cooperation between the bureau and the budget committee on all items with significant budgetary implications. the new approach is designed to ensure that the available resources are used in the most rational way possible and to identify possible savings. it is to be welcomed that reasonable estimates of expenditure have been made for the new member's statute, especially as there is a possibility to adjust the amount of the expenditure at a later stage. it also welcomes the inclusion in the preliminary draft for 2009 of the proposed 65 new posts to strengthen parliament's legislative activities and services for members, while placing 15% of these in the reserve. it also welcomes the continuation of the priorities set in the 2008 budget for interpretation and library analysis services. the successful completion of this year's budgetary procedure will also require immediate debate and concrete decisions on parliament's property policy.
in writing. - i supported mr lehtinen's report because the transparency of the rules protecting european consumers is good for them and also for competing producers. economic changes in the new member states have led to the introduction of new rules for the operation of market operators. today, the consumer's offer is increasingly enriched in terms of products and services. however, i believe that the position of consumers, especially in the new member states, where we all remember the origins of the free market, remains relatively weak in relation to the large companies. it requires greater transparency and the improvement of the appropriate legal framework to ensure that consumers' rights are adequately protected. i also welcome the part of the report in which the rapporteur advocates support for small and medium-sized enterprises in the eu. in my region, lesser poland, they account for 95% of the companies, most of which have a short experience (30% are less than 5 years old).
in writing. - consumers are at the heart of the common market and should therefore be its main beneficiaries. however, i believe that a balance should be struck between legislation that strongly protects consumers and the conditions under which businesses operate. no one is questioning the right of consumers to pursue their claims. however, i believe that we should ensure that consumers in particular are able to enforce their rights quickly and effectively. i believe that extrajudicial remedies should be particularly strongly emphasised when dealing with consumer complaints. i would like to point out that according to business europe, as many as 90% of consumer disputes are settled out of court. the cost of such proceedings is also important, and is considerably lower than the cost of involving the courts. i believe that the amendment voted in the european parliament, which calls for the creation of a european system of collective actions, does not guarantee more effective consumer protection. this issue should be considered by the european commission, and we should refrain from making a decision until the results are published. it may be that this matter is sufficiently regulated by the legislation of the member states. moreover, i fear that this system will create conditions for litigation where the real beneficiaries will not be consumers but the legal community, which will benefit from higher rates for litigation.
in writing. − the european union's consumer policy strategy for 2007-2013 sets out the right direction for consumer protection, but it should be noted that this is far from being enough. we must propose a plan of concrete and consistent next steps which will help to make consumer protection a part of all eu legislation. we must realise that consumer protection is not a separate area of european policy, but is part of all the european policies which make up the european internal market. so without the right safeguards, the single market project will not be completed. we must also remember that eu consumer protection has an external dimension - to mention just one last problem with chinese toys. our aim should be to achieve full consumer confidence in all products in circulation on the internal market. moreover, a genuine internal market should offer a european system of collective redress. in developing it, we must draw on the lessons of the unsatisfactory american class-action system.

in writing. − to begin with, i would like to stress the importance of debate and action on anti-discrimination and equal opportunities. however, as the rapporteur herself notes, some member states have not yet fully implemented the directives on equal treatment for persons irrespective of racial or ethnic origin (2000/43/ec) and on equal treatment in employment and occupation (2000/78/ec). in view of the problems encountered in implementing their provisions, it seems crucial to focus on the correct transposition and more effective enforcement of the provisions of these directives. the situation will not be improved by the inclusion of further categories of persons in further legislative acts. the most important thing is to carry out education and information campaigns and awareness raising activities, mainly at member state level, which will be the appropriate response to these problems. the challenges of discrimination and equal opportunities are not the same in all member states. that is why i am opposed to the creation of further legislation which will not make the problems of equal opportunities and discrimination disappear. i believe that discrimination against disabled people, whose specific situation requires the urgent development of a comprehensive proposal and, above all, its implementation at the level of member states' laws, requires a separate examination. i hope that the european commission will soon take up this initiative.
in writing. - indirect and direct discrimination on grounds of sex, age or disability is still present in europe. the online portal pracuj.pl conducted a survey among working people, job seekers, employers, students and graduates. according to the survey, the most discriminated against groups in the labour market are people aged over 50 and the disabled. the most common manifestation of discrimination in the labour market is the use of prejudices and stereotypes in selecting a job candidate - nearly 62% of respondents consider this a major problem. next in line are: unequal access to job offers/no suitable job offers (56%), reluctance to take on a permanent/contractual job (44%) and lower than average wages in the environment or industry (43%). i believe that anti-discrimination policy, as one of the eu's fundamental principles, has a special role to play in this respect.

mr. chairman, please! i shall not say anything new if i start by congratulating and thanking the rapporteur for a great report. the international community has recently received a document from the ipcc that provides a broad scientific analysis of the problem of global warming. we are talking about it in our report and in our resolution. most researchers, as well as the governments of the countries participating in the panel a hundred or so countries accepted this document at the ipcc fourth forum. but there are also voices denying the value of the document. we heard them in this room, too. so it's worth looking at these controversies first. first, though, today almost everyone agrees that global warming is real, even if, temporarily, some part of the earth is colder than it has been in years. so, warming seems indisputable, thanks in part to the ipcc report. and it's not so much that we need to be showing more evidence of the coming global warming cataclysm, but rather that we need to be showing and proving what's causing the global warming. remember, the vast majority of scientists who are serious about this issue agree that man is largely, but not exclusively, responsible for global warming. in particular, the emission of greenhouse gases. however, it is worthwhile to make further efforts to document and prove this claim. the study of the causes of warming should be pursued with determination, and this should also be an important conclusion of our considerations. but today, remember, this is the most important thing, the probability that the warming is caused by human-made greenhouse gases is so high that we have to act. the european union has therefore become a world leader in reducing emissions. but it is all the more important for us europeans to reach a global agreement on this issue in poznan and copenhagen. let's remember that we can't save the planet on our own. but to neglect our own actions today would be inexcusable. this is our civic responsibility.

in writing. - mercury is one of the most potent environmental poisons. it's a metal that under normal conditions is a liquid with a high vapor density. it is not biodegradable and therefore persists in the environment for a very long time, accumulating in food chains that can enter the human body in significant concentrations. the development of industry has made mercury a metal with special properties and a low cost of extraction. the use of mercury in the production of energy-saving lighting seems difficult to eliminate. it is therefore necessary to develop effective collection systems for such waste and to apply safe disposal technologies to prevent further environmental degradation. one of the largest mercury poisoning incidents occurred in japan between 1953 and 1960. the inhabitants of minamata bay were massively ill, showing signs of nerve damage, which was often the cause of death. the eu should make every effort to ensure that mercury is stored safely. the export of metallic mercury should be banned.
in writing. - caring for the environment is our common responsibility. but the world is not handling it well, and it is being downplayed and put off. in 1998, the european council decided to protect the environment through criminal law. the adoption of the new directive has defined a set of offences which are subject to criminal sanctions in all member states. i believe that the responsibility of manufacturers, exporters, importers and carriers for their products and services should be further emphasised, so that there is no room for manipulation and evasion of responsibility. however, in order to enforce the new rules and reduce environmental crime, measures are needed to provide the necessary resources, training for staff, etc. i believe that the budget of the european union should provide funds, at least for the new member states, which have a lot of work to do in a short period of time. the objectives set out above can only be achieved through the solidarity of all member states. otherwise, regional disparities will only grow.
in writing. − i am voting in favour of the report on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the protection of the environment through criminal law (com (2007) 0051) because the introduction of new legal rules and the definition of a community-wide minimum list of environmental crimes will ensure more effective application of community law. although the rules are uniform in all the member states of the community, the way in which they are applied varies, this encourages the reprehensible practice of dishonest traders to locate their business in countries where criminal penalties for offences are more lenient. this is particularly true for the new member states. it should be emphasised that organised crime is playing an increasing role and that environmental crime is increasingly transnational. i agree with the rapporteur that the legal framework set out in the proposal for a directive is an important contribution to effective environmental protection and can guarantee uniform and fair enforcement of environmental law in the eu. in order to effectively enforce the law and effectively reduce crime, it is necessary to provide adequately trained services. the proposal to clarify the obligations of the member states in this respect is therefore justified. the adoption of a set of environmental offences and related criminal sanctions will be a very important instrument in the uniform enforcement of environmental law in the eu.
in writing. - ladies and gentlemen! i am in favour of simplifying reporting procedures and forms of communication between public administrations and businesses. the bureaucratic requirements for entrepreneurs are absurdly extensive these days. the report is intended to improve communication and, in addition, recommends the implementation of xbrl, which is an open standard, i.e. accessible even to the smallest companies. i have therefore decided to support this report.
in writing. − the commission's communication on a simplified business environment for enterprises in the areas of company law, accounting and auditing proposes measures to reduce administrative burdens and to ensure that european companies can compete effectively on a global scale. not only do member states not use optional measures to reduce red tape, but they often back up community concessions with stricter national rules, depriving local businesses of the possibility of simplifying procedures under eu law. the commission should therefore focus on encouraging member states to harmonise the classification of financial reporting requirements and to embrace new technologies to reduce costs. moreover, a solution in the form of a common corporate tax base would make the statute of the european company more useful and effective. the proposal to exclude 'micro-enterprises' from the application of the accounting directives is also welcome, which would in practice mean exempting them from the obligation to keep accounts, to submit annual accounts or to publish reports required by european legislation. the proposed solutions are commendable, but further simplification of the union acquis in the area of company law and its effective implementation in the member states appear to be necessary for european businesses to compete successfully in an increasingly demanding global market.
in writing. - mr president! - what are you doing? the european union is not seen as a friendly area in the sense of simplicity in the rules of doing business. rather, it is widely believed that this is an over-regulated area, against global standards, which creates particular difficulties for small businesses. therefore, any step towards simplification of the rules, as announced in the european commission's communication of 10 july 2007, should be welcomed. the most important and desirable effect of simplification should be to encourage small firms to operate in the european single market, which has so far been difficult for new businesses from central and eastern europe to access. the measure to achieve this is not only the repeal of redundant provisions, in the two variants proposed by the commission, but also the harmonisation of national provisions. however, this does not mean tax harmonisation, as is suggested in paragraph 23 of mr lehne's report in the 'soft' form of the harmonisation of the corporate tax base. the rapporteur favours the second of the options proposed by the commission, which is more modest and which, in the light of the european union's regulatory inclinations so far, would in any case reverse the unfavourable trend that undoubtedly reduces the competitive chances of european companies on the global market.
in writing. - mr president! - what are you doing? despite increasing access to higher education and an increasing number of female university graduates, we still see a low representation of women in top academic positions. women, although they represent the majority of the teaching staff (over 50%), are mostly in lower positions. i support taking into account the needs of families by allowing flexible working hours, better childcare services and access to social security abroad and to provide parental leave conditions that give men and women freedom of choice. the interruptions that women take in their scientific careers for family reasons must not have a negative impact on their future career opportunities and thus give men an advantage in pursuing a scientific career. i supported the report by mrs britta thomsen because i think it rightly raised the issue of gender stereotypes which are still present in many countries of the european union.
in writing. - as a female professor who has worked for many years at a polish university, i am aware of the importance of the issue and therefore support britta thomsen's report. the report is interesting in that it tackles the issue of gender discrimination in science, and identifies the social, cultural and economic barriers that still leave women underrepresented in science. we are few in the public sector and higher education (35%) and only 18% in the private sector. how can we without women in science build a knowledge-based society, develop european science and economy, meet the challenges of the lisbon strategy and meet the expectations of europeans at the dawn of the 21st century? the conditions must therefore be created to allow women to be more widely involved in scientific life, to open the doors not only to academic laboratories but also to the highest academic positions. it is a shame that in a world of science where advancement is determined by merit, women are three times less likely to be appointed to a professorship than men. and it's not just because they're more involved in their family life. it is difficult to implement gender equality policies in european universities, since women are so rarely members of their decision-making bodies. the shameful example of the european research council, where only five women sit on the 22-member scientific council, is enough.
in writing. − women's participation in the labour market is steadily increasing throughout the european union. poland is no exception, although the participation of women in the labour market in poland is still below the eu average. however, i would like to emphasize that polish women are much more likely than their western counterparts to hold senior positions. it's very important to me that women are activated professionally. the situation of women scientists must also be considered in this context, since it coincides with the situation of all women who are faced with the need to reconcile professional obligations with family life. however, i do not think that the way to increase women's participation in the labour market should be through the establishment of parities. the qualifications and competences that women have acquired through appropriate education should be the primary determinants of employment. proposals to make recruitment procedures, competitions for management posts and the award of research grants more transparent seem to be appropriate. however, these changes should be accompanied by labour market reforms. science in the eu needs support. given the importance of science for economic development, we should be keen to promote science and technology as attractive fields of study for both sexes. so we should focus on encouraging young people to take up these fields of study.
in writing. - women have made a major contribution to the development of science. a fine example is the polish nobel laureate in physics and chemistry, maria skłodowska-curie. the university, the hospital, the street are named after this scholar. women face greater challenges than men in choosing a career in science. this includes the birth and rearing of children. therefore, women scientists should be supported by developing preferential maternity leave conditions, special grants for women who are raising children and working in parallel with their scientific work. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. careers and research should not be determined by gender but by personal choice, ability and knowledge.
in writing. -history teaches that theories widely accepted as true in the past may, based on new scientific discoveries, be unsupported by facts. i believe that the science of climate change, of warming, is not yet well established. certainly not enough to create laws with a clear conscience to create certain attitudes of the european community countries. the increase in the average temperature of the earth's atmosphere is one thing, but the question of how much human activity has contributed to it remains unanswered. the scientific community is divided. some scientists believe that large climate fluctuations are a natural phenomenon that has been cycling on earth for thousands of years, and the appeals of climate scientists are designed to instill fear in people so that they can finance their research. others argue that man's ability to predict long-term climate change is limited, accusing the ipcc of being a political, not a scientific, agency. another controversial point is the supposedly large number of scientists who support the theory of man-made climate change. the counter-arguments presented above are readily available. they are also undeniable, leaving doubt, but also the question: "can we build coherent policy in any field on the uncertain scientific arguments put forward by lobby groups?"

on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. caution is reason enough to work toward the effective elimination of depleted uranium weapons. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the protection of the environment and the environment from the effects of nuclear weapons is a very good one. however, a moratorium on the use of such weapons can be introduced today and the issue can be taken into account in a renewed european security strategy. the task today is to begin work on an international treaty based on the un system that would regulate the use, production, stockpiling and testing of these weapons.
depleted uranium is 70% heavier than lead, and therefore even a very small-caliber projectile can, with its kinetic energy, pierce through the armor of a tank. and that's what made this depleted uranium so useful in military thinking. and there's about a million and a half tons of depleted uranium in the world. so it's understandable that it was a temptation. but it turns out that the effectiveness of these weapons is not as high as expected: 70% of the destruction of iraqi tanks were the destruction of other weapons. the problem, of course, is the effects of using these weapons. and let's be clear, there is no final solution here. after all, thousands of people work in uranium mines for many years, and there are no such obvious effects. but the case is still, of course, questionable and for that reason, we have to decide on a moratorium to finally clarify the matter.

the rapporteur. −"prevention is better than cure" is the main idea of the animal health strategy proposed by the commission. the idea is obvious. we all remember the problems of bse and bird flu, when it was necessary to kill millions of animals. it was a very sad experience and we all want it to never have to happen again. this experience shows us that we should improve cooperation at european level to better protect animal health, which is very closely linked to human health because of the possibility of indirect or direct transmission of diseases from animals to humans. i would like to draw particular attention to a few points in my report. first, the promotion of better animal welfare standards. the report emphasises very strongly the close link between these two values and we expect that both values will be very closely present in future policy. the second thing is fair competition. european producers are required to meet a wide range of veterinary, animal health and welfare standards, but the same standards are not required of importers. the report emphasizes this. the same standards should be required of our producers as those who export animal products to the european market. this is a great challenge for our negotiators in the world trade organization negotiations. the third issue is strong support for the vaccination program. we think it's a very important tool to reduce disease. this also requires a different approach: products derived from vaccinated animals should not be discriminated against on the market. several sections of the report deal with this issue. the fourth problem is the compensation system, the compensation system. it should, firstly, encourage the reduction of the risk of disease and, secondly, take into account not only the direct losses associated with the eradication of disease outbreaks, but also the indirect losses associated with the crisis in the market. the fifth point is better control at the external borders of the union, which should not be limited to documentary checks but should be real, should effectively prevent the illegal import of animals of unknown origin into the union. the sixth issue is the duration of the strategy. we are a little late 2013 is too short a timeframe for these legislative plans to actually be implemented. a longer-term perspective is needed to implement these ambitious plans. the seventh issue is the financing of the strategy's objectives. in the draft report, we criticise the fact that these ambitious objectives are not sufficiently supported by financial means and should be financed from the union budget. in conclusion, mr president, i will say three sentences in english, so as not to distort the quotation to which i am referring. in writing. - i support the ep resolution on visa negotiations with the usa. they shall be conducted on behalf of all the members of the union. the us government and the governments of countries that have already entered into bilateral negotiations should take into account the eu's ownership and its treaty competences. clear rules are needed for bilateral visa-free talks with the united states, but there are issues within the union's competence. this is a two-way street. unfortunately, for poland, which unilaterally lifted the visa requirement for us citizens on 15 april 1991, this asymmetry is very clear. i'm not convinced that the argument that it's decided by an overly high visa refusal rate is valid. these renewals, i believe, are often the result of an arbitrary decision by a us consular officer who - sometimes on no apparent basis - concludes that someone would illegally extend their stay in the us. such assumptions are grossly unreasonable and sometimes even offensive. the dollar's exchange rate against the zloty is no longer a reasonable argument for black-market labor. today, it's important to travel for tourism, business, to visit friends and family. i think the united states is losing out on this, too, by closing its borders to allies and keeping them airtight against potential terrorists. how can we build transatlantic cooperation if we don't trust our allies? - that's not a rhetorical question. many of my constituents are paying attention to this problem.
in writing. − the 2005 paris declaration established a programme for the effectiveness of international aid, focusing on the fight against poverty. the document sets out specific commitments to promote more effective aid based on international cooperation. it seems that this will be effective aid in the full sense of the word and that those who need it will receive it and not have to bear the cost of it. unfortunately, it is not uncommon for people who receive 'aid' to have to pay for it. in many cases, it is an instrument of economic dependence of the weak on the strong, the poor on the rich. in the early 1960's, a hindu man observing the aid given by developed countries to his country commented to the world food organization: 'for god's sake, stop helping us.' i believe this time will be different.

rapporteur. − mr president, i should like to comment and express the views of parliament on foreign policy during this debate, which is more than just a routine annual debate on foreign policy and the state of play of foreign policy in the union: the participation of mr solana with us is a testimony that it is a special debate. thank you for coming, mr solana. first, we are at a very important juncture, if not a turning point, in terms of foreign policy because of the lisbon treaty innovations. we have to look back in order to evaluate as usual, but we also have to take a forward-looking approach. we have high and growing citizen support for foreign policy, for one which is genuine and robust. member states’ perceptions increasingly change, seeing that speaking with one voice and acting in common is the only way to have an effective union foreign policy. entering this new chapter of eu foreign policy, we are moving towards a qualitative change. the new foreign policy should draw its legitimacy not only from its intergovernmental source, but also from european parliament scrutiny, hence, as we will see, the growing importance and role of the european parliament in shaping this policy, as we called for in our report. we need an integrated and holistic approach to foreign policy, with cohesion, convergence and complementarity of all the institutions involved, including the member states. the european union should continue its role as peace-maker and mediator, a soft power helping to stabilise, reconstruct and reform, a supplier of assistance and humanitarian aid, as a normative power, value-projecting and promoting democracy, freedom and human rights, but at the same time we should complement the soft dimension with a harder one by developing the esdp dimension and our military capabilities to be prepared for power projection also. we should complement our reactive policy to short- and medium-term challenges with a more long-term strategic approach and definition of european interests in the long term, by addressing the true causes and not only the effects of some changes around us like darfur, which is both a climate and a conflict situation. we should continue being active on various geographical priorities, but also face new challenges and horizontal issues like climate security, energy security, space security, cyber-security, migration flows and many others. while aspiring to be a global power and a global actor, we should change the balance between being a payer, as we are and we want to be, and being a key player in the world arena. the new treaty offers a huge potential for a coherent and effective foreign policy, but we all know that implementation will be crucial. we need collective will and cooperation, not only in the institutional triangle but also with member states, and we have to avoid rivalries. we tried to table a constructive approach in this report. we are concerned by some failures of foreign policy, but we look more to the future. we recognise positive evolution, progress and successes. we recommend challenging the failures but building on achievements, and identifying room for further progress. the european parliament’s ambition is not only to scrutinise the foreign policy, to make recommendations on which to base solutions and choices for the executive branch, but also to invest in its own foreign policy-making, which i call ‘parliamentary diplomacy’, as it is run within our competence at parliamentary level. on priorities, we believe that we need a focused approach and a limited number of priorities. we underline the need for value-driven foreign policy, not because we are excessively idealistic or naive, but because a world around us which shares our own strong universal values will best serve our interests of security and prosperity. parliament considers the foreign policy of the union as a contribution to strengthened european identity and also as value added for eu citizens and as part of the european commission’s trajectory of a europe of results. we consider foreign policy as a key eu policy to be equipped with a proper institutional set-up, which the lisbon treaty brings about, proper instruments, and adequate financing out of the eu budget. we need a set of instruments at our disposal, and that is something which lies ahead of us.
mr. chairman, please! i would like to recall that in last year's council report on the main aspects and basic choices of the common foreign and security policy, parliament expressed its deep concern at the announcement by then russian president vladimir putin that russia would withdraw from further participation in the treaty on the limitation of conventional forces in europe. despite the explicit declaration of the european parliament, the union authorities have not taken any serious action in this regard. in july 2007, the russian state duma unanimously adopted a law suspending russia's participation in the treaty. this is of fundamental importance for european security, since russia has the largest conventional armed forces on our continent. i therefore consider that the matter of the re-accession of the russian federation to this international agreement is a matter of priority. the authorities of the union and its member states should use all possible means to bring this about, not least because russian military spending has recently increased by 700%.

vice-president of the commission. - mr president, i have to say something. i believe, as did javier solana before me, that this debate has shown a broad consensus on the basic orientation of european foreign and security policy, and i am very pleased about that. i would like to make three brief points. i would like to return to the question of security. i don't think we're that far apart. none of the major global problems we face today and in the near future is without a security dimension. even the crisis in the financial markets has a security dimension. the food situation has one, the raw materials situation has one, not to forget the classic issues. however, there is no danger of a militarization of our foreign policy or of the european union, because the military response to these risks is rarely an option. if anything, it is usually to create a safe environment in which to do the real task, which will be of a civil and political nature. but we must be able to do both. we must be prepared for both, and that is precisely the consideration that european policy is going to give. we are also particularly well placed to help to deal with crises in the world because we have a wide range of instruments at our disposal to implement our strategies. the european union can rely not only on the cfsp and the esdp but also on various community instruments, such as the instruments for stability and development cooperation in general, but also humanitarian aid and civil protection. we must ensure that we always choose the right instruments and that the various players work together in a coherent way. there can be no doubt that one of the main benefits of the lisbon treaty when it comes into force is that it will significantly facilitate precisely this coherent and more effective interaction. let me conclude and summarize once again: what really matters is our collective and political will to actually use our opportunities. the opportunities are there, we just have to want to take them. we need to use them in a way that we can pull together. under the circumstances, we really have no choice. we simply cannot afford to act inconsistently or to use resources inefficiently. we must instead pool and concentrate our resources and instruments if we are to achieve a truly common, credible and coherent eu foreign policy. only then will we be able to meet the madam president! the council regulation is an interesting example of preventive legislation, a regulation against illegal fishing that threatens the sustainability of fish stocks. the chances of this particular document being effective are first and foremost created by the clarity of the solutions proposed. a precise definition of the legislator's intention. the rapporteur has captured the specific nature of the regulation very well, with very helpful interpretative exercises that simply facilitate the correct reading of the most important provisions. the governments of the southern and eastern baltic states have made extensive references to this important legislative initiative. however, the council's proposed criteria for punishing illegal fishermen are still the subject of debate in the scientific community. the question is asked again: does the idea of seeking to guarantee the effectiveness of the penalty by formalizing it to a great extent take account of the diversity of the fishing potential of european waters? should the possibility of making the amount of the fine dependent on the size of the fish stocks and the fishing quotas in force for overfished species not be taken into account in future legislative work? i believe that the recently published revised assessment of the ics in relation to the baltic ecosystem is a harbinger of a softening in fisheries policy, a process of adjustment to the european union's revolutionary approach to conserving resources. the european parliament's committee on fisheries has proactively added a special amendment which treats the first year of application of the regulation as a transitional, adaptation period allowing member states to take the necessary adaptation measures.
madam president! the european union is an active participant in the search for global solutions to the use of advanced fishing gear. instead of a total ban on their use, it advocates strict restrictions on their use. the regulation in question is a modus vivendi. however, the legislative effects achieved are not always based on a clear and convincing record. the smaller fisheries, which lack the possibility of regular detailed surveys, are simply concerned about whether they will be able to meet the requirement to draw up an appropriate fishing plan, including the requirement to determine the depth at which fishing gear will be used, or - which is of particular concern to poorer fisheries - the configuration of the seabed.

the next item is the commission statement on the 40th anniversary of the customs union on 1 july 2008.
mr. chairman, please! the customs union is an essential element of the internal market of the european union, which cannot function properly without common rules at its external borders. in addition to its obvious function of collecting customs duties, the customs union plays a huge role in protecting the health and safety of our citizens. in recent months, we have spent a lot of time in parliament discussing, among other things, the safety of products, in particular toys and counterfeiting. we all want to have products that meet certain criteria, and above all that do not endanger our health or our lives. i would like to remind you that, contrary to popular belief, counterfeiting is not limited to high-end and expensive products, but also to car parts and everyday products such as food and medicines. many of these products are placed on the european internal market from third countries. the scale of this phenomenon is illustrated by the numbers. in 2007, customs authorities seized some 128 million counterfeit products. this represents an increase of 70% compared to 2005. the drug alone accounted for 380 percent of the total. of course, the reasons for this increase may vary. this may be due to an increased flow of counterfeits into the union, but also to an improvement in their detection by customs. but let us remember that standards alone are not enough if there is no effective control at our borders, and especially no control carried out in the same way at every section of our external border. the effective fight against counterfeiting entering the union requires enhanced cooperation between the customs authorities and supervisory authorities of the member states of the union, but also with the customs authorities of third countries. this amplification must keep pace with technological change. it is therefore essential that customs services throughout the european union have the appropriate equipment to enable them to carry out their tasks effectively.
mr. chairman, please! the customs union, which was established on 1 july 1968, was the first step towards deepening the economic integration of the then six member states. it can be considered a success story in the history of european integration. as we celebrate the 40th anniversary of the customs union, it is also worth noting that this is a perfect example of how effective cooperation can be achieved among 27 member states, since there is not just one customs service of the european union, but 20 national customs services with different competences and different forms of organisation, which cooperate with each other on the basis of a common european policy and a common legal framework defining the rules and procedures in force. the customs administrations of the 27 member states must act as one single administration. forty years ago, the customs union was designed to abolish customs duties at internal borders between member states and to bring about the single market. customs offices now work together to protect the external borders of the european union and to take action to combat smuggling, seize dangerous counterfeit goods and other tasks, which, congratulating the commissioner, were also included in the european commission's strategy for the development of the customs union presented in april 2008.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all allow me to express my thanks for the very interesting debate that has just taken place. i have carefully noted the comments made, since they are extremely useful for me and the commission – and the customs services – in taking into account the political priorities expressed by the european parliament. i was very much impressed by the explicit expression of appreciation and support for the work of the customs union; i can assure you that it will continue. what are the guarantees? the guarantees are that we have the instruments, we have the strategy, and we have the legal basis, the modernised community customs code with rules and procedures that guarantee the facilitation of legitimate trade and also the protection of the internal market, the safety, the health and the life of our citizens. we have the id technology in the framework of ecustoms, and we have a very wide cooperation network: cooperation among the customs authorities of the member states, cooperation with other law enforcement agencies, cooperation with business – and referring to the contribution of mr harbour, i should like to say that in frankfurt last week i had the chance to get information on the medifake project, which is about counterfeit medicines, and if any distinction may be drawn between the different kinds of fake products, certainly pharmaceuticals are the most dangerous. i am happy to tell you that just a couple of days ago in the country i know best, in hungary, there was an agreement between the customs authorities and the association of pharmaceutical factories in hungary on how to prevent fake pharmaceuticals from getting onto the market. we also have cooperation with international organisations, with third countries like china, and i must say that, in what are now more than three years of dealing with this portfolio and holding regular meetings with the chinese authorities, i have certainly witnessed some improvement in the chinese attitude. they are more concrete; they are speaking more to the point; they are more cooperative, more constructive. probably the reason is that for them it is more and more a question of political prestige. china, which is playing a more and more important role, not only in world trade but also in world politics, cannot afford to be labelled as the main source, as the main country of origin of those fake products that endanger the safety, the health and even the life of the citizens of other countries. another reason is that, as much evidence has proved, china is becoming more and more a target country and not merely a country of origin. at least two speakers mentioned the 100% scanning initiative of the us congress: i want to tell you that we are really trying to exert pressure on the us administration, and indirectly even on us legislation, because we are absolutely certain – and we keep saying it – that this initiative would result in the disruption of international trade in maritime shipping, it would create a false sense of security and it would just divert attention and resources from the real issues. we hope that finally we will be successful. so with your support, with the support of parliament, with the support of committees like the imco and inta committees which have been very actively supporting the customs union, i am sure that the successful activities of the customs union in the next, fourth year will be guaranteed. thank you very much for your contributions and support.

in writing. - i voted in favour of the report on the legal protection of computer programs (rapporteur lidia geringer de oedenberg), because i believe that, as they play a huge role in the functioning of modern society, they should be afforded appropriate legal protection, granted in accordance with the provisions of copyright law, just like literary and artistic works within the meaning of the berne convention. only computer programs expressed in the correct form should be protected. the concepts and principles on which the individual elements of a computer program are based may not themselves be subject to such protection. of course, mathematical procedures, programming languages or algorithms cannot be protected in this way. such protection should be granted to both natural and legal persons in accordance with national copyright legislation. it should be noted that if the scheme has been drawn up by employees in the course of their duties, the employer or the contractor is entitled to exercise the property rights arising from the scheme (unless otherwise agreed in the contract).

mr. chairman, please! the involvement of the european parliament in committee procedures is necessary in view of the development of its legislative powers, in particular in the context of the codecision procedure provided for in article 251 of the treaty. this is the aim of the council decision of 17 july 2006 and article 5a introducing a new procedure whereby parliament will decide jointly with the council on the admissibility of proposals for certain implementing measures. the new procedure, known as the regulatory procedure with scrutiny, will cover measures of general scope designed to amend non-essential elements of a basic act adopted under the codecision procedure. the council's decision is revolutionary for the legislative process, as it will allow parliament to veto the commission's proposal for implementing measures. as a result, it will be possible to modify the proposal or return to the legislative path. it is essential that the adjustment package is adopted as soon as possible to allow the new procedure to be applied immediately to binding legislation. i therefore propose that the commission's proposal, which includes a list of legal acts to be adapted to the new procedure, together with the amendments proposed by parliament's competent committees, be adopted in the forthcoming vote. at the same time, i would point out that the way in which parliament makes use of the opportunities it has to offer will be crucial to the success of the current reform of comitology. the requirement of an absolute majority to reject the commission's proposal for implementing measures or the lengthening of the procedure, for example by the need to translate documents into 23 eu languages, may have a negative impact on the procedure. it should also be borne in mind that parliament may come under increased pressure from various circles interested in influencing the final shape of implementing measures. the additional challenge, both in terms of substance and organisation, will also be to take account of the huge number of implementing acts that will be submitted to parliament in the future.
