mr. chairman, please! the common market means more competition and, consequently, higher standards. they require market participants to make the appropriate investments and improve the capacity of transmission networks. this in turn improves security of supply and avoids disruptions to the energy supply. the creation of a common energy market is very important, because we are seeing a continuous increase in energy demand. this is an important step forward, but it is still not enough to ensure europe's energy security. we must build a common energy policy in a spirit of solidarity. it is necessary to develop appropriate mechanisms to allow member states to assist each other in the event of energy crises. but even more importantly, europe must finally start to speak with one voice in its external energy policy. only a coherent, effective and, above all, common policy will guarantee our energy security.
in writing. − the european parliament has taken a key decision towards a common electricity market by advocating mandatory ownership of energy companies in the european union. only the division of the companies in the sector into companies responsible for the production and transmission of energy guarantees the creation of a competitive and open market, from which conflicts of interest will disappear. the consumer is the main beneficiary of the proposed names. the proposal voted on significantly strengthens the rights of consumers, giving them, among other things, the right to withdraw from an electricity supplier contract without additional charges or the right to change energy supplier within a short time. let us not forget that the electricity market is currently dominated by monopolies that exploit their position in non-competitive markets. i believe that price limits will protect consumers from abuse by energy companies, while not discouraging new entrants to the market. of course, the solutions proposed will not solve all the energy problems we are facing today, such as rising oil prices, but they are the right move towards a more competitive market. the discussion will continue in the council. unfortunately, it is unlikely that all the european parliament's proposals will be upheld. as the rapporteur rightly pointed out, many member states protect the interests of national groups.
in writing. - the rapporteur has prepared a very thorough and reliable report. i believe that the european parliament's proposal in this form will allow the work to continue on the integration of the eu energy market. i hope that we can reach an agreement on all cross-border issues.
in writing. - the rapporteur has prepared a very thorough and reliable report. i believe that the european parliament's proposal in this form will allow the work to continue on the integration of the eu energy market and to strengthen the agency's powers in relation to all cross-border issues, which will result in effective cooperation between member states.
in writing. - in poland, the number of accidents involving pedestrians increased by 5.7% and those involving cyclists by as much as 16.8% last year. i support mr ferrari's report and i think that it is necessary to increase safety requirements, but we must also remember that the costs of introducing them should not be focused on vehicle owners. for the lesser poland voivodeship, which i represent, the accident rate is the lowest in the country (at 7/100), although there are many dangerous points due to excessive traffic and inadequate road infrastructure.
in writing. - i would like to underline the importance of this report and congratulate the author on the result achieved. it is a fact that every year in the european union, 8 000 road users, mainly pedestrians and cyclists, are killed and another 300 000 are injured. this situation not only brings individual tragedies but also has serious economic and social consequences. therefore, union action to better protect pedestrians and other vulnerable road users from injuries caused by motor vehicle collisions should be considered highly desirable. since october 2005, according to the current regulations, some vehicles have to undergo a series of performance tests based on the recommendations of the joint research centre. in addition, the union proposes to tighten up the testing requirements for cars entering the european market after 2010. the regulation allows active and passive safety measures to be combined and provides for the introduction of collision avoidance systems in the future. there is no effective pedestrian collision protection system on the market so far, and the commission is right to encourage the industry to develop such a system. i also share the rapporteur's view that technical possibilities for raising passive safety standards should be continuously monitored and possibilities for increased safety requirements monitored accordingly.
in writing. - report on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the protection of pedestrians and other vulnerable road users (2007/0201) there are currently no collision avoidance systems on the market that can effectively and correctly recognise pedestrians or other unprotected road users while maintaining all the necessary conditions. i share the rapporteur's view that it is essential to introduce measures to reduce the number of injuries and, above all, the number of fatalities among pedestrians and other vulnerable road users. it is worth emphasising that the proposed amendments aim to tighten the provisions of the regulation where possible. i am voting in favour of the report because i believe that we should not only monitor the development of active safety technology but also examine the possibility of introducing stricter requirements for passive safety (vehicle design).
in writing. - pedestrians and cyclists are very common victims of road accidents. protecting their lives is a major challenge for the automotive industry. a very good solution is the epp (electronic pedestrian protection) system, which helps to mitigate the effects of a collision with a car. this solution absorbs the force of the impact on the front of the car, thus reducing the extent of the injury. another equally effective method, which provides protection for pedestrians by actively covering the engine, was used in the c6. when the pedestrian is hit, the engine's mask automatically lifts. the cap is raised by 65 mm in 0.40 seconds by a shock detector and pyrotechnic mechanism, and a separate mechanism keeps it in the raised position despite the shock force, thus absorbing the energy generated by the distortion. a beam equipped with energy absorbers also has a protective function in the event of a light impact. all vehicles should undergo as many tests as possible to improve safety on eu roads.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report by mr galeote quecedo gerardo on the proposal for autonomous community tariff quotas for the importation of certain fishery products into the canary islands. the report proposes to suspend the common customs tariff on imports of certain fishery products into the canary islands for the period 2007-13. it should be noted that the provisions to which the request relates expired on 31 december 2006. the proposal to open and manage duty-free tariff quotas is in line with article 299 (2) of the ec treaty, which provides for specific measures to assist the outermost regions. i therefore vote in favour of the report because i believe that the exceptional geographical situation of the canary islands in relation to the sources of supply of certain fishery products, which are extremely important for domestic consumption, creates additional costs for the sector. these natural difficulties arising from the situation can be remedied, inter alia, by temporarily suspending the levying of customs duties on imports of the products concerned from third countries.
madam president! the world and europe are in a situation where oil prices can determine not only economic growth but also the depth of the crisis, which has its origins in the food market, in fisheries, and will soon have problems in the transport sector. what action? the long-term is the construction of a stable energy policy, understood very broadly, which is what we are talking about so much in the union and in parliament. short-term action: we need to target aid to specific areas, i.e. specific support for farmers, fishermen and also for transport operators, already in the second half of this year. i emphasize: the deliberate allocation of specific aid during a specific part of the year. action should be taken to limit speculation and monopolistic practices. finally, let us be clear: tax policy needs to be reviewed at both eu and national level.
mr. chairman, please! fishing is a very specific sector of our economy. the economic operators are very fragmented and dispersed. these are often family-run, local businesses with limited catch sizes and therefore no ability to increase production to generate a satisfactory income at increased costs. you can say, costs go up, so fish prices have to go up, but these relationships have a limit, how much, what price can the consumer pay? what about their reason? to counter the current difficult situation, i propose to grant certain fuel subsidies to fishermen, subsidies dependent on oil prices. fishermen and their families have no possibility of earning extra income in another activity. in conclusion, fisheries policy needs a new approach.
the chairman of the council. - i would also like to emphasise in my concluding statement that the council is aware of the difficult situation of the fisheries sector in the european union, but it is necessary to distinguish between two aspects: the specific characteristics of the fisheries sector and the high fuel prices, which, as already mentioned, affect many, practically all sectors, including, of course, the fisheries sector. the council is very active in seeking solutions: intensive consultations are under way, culminating next week in the agriculture and fisheries council, and short, medium and long-term measures are being sought to preserve european fisheries, to overcome the current difficult phase, to preserve both coastal and high seas fisheries. i can assure you that i have followed this debate closely and that the president of the fisheries council will be fully informed of the views expressed in this debate, including your initial reactions to the proposals and plans presented by the commissioner.
member of the commission. − mr president, i would firstly like to thank everyone for their comments, for the various points that they have raised and also for the general expression of support for the package that the commission intends to propose. i would like to say that this is not the end of the whole process but just the beginning. we still need to steer these proposals through council and parliament and i would repeat that we need your full support in order to get these proposals through as rapidly as possible, especially in those parts which would require legislative amendment. what i have presented represents, in my view, the limits of flexibility in addressing the short-term crisis, with a view to putting in place a medium- and longer-term perspective of restructuring, in order to regain sustainability of resources and the profitability of the sector. i agree that these measures should not be seen in isolation but also within the context of the ongoing discussions concerning iuu, discards, eco-labelling and various other measures which we are in the process of having adopted. with regard to iuu for example, i hope that on tuesday of next week a decision will be taken in council on the proposed regulation to effectively combat iuu fishing, on which the european parliament has given overwhelming support. i would like to say to mr davies that we are not proposing to throw money at the problem, but to provide assistance with a view to restructuring – as i said, to regain sustainable fishing and profitable fishing. i would invite mr davies to examine what we would be proposing and, if he has any specific comments to make, i would certainly welcome them. yes, we will work to enable the proper market mechanisms to operate rather than continuing to allow a few huge operators to dominate the market when setting fish prices. in response to what mr allister said, the package makes it more attractive for member states to take up what is available under the european fisheries fund, and therefore we hope that member states will fully engage. we will be discussing this in next week’s council in order to implement effectively these measures that we are proposing. i will just go very briefly through the measures that are envisaged. first of all, we are looking at the emergency measures, where we are proposing assistance for temporary cessation for fishing vessels (and this also goes in the direction of sustainability) for a maximum period of three months in addition to what is already in the european fisheries fund, and not linked exclusively to biological reasons. such a measure may finance cruise costs and fixed costs of vessels. this measure will only apply in cases where there is an explicit commitment that the enterprises benefiting from it will be included in a restructuring plan within a period of six months. a second provision relates to the increase in the eff aid intensity for fuel-saving equipment. we are proposing that the mandatory private financial participation will be at a lower rate and will therefore be at 40% of its present level. we are also proposing to extend further a number of socioeconomic measures which are eligible under eff. on de minimis aid we are looking at making provisions so that if, on an economic analysis, it proves to be feasible, then our proposal would be to extend the de minimis aid from eur 30 000 per enterprise to eur 30 000 per vessel but with a maximum cap of eur 100 000 per enterprise. the longer-term measures would relate to eff premiums for permanent cessation of fleets in restructuring, so that we would lift any limitations on access to permanent cessation premiums; and additional aid for temporary cessation, so that beyond the first three months that i mentioned, we will be proposing that there will be an additional three months to be taken during the period of restructuring, where vessels will be necessarily laid up because of the restructuring process. this would be up to the period of 1 january 2010, and for an additional three months if the restructuring needs to go beyond 1 january 2010. so it would be a maximum of six months beyond the three months given as an emergency aid. we are also providing for increasing the aid intensity for modernisation schemes. today the private financial participation is 60% and 80% for gear and engine replacement respectively. we are proposing to reduce the private financial participation to 40%. we are doing this because we realise that the private sector – the private entrepreneurs, the fishermen – are not in a position to be able to significantly part-finance any restructuring out of their own pockets. we are trying to make it as easy as possible for fishermen to undertake restructuring by providing the lion’s share of the expense that will be incurred. we are also allowing for the granting of partial decommissioning. in other words, if there is a group of vessels and that group of vessels represents, say, 100 000 tonnes, and they undertake to decommission 50 000 or 60 000 tonnes, leaving 40 000 tonnes by virtue of which they want to construct new vessels, then for the amount partially decommissioned – for the 50 000 or 60 000 tonnes – they would be given decommissioning aid. obviously that would mean that the size of the fleet would be reduced. you would have a newer fleet but this would mean that the compensation would have been paid for the amount by which it had been reduced. we are also proposing social aid in the form of decreased social security contributions. in other words, what we are proposing is that there will be the possibility for the contributions payable by fishermen, and not the contributions payable by the enterprises employing them, to be exempted on condition that the remuneration of the fishermen is not reduced and on condition that the fishermen remain in receipt of the same social benefits under any existing schemes. with regard to market measures – a point mentioned by mrs fraga – i would like to state that there are various measures which we are proposing: increasing fishermen’s bargaining position vis-à-vis the processing industry and distributors by joining forces with larger pos or local marketing associations; establishing a price monitoring system to better understand the factors determining market prices; improving predictability of sourcing for eu-origin products for the industry; promoting quality initiatives like labelling and better handling and processing; promoting information to consumers; health and nutrition; responsible fishing; market audit assessment; developing tools to analyse the value chain and prices; and verifying the correct implementation of the monitoring of labelling measures and iuu. we are also making available from our own funds – from other fisheries funds – for the first year, eur 20-25 million in order specifically to launch other projects in cooperation with the sector in the area of market monitoring, labelling etc. we are prepared to reopen discussions with member states – even though we have just concluded them – on the existing operational programmes in order to ensure that the european fisheries funds are focused more on these restructuring programmes. we are facilitating the use of the european fisheries fund. for example – just to mention one point in addition – it is proposed to double the eff pre-financing amount paid by the commission after the adoption of the operational programmes from the current 7% to 14% of the total eff contribution. i have two final points. mrs fraga said that we could have done more before. i would like just to introduce a nuance to this. we could have acted differently before. we could have avoided incentivising and encouraging over-capacity and not thrown precious public money at unwarranted huge increases of capacity way beyond what the stocks of our fish can reasonably sustain. concerning mrs doyle’s remarks – that the cfp has failed miserably – i simply do not agree. it is because of the cfp that we can put forward proposed common solutions as we are doing now, instead of witnessing individual member states joining in a race downhill in the direction of the total destruction of fishing.

in writing. this is a very important debate for all coastal countries and consumers alike. as the participants in the debate recalled, we all lived with the feeling that oil prices would never rise. of course, this was after years of neglect and the lack of imagination of the institutions in charge. today, the mere fact of taking boats and canoes out to sea has become unprofitable, and the price of fish does not compensate for the cost. many fishermen may be forced to retire, which could upset the whole economy. i think that few people listened to the fishermen's voices, and it was only after the crisis that the conscience of many people was awakened, and the problems of the sector started many years ago. there is still a lack of a comprehensive debate on this sector, a substantive and frank debate. we must solve this deep crisis now and take care of the fisheries sector.
the next item is the statements by the council and the commission on the preparations for the eu-russia summit (26-27 june 2008).
the chairman of the council. − i am very pleased to present to you today the preparations for the eu-russia summit, the 21st eu-russia summit, which will take place later this month, on 26 and 27 june, in the town of hanti-mansisk, in western siberia. the presidency considers this forthcoming summit to be a great opportunity, in particular for both sides, the european union and the russian federation, to open a new chapter in their relations. above all, we must be prepared to take advantage of the potential positive impetus that the newly elected russian president medvedev could bring to eu-russia relations. the central objective of the summit is, of course, to open negotiations with the russian federation on a new framework agreement. the presidency is very pleased that the council adopted the negotiating mandate for the new agreement on 26 may. the presidency has worked hard in recent months, together with the commission at the highest level, to resolve the remaining problems on the part of the european union. during the negotiations that will now follow, the negotiations for a new agreement, the european union will seek to further deepen cooperation with the russian federation in all areas of common interest, while also addressing those issues where our positions, the positions of the european union and the positions of russia differ. in addition to this, the summit will, as usual, be an opportunity to assess progress in the implementation of the four common spaces. let me very quickly highlight the current main features under each room. as regards the first, the common economic area, we will be advocating at the summit the use of an early warning mechanism in the energy sector. we will reiterate that the establishment of predictable and established rules is of the utmost importance for foreign investment in russia. the european union also intends to underline that formal negotiations on a deep and comprehensive free trade agreement can begin as soon as russia has finally acceded to the world trade organisation. as regards the long-standing problem of charging fees for trans-siberian flights, the european union will continue to advocate the signing of the existing agreement. in the context of the second common area, which concerns the area of freedom, security and justice, the european union intends to express its concern at the situation of human rights, democracy and the rule of law in russia, in particular in the light of the recent elections. i should add that the presidency shares the european parliament's concerns in this respect. the summit will also provide an opportunity to assess progress in the implementation of visa waiver and readmission agreements. in the context of the third common area, external security, the european union will give priority to the need for more concrete action to continue cooperation within the common neighbourhood. in particular, we will emphasise that russia must work towards a settlement of the conflict in transnistria and georgia. we would also like to welcome russia's participation in the eufor operation in chad and agree on further cooperation within the framework of the european security and defence policy. as regards the fourth common area, research, education and culture, the summit will welcome the first meeting of the permanent research partnership council, held in slovenia in may. finally, the summit will also be an opportunity to discuss current international issues such as frozen conflicts, the middle east, iran, afghanistan and others. ladies and gentlemen, i would like to conclude by saying that the summit will also place a strong emphasis on the efforts of both sides to ensure the stable and democratic development of the countries in the common neighbourhood. concrete cooperation between the european union and russia in the framework of the common neighbourhood is essential to resolve problems of european and russian interest and concern to both sides, in particular frozen conflicts. i'll finish this and listen to your argument with interest. (applause) i would like to thank you.
member of the commission. − mr president, with a new russian president in office, as has just been said, and also with our mandate finally in place to negotiate a new agreement with russia, i think we have an opportunity to redefine this essential partnership with our largest neighbour based on a number of common interests. getting the eu-russia relationship right is one of the most important challenges in european foreign policy: we all know that. the launch of negotiations will be the centrepiece of the first eu-russia summit with president medvedev in khanty-mansiysk at the end of june. right after that the negotiators will begin the first session of their work. the new agreement between the eu and russia gives us the chance to update the legal framework underpinning our relationship so as to reflect the substantial changes in both russia and the european union, because we have changed a lot since the current partnership and cooperation agreement was negotiated in the 1990s. i believe it will also help us to unlock the potential of our relationship, because there is huge potential, and to pursue the interests of our member states much more vigorously. the hallmarks should be: results-orientated political cooperation, deep economic integration, a level playing field for our energy relations enshrining the principles at least of the energy charter treaty, and ever closer relations in the field of freedom, security and justice, as well as a progressive opening of our educational and scientific systems to each other. at the same time, we should continue to implement the cooperation with russia under the four common spaces, which the president-in-office of the council has just mentioned, and their road maps. they indeed comprise a wide range of actions giving concrete expression to this strategic partnership. the new agreement should also provide the legal framework to build on these for the future. the summit will also be an opportunity to hear at first hand where president medvedev sees russia’s priorities with the european union. i think we always have to look to what he has said, for example in an important financial times interview where he said he wants more rule of law in russia and he also wants a greater modernisation of the russian economy. of course, we will judge him by his deeds. while there will certainly be, at the beginning, strong continuity of policies in russia, the new president has stressed his commitment to the rule of law and the modernisation of the russian economy, and i think we should encourage him to match all his words with clear action, and with action that should happen soon. while we pursue our common interests with russia, we must nevertheless remain clear and firm on democracy and human rights. we will continue to remind russia of the commitments that we have both signed up to, notably, for instance, with the council of europe and also the osce. we are often close partners with russia in tackling international challenges, for example as members of the middle east quartet – most probably we will again be in berlin next week – but we also need, as our colleague has said, to see a russia that pursues a positive agenda with its other neighbours; so it is true that we are concerned that recent russian moves in georgia could undermine stability in the region. therefore during my visit to moscow some 10 days ago i had a very long conversation with foreign minister lavrov in which i discussed this important issue. we should gradually establish with russia a continuous high-level non-confrontational dialogue covering all the aspects of conflict resolution, including peace-keeping and peace mechanism aspects, since russia indeed will clearly remain an essential actor in any peace efforts regarding the frozen conflicts. on the other hand, it is natural that tblisi is seriously concerned about maintaining its territorial integrity and in the summit discussion on frozen conflicts we will certainly firmly underline that georgian and ukrainian sovereignty and territorial integrity must be respected; but i think we also need to be pragmatic, realistic and have an inclusive approach from the georgian side. in my regular contacts with both georgia and russia, i am indeed urging pragmatism and an end to the setting of mutually exclusive conditions: these will not work. in conclusion, the eu-russia summit is a chance to embark on a constructive relationship with the new administration, defending our values and promoting our common interests. i look forward to your input and to the discussion in the house. (applause)
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the upcoming eu-russia summit will be the first meeting between eu leaders and the new russian authorities elected after the recent elections. it will therefore be an excellent opportunity to gain a better understanding of russian policy and how it is being pursued. some light on what this policy might look like will be shed by president medvedev's speech in berlin. it contains a number of promising statements on the fight against corruption and the rule of law, except that his predecessor, president putin, made similar statements at the beginning of his presidency, and we know what the reality was and is. but that speech also included a worldview that we might not want. according to her, the european union, or rather the countries of the european union, are reduced to the role of a purely economic partner of russia, which wants to carry out political activities in a much wider space from vancouver to vladivostok. there is another subject worth considering, one that is much more detailed but urgent. it's russia's relationship with georgia. in abkhazia, part of georgia, as a result of the 1994 agreement, russian troops from the mandates of the commonwealth of independent states, i.e. the post-soviet grouping of countries, are stationed. all indications are that they are not peacekeepers, but simply parties to the conflict between abkhaz separatists and the georgian government. the russian aircraft's downing of a georgian unmanned aerial vehicle is a clear indication of this. recently, by a unilateral decision of the russian authorities alone, these forces have been significantly strengthened. in this situation, it would be of the utmost importance that the european union should be involved in the solution of this conflict as a reliable and trustworthy actor.
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. for some time now, we have been witnessing the startling practice of the russian gazprom collecting former prime ministers of european union countries. the best example of this is former german chancellor gerhard schröder, who first signed the nord stream pipeline agreement with russia and then became a member of the company's supervisory board. we're seeing similar moves in southern europe with another russian company's project, the south stream pipeline. i would like to emphasize that none of the western energy companies are as closely tied to the state as gazprom is to the kremlin. with his designs, we are dealing with cold political calculation, when normal market rules simply do not work. it is high time that the european union recognized this and took action to prevent a state-sponsored company from turning the pipeline into a tool of political pressure. russia's energy dominance will inevitably lead to further increases in energy prices in europe. russia will also be able to force even bigger political concessions for gas and oil supplies. the european union must, of course, build a good relationship with russia, but to do so effectively it must show unity, a unity which we do not have at the moment. i would like the forthcoming eu-russia summit to be a demonstration of the european union's solidarity with russia's energy expansion.

the rapporteur. - mr president! - what are you doing? i wanted to welcome to our ranks, in his new capacity, commissioner tajani. commissioner, i voted for you, and i think i did the right thing. the dangerous goods directive updates de facto four commission decisions and brings them together in one legal act. it covers the transport of dangerous goods by inland waterways which has not been subject to union legislation until now. this proposal also transposes into community law international rules on the transport of dangerous goods, but extends them to national transport. we expect to achieve a higher level of safety as a result, as well as improved intermodality for the transport of dangerous goods. i would remind you that parliament adopted 42 amendments at first reading. in those 42 amendments, the essence was that member states which do not have a rail system do not have to transpose and implement this directive. secondly, a transitional period of up to two years was introduced to adapt to the effective application of those provisions. thirdly, the principle has been introduced that member states may lay down specific requirements for the national and international transport of dangerous goods within their territory, taking into account the specific characteristics of both road vehicles, railway wagons and inland waterway vessels. they may also specify routes and special types of transport and lay down rules for the transport of dangerous goods in their territory by passenger trains. the commission and the council agreed to those amendments. the council considered it appropriate to introduce two new amendments. first, an additional paragraph is proposed in article 1 which allows member states to regulate or even prohibit the transport of dangerous goods within their territory for reasons other than safety during transport. and secondly, the council proposes a new paragraph 8 which provides that the commission provides financial support to the member states for the translation into their official languages of the agreements on the international carriage of dangerous goods by road, the international regulations for the carriage of dangerous goods by rail and the 'european agreement concerning the international carriage of dangerous goods by inland waterways'. as rapporteur, i support these two council proposals and i am calling for them to be adopted. in conclusion, i would like to express my great satisfaction with the effective, efficient and very cooperative cooperation with both the commission and the council.

madam president! the challenge of equipping cars with electronic stability control systems and accident notification has become a challenge of the times. there are many reasons for this. the first is the need to improve the safety of vehicle and road users. there are 41,600 fatalities on european roads every year. the loss of health and disability of the next thousands of road users speaks to more than any of us can imagine. the death toll would be much lower if aid reached those in need in time, so the introduction of an accident notification system is another necessary solution. the third important factor that has a major impact on the number of accidents is the state of the roads. road investment is particularly necessary in the new member states and in lagging regions with poor infrastructure. the modernisation and expansion of the road network also requires attention to the surrounding area. roadside trees near the roads are also a major factor in the increase in road deaths. modernity in the automotive industry is not just about the safety of vehicles and people. it also reduces the harmful environmental impact of co2 emissions from cars. it is good that the rapporteur also sees this problem and many other issues. so i give her my full appreciation for a job well done. i can't agree with just the term "intelligent car". i agree with my predecessor, who said in his speech that this concept is reserved for the rational. if we accept this category of thinking, we will arrive at a situation where 'intelligent cars' will be driven by technically competent drivers. and with whom will we then conduct the educational activities so important in the context of improving road safety and using the new achievements of civilization?

mr president, the nord stream baltic pipeline has been a controversial project since the day the former german chancellor took a senior executive position in the company managing the venture. it has raised justified concerns about energy security issues in several countries around the baltic sea. it has become a classic example of the principle of european solidarity gone wrong. there can surely be no doubts regarding the geopolitical importance to russia of the nord stream project. however, it is not these issues we are debating today. today we are discussing another very important aspect of nord stream’s pipeline: its environmental impact. i was, therefore, very surprised that commissioner dimas first stressed the importance of the energy supply and business aspects of the project, only later referring to the environmental impact. i would have expected a different set of priorities from the commissioner for the environment. we all agree that the baltic sea is a unique and fragile environmental environment. numerous experts share the concerns of petitioners and are rightly suspicious of an environmental impact report penned by nord stream’s experts. please note that the very countries around the baltic sea which feel the non-environmental threats of the pipeline most keenly will also suffer any environmental damage directly. adoption of amendments that play down the environmental threats will, frankly speaking, add insult to injury.
mr. chairman, please! the northern gas pipeline and the european union's approach to the northern gas pipeline is for me a test of the quality of the european community, of whether the european union is really acting on the principle of solidarity. it's also a test of environmental attitudes. if in much smaller projects with much less risk to nature and people, several alternative projects are required to choose the most optimal one, then in this powerful project, which can potentially be a strong risk not only to nature but also to people, the more should the designers be asked to choose several alternative solutions and only from these few alternative solutions should the most beneficial and least harmful to people and the environment be chosen. it's strange that with this huge project, such a road was abandoned.
mr. chairman, please! the planned northern gas pipeline, linking russia and germany, is set to be the longest undersea two-channel gas pipeline in the world, and also the shallowest, making it particularly vulnerable to damage. there is no doubt that the scale of long-term works in the vast baltic sea area poses a serious threat to the natural environment, biodiversity and habitat, to the safety and smoothness of navigation and, in the event of an ecological disaster, to the health of the baltic sea region's population. under the espoo convention and due to the serious environmental risks, alternative pipeline routes that do not affect the marine environment, in this case onshore pipeline routes, should be considered as a priority. the investment in the baltic sea is not a bilateral matter between germany and russia, because in the event of an ecological disaster all the baltic states will suffer. such a major project should only be undertaken in the spirit of european solidarity and with the agreement of all the baltic states after a thorough and independent environmental impact assessment of the pipeline has been carried out.

infrastructure projects. however, both the environmental impact and the opinions of the public and the environmental authorities are the subject of the environmental impact assessment, which is chemicals needed to treat the pipeline before it is put into operation. the report also contains a list of substances that may be used in the manufacture of certain chemicals. however, it appears that exist. other chemicals are likely to be used. but it does mean that we must wait for the completion of the environmental impact assessment process, as provided for by law, to be able to discuss compliance with community legislation and policy, the impacts, the risks, the measures and to decide on the conditions to be imposed on the project owner. the transparency requirements foreseen in the environmental impact assessment process ensure that all interested parties, including the european parliament, will have access to all relevant information. it is interesting that from many quarters today it was heard that the commission should have more powers either to make environmental impact studies or to enforce various policies. the commission has specific responsibilities; has neither the means nor the competence for studies and environmental assessment studies; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. the role of the commission, as stated in the treaty, is to ensure that member states correctly apply and fully respect all the rules of community law, including international agreements ratified by the community. the commission may only intervene if it has serious grounds for believing that there have been breaches of relevant legal obligations under community law, including european union environmental law. at present, there is no indication of this, as the environmental impact assessment process is still ongoing. i can assure you that the commission will not hesitate to intervene whenever necessary. finally, i can only reiterate here that the commission expects the member states to comply fully with their obligations under community law. this is a basic condition for any final approval decision. i thank you again and i thank mr libicki for his report and for the opportunity he has given us to discuss this very important issue of the pipeline and the environmental impact it people in their efforts to build a stable and democratic state, and these tragic events demonstrate the importance and urgency of our discussions this morning. the council, like parliament, is convinced of the need for a long-term commitment in afghanistan. our aim must be to help the government develop the structures of a modern and democratic state that can function and ensure the security of its citizens, respect the rule of law and promote economic and social development. i have to say that the combined efforts of the afghan authorities and the international community have relations between afghanistan and its neighbours is essential for the lasting stabilisation of that country, given, of course, the multidimensional nature of certain problems that mr brie has highlighted, in particular the production and trafficking of drugs. in any event, these few comments on the report presented by parliament cannot hide the very close general agreement between the council and parliament on the policy to be pursued in afghanistan, and i take this opportunity to welcome and encourage the initiative presented in mr brie's report, which aims at strengthening cooperation between the european parliament and the afghan parliament. for all these reasons, the union will continue to act and play a major role in mobilising the international community in support mr. chairman, please! the european union's approach to energy problems is full of contradictions. we are hearing more and more calls for coherent, joint, long-term cooperation and strategy, and at the same time, more and more examples of uncoordinated actions, piecemeal proposals, investments that serve the interests of some at the expense of others. the reports presented are an attempt to put the problem in order or to draw attention to underestimated issues and dilemmas. the rapporteur should therefore be commended. the world has never seen a case in history of a second commodity whose price would rise as much as oil and gas prices in such a short period of time. so it's safe to say that there was a mistake in predicting what would happen. there is no doubt, then, that this economic dilemma must be solved in two ways. first, by increasing the supply of energy resources, including new, more efficient energy sources, and second, by slowing down the growth of demand through new, more energy-efficient technologies. the european union must be effective in this respect and must not allow the privilege of a monopoly access to raw materials or a capital advantage to determine the market situation. that is why access to the gas transmission network, research into new technologies, new agencies are useful proposals. today, time is of the essence, and therefore urgent action and implementation is needed. therefore, the threat to climate stability posed by co2 emissions should be re-examined by scientists for its validity, lest it be found that reducing emissions will only benefit a select few, and mainly the companies, and not consumers, while destroying hard coal.
acting president of the council. - mr president, i thank you for allowing me to speak, because i am obliged to leave you to take a train because of very heavy agenda constraints. i would first like to thank the european commission and the members for this interesting debate and for all the work that has been done on this 'internal energy market' package. as many of you have noted, the adoption of this package will have direct consequences for the lives of our fellow citizens. we are dealing with a subject which expresses the expectations of europeans. it seems to me that the improvements our citizens expect can come from two directions. the first is the need for consistency in the rules and mechanisms applied in the european union, to which this package will contribute. the second is the need for clarity and readability for market players and consumers. in the case of the latter, annexes a to the directives must be transposed by the member states in particular. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the consumer is informed and that their concerns are heard, and that the situation of vulnerable consumers is of course better understood. but the work is not yet done. there are still points of convergence to be found, particularly for the application of effective separation not only to gas, since our positions are already quite close, but also to electricity. the french presidency will give concrete form to the general orientation of 6 june at the energy council on 10 october. only then, on 10 october, will we have a stable position from the council. we still need to work on the third country clause in particular so that the concerns of all member states are taken into account. the presidency will then forward its common position to the european parliament so that the internal market package can be completed by the end of the parliamentary term; that's what we're trying to do. i hope that our joint efforts will be rewarded in a constructive spirit and in a spirit of compromise between all our institutions.
mr. chairman, please! each plan should include decisions that are both temporal and spatial, but the current commission decisions hamper the implementation of earlier ones, e.g. the market holds back the plans for investments in cogeneration, as it is not profitable to convert the plants into efficient plants, which are burdened with emissions purchases and network problems. the commission also divides the eu countries into better countries that can increase emissions and worse countries that must reduce them. the latter, of course, are mainly central and eastern european countries. under the kyoto protocol, the reference year for counting emissions in the ets should be the 1990s, not the 2005 imposed by the commission. it would be both fairer and more supportive. leadership in the area of climate change cannot be at the expense of poor communities. efficiency and savings should be the priority, and renewable energy should be seen as a complement, not an alternative. the future is clean coal in the medium term and nuclear energy in the long term, as we have seen.
mr. chairman, please! the regulations discussed here are intended to facilitate the integration of national gas markets and to enhance enforcement at european level. the gas market should be considered separately from the electricity market, given the european union's high import dependency. ownership unbundling can be a highly effective instrument for ensuring the creation of a single gas market in the european union and the emergence of fair competition in the union energy market and can, as a result, lead to lower or at least stabilised energy prices. however, caution is in order. the process of market liberalisation requires specific structural changes, for which not all eu countries are prepared. market liberalisation and ownership unbundling in poland, without introducing them by the main energy producers in the union, may give western european companies an advantage over polish ones. europe needs an energy model that not only ensures competitiveness in regional markets and the european single market, but also guarantees the protection of the final consumer and, above all, energy security.
mr. chairman, please! one of the fundamental issues to be addressed is the problem of guaranteeing the security of supply of raw materials. energy policy must take into account the fact that the potential for diversification of gas import sources varies considerably from one country to another. the fact is that they have different possibilities of obtaining and purchasing this raw material. i have already stressed on many occasions the need to develop a coherent energy policy that will ensure the energy security of the individual member states. the measures to implement ownership unbundling in the natural gas market will certainly improve the competitiveness and quality of the services provided. however, given the wide diversity of gas and energy markets, i support the rapporteur's proposal that these sectors should be regulated separately. the gas market will only be truly competitive if customers have full access to information on their natural gas consumption levels and the possibility to switch suppliers.
rapporteur. − madam president, i thank all my colleagues for the discussion – it was a very good, very deep discussion – especially the shadow rapporteurs and all the colleagues who prepared opinions in other committees. i congratulate both rapporteurs, mr paparizov and mr la russa. i entirely support your reports – and of course i support my report as well, but i am probably not very objective on that. as you can see from the discussion there is not much controversy on the set plan, but there is one thing on which i should like an answer. adina-ioana vălean is not in favour of the ccs installations – the ccs commercial demonstration installations – because the companies we would like to support are doing business. i would like to give an example. the same companies receive enormous incentives from citizens’ taxes for renewables. there are also commercial renewable installations and companies are doing business – nothing else – and i very strongly support these incentives for renewables. if you really want to solve the climate change problem on our planet we must solve the ccs question because we do not know the true answer for that. so from that point of view, as in the case of renewables, we should also have incentives for the first movers on ccs. i give my thanks and congratulations to both commissioners. you are doing great work on the energy issue, as well as on r&d and innovation.
in writing. mr president, europe's fundamental weakness in its relations with russia is the lack of a common, free energy market. there are now several energy hubs scattered across europe, each managed by national regulators. it is natural that the efforts of national governments to secure cheap energy and jobs in the sector are given priority. however, in this way, divided by national egoism, we lose to gazprom's energy offensive in europe. an integrated european market and a supportive attitude towards non-eu suppliers can ensure our energy security even before we diversify our energy supply. so far, the eu's failure to create a liquid and competitive energy market has been relentlessly exploited by the russians. opening the european internal gas market to competition leads to greater efficiency and strengthens the rights of consumers and national regulators. the creation of a kind of interconnected vessel system will make it easier for individual member states to respond to energy supply crises and thus reduce the threat of energy blackmail. we must stop russian companies from expanding into europe and force russia to reciprocate in its treatment of energy investments. i fully agree with the rapporteur that member states should promote the integration of national markets and cooperation between network operators at european and regional level.
in writing. the liberalisation of the natural gas sector is a very important part of the attempt to create a common internal energy market. the natural gas market is currently dominated by large companies, which often control the production and distribution of gas. a well-functioning internal energy market is essential for achieving the objectives of the lisbon strategy, but also for ensuring affordable prices for energy consumers. in this debate, however, we should not forget the energy security that must be ensured by diversifying the supply of imported energy resources. this does not mean that the energy market is the same in every area. the natural gas market is indeed significantly different from the electricity market and it is therefore not possible for the regulations resulting from the work on the regulation of the electricity sector to be transposed into the regulation of the natural gas sector. the real liberalisation of the natural gas market should be based on the ownership unbundling of transmission system operators, only then will we avoid unnecessary conflicts of interest and fair and non-discriminatory access to the network. in order to ensure a level playing field in the common energy market, investors from third countries should be subject to the same criteria as regards ownership and independence as companies from member states, and we should emphasise this very strongly. i hope that the european market will soon be an open market, where the activities related to the supply and production of energy are effectively separated from the operation of the grid, resulting in greater transparency in the operation of the market.

in writing. − a regulation adopted by the european parliament transforms the rules governing the provision of air services within the community, to the benefit of both air carriers and passengers. the regulation is important for the proper functioning of the internal market. it creates a more competitive environment for european airlines to compete with their international competitors. it will create a level playing field in the award and withdrawal of concessions, which should eliminate the distortions of competition that exist on the market, caused by, inter alia, divergent rules on concession requirements, discrimination against certain eu carriers on grounds of nationality or discrimination in the operation of routes to third countries. however, the consumer should be the main beneficiary of the changes. the need to include all taxes and surcharges in air fares will strengthen price transparency and the principle of voluntary surcharges. this will eliminate the exposure of consumers to higher tariffs and will result in more informed consumer decision-making. in addition, the inability of financially uncertain airlines to continue their operations will eliminate the risk of financial risk for passengers in the event of the bankruptcy of the air carrier.

on paper. as the representative of a country that joined the eu in 2004, i fully support all of the elements of elmar brok's report which underline the importance of successive enlargements and their positive impact on building a strong, cohesive, citizen-friendly and prosperous europe. i agree with the statement that the prospect of eu membership, which is already recognised, has a very positive effect on the internal policies of the candidate countries, encouraging them to speed up the restructuring of their administrations, reform their education and higher education systems, pay more attention to respect for human rights, including minority rights, combat the pathologies of public life, in short, adopt the values that have long guided the european union. i also believe that the report should emphasise even more the openness of the european union and its readiness to welcome new member states. this is particularly important for my country, poland, especially in the context of the expectations and european aspirations of our eastern neighbours, mainly ukraine. it would be very bad if our neighbours perceived our eastern border (the schengen border for the whole eu) as a new wall that permanently separates them from us. the views sometimes expressed in this context that further enlargements of the union should be conditional on its so-called 'absorption capacity' are therefore highly ill-considered and, consequently, dangerous to the objectives the eu sets itself.

in writing the prospect of eu membership is thus a driving force for change in the countries concerned. it calls for the necessary political and economic reforms to be carried out and for the copenhagen criteria to be met. for the prospect of membership to be credible, on the one hand, progress in the negotiations must depend on the pace and scale of reforms in the candidate country. on the other hand, we need the union's capacity to accept these countries, we need a strong and cohesive community, and above all a community of solidarity. it is very important that the citizens of our countries see the benefits of the accession of new countries. enlargement brings benefits, economic and social development to both new and old member states. the successive enlargements of the european union have been a success. the success of the acceding and the existing member states. the success of europe. i am very pleased that the report emphasises that the eastern european countries still have an open path to membership of the european union. this, together with the recently adopted eastern partnership programme, should encourage them to make efforts to move closer to european democratic, economic and administrative standards.
in writing. previous enlargements of the european union have undoubtedly benefited both the union itself and the countries that have acceded to it, and have contributed to stimulating economic growth and strengthening stability, development and prosperity in europe. it is very important to create the conditions necessary to ensure the success of future enlargements, to improve their quality on the basis of the experience gained in the past. the eu must be open to new countries, but the enlargement strategy should comply with the eu treaty and reflect its commitments to all candidate and prospective member states, with full and rigorous compliance with the copenhagen criteria as an absolute condition. at the same time, we should closely monitor the progress of these countries in building the rule of law, an independent judiciary and respect for fundamental rights. the union must take action to increase its capacity to welcome new countries. the necessary internal reforms are needed to increase efficiency, social cohesion and democratic accountability. the lisbon treaty is the answer to these requirements, and without it, further enlargement of the union becomes very difficult. at the same time, however, the success of the eu's political integration process can only be achieved if there is clear and lasting public support for eu membership in each of the candidate countries and for the union itself as an economic and political project.
in writing. we like to say that the european parliament is the only real place where the views of the citizens of the union can be expressed. it is a pity, then, that this is the only place where we can convince each other that the enlargement of the european union is a great success. it's all our fault that not everyone in the community has the same opinion. this in turn leads to a lack of understanding of the need to reform the union. however, i cannot accept the argument that the absence of the lisbon treaty is the main reason for the impeding of enlargement policy. the treaty itself doesn't solve anything. it takes vision and strategy. the european union will not be a political and geographical entity until all european countries are in it. it is not true that citizens of countries wishing to join the union expect it to happen immediately or in a very short time. but they need a clear signal that there is a place for them here. without this declaration, it is difficult to expect them to undertake the effort of comprehensive reforms that involve much sacrifice and hard work. we cannot forget the europeans from the balkans and eastern europe. the european neighbourhood policy is a good instrument for regulating cooperation with the countries neighbouring our continent. the european union's neighbours, on the other hand, have a right to expect a more clear and effective cooperation policy, one that does not lead to more lobbies or waiting rooms. if so much energy is being devoted to the creation of a mediterranean union, which is particularly supported by france, then at least the same energy should be devoted to the creation of euronest.

question no 45 by paulo casaca (h-0479/08) subject: execution of the perpetrator of an attack on the united nations according to the enewsletter hands off cain, no 107 of 6 june, leandro despouy, the united nations special rapporteur on the independence of judges and lawyers, has reaffirmed the un’s belief that the iraqi authorities' execution of awraz abdel aziz mahmoud sa’eed for carrying out the attack on the un headquarters in baghdad in august 2003 – which killed, amongst others, sérgio vieira de mello, un special representative for iraq – prevented the international community from learning who the real perpetrators of the crime had been. what steps did the commission take to voice the eu’s blanket opposition to the death penalty? what measures is the commission intending to take to clarify the reasons underlying the speed with which awraz abdel aziz mahmoud sa’eed was executed, despite the express requests made by the united nations, which legitimately wanted to discover the underlying reason for the attack on the un and identify the organisers thereof?
member of the commission. − mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european commission, together with the member states, is the leading institutional actor and donor in the fight against the death penalty worldwide. its work in this area is a key priority of the eu's external human rights policy. the general principles for the policy of the european union towards third countries on the death penalty, adopted in 1998 and revised in 2008, set out the criteria for issuing demarches and the standards to be used. the abolition of the death penalty is one of the main thematic priorities for assistance under the european instrument for democracy and human rights. since 1994, the commission has funded some 30 projects worldwide with a total budget of approximately eur 15 million. commissioner ferrero-waldner spoke out categorically against the death penalty, whether in practice or in law, in a public statement on 10 october 2007, on the occasion of the world day against the death penalty and on subsequent occasions. the event referred to in the honourable member's letter is known to the commission. iraq is one of the countries to which the european commission sends frequent demarches on the death penalty. in the present case, the demarche was sent in june 2007. the european union and the commission have repeatedly called on the iraqi government, including the supreme court, to abandon the use of the death penalty and to commute all death sentences handed down and not executed. they also called on the iraqi government to immediately impose a moratorium on all executions. it goes without saying that in the case of the bombing of the un complex on 19 august 2003, such a moratorium would have allowed for a full cross-examination of all persons who could provide any evidence necessary to ensure that none of the perpetrators of the attack would go unpunished. the commission is of course concerned by the haste with which the case was handled. but our main goal is to advocate for the universal abolition of the death penalty. the commission continues to work closely with the member states of the european union in an effort to interpret our position and concerns towards the iraqi side.
member of the commission. - the european commission and the european union are exploring all the options available to us in order to strengthen our capacity to gradually eliminate and reduce the use of the death penalty, particularly in the areas where it is most frequently used, including iraq.
question no 46 by claude moraes (h-0427/08) subject: anti-discrimination horizontal directive the european commission announced that this spring would see the launch of the new horizontal directive prohibiting discrimination. what is the latest development regarding the scope of the directive? will there be a far-reaching anti-discrimination directive including all of the remaining grounds of article 13 of the amsterdam treaty – namely age, disability, religion or belief, and sexual orientation, as supported by a majority in the european parliament? if not, could the european commission give its reasons, and outline its detailed plan of action for the coming months?
member of the commission. mr president, madam member, ladies and gentlemen, last week the commission adopted a proposal for a directive prohibiting discrimination on grounds of age, disability, sexual orientation and religion or belief outside the labour market. discrimination on these grounds in employment is already covered by directive 2078/ec. we have therefore fulfilled the commitment we made to you at the beginning of our term of office and we have heard your repeated calls, lastly at the may part-session, to put forward such a proposal. this proposal for a directive builds on principles already adopted by the member states under existing directives. it includes, for example, provisions to ensure the protection of victims of discrimination and to deal with harassment and bullying, but also provisions on the establishment of equality bodies. as i have already said, the proposal for a directive deals with discrimination on the basis of four grounds of discrimination, but the fact that we put all these grounds on an equal footing does not mean that the provisions for all these types of discrimination are the same. the draft directive therefore takes account of the specific characteristics of each type of discrimination in order to make the directive as effective as possible. in particular, it allows, depending on the context, to take age into account, and to take age and disability into account in the insurance and banking department, to the extent that this is appropriate and justified, but i emphasise the words appropriate and justified. this should not be an arbitrary exclusion of the elderly or disabled from these services. in the case of disability, the principle of equal treatment implies a positive commitment to ensure universal access for disabled persons and, in individual cases, to make appropriate adjustments. these measures do not represent a disproportionate burden, and the proposal for a directive clearly states that account should be taken of the size, type and resources of the organisation, the estimated costs, the lifetime of goods and services and the likely benefits of disabled access. this proposal represents an important step towards filling a large gap in the legal system for protection against discrimination. we are aware, however, that protection against discrimination based on sex is still not as strong outside the workplace as it is in the case of racial discrimination. directive 2004/113/ec does not cover the field of education, as can be read in the explanatory memorandum to this proposal. we believe that it would be premature to propose an amendment to that directive, as the deadline for its implementation has only recently expired. but in 2010, when we report on the implementation of the directive, we can propose an amendment if necessary.
member of the commission. - it is clear that a directive of this kind, which is fundamental and protects the fundamental values of the european union, the european community, is viewed from a number of angles and that there is, of course, frequent pressure to limit its effectiveness for a variety of reasons. the commission is aware of this, which is why we have tabled this comprehensive proposal and we are of course prepared to defend it against any unjustified objections in the further discussion.
member of the commission. − in general, the directive protecting workers in the labour market also protects them against age discrimination. i cannot comment specifically on the statement in the british press, because it always depends on the specific circumstances of the case, but i can say in principle that the directive has no exceptions in this respect, it has no exceptions that protection no longer applies from a certain age.
