member of the commission. - i can only say that mr crowley has, in a few words, made a fairly perfect analysis of the problem. yes, that's exactly what it is. and that's why we're staying active. this is not a closed question for the commission.
member of the commission. you are absolutely right, the council's deliberations are deliberations on any fundamental political consideration and they are not secret deliberations. the opinion of all the member states was gradually formulated, with the exception of the federal republic of germany. that is the situation, but it does not mean that, as i said, we are not at the end of the road and will look for other ways and options to reach unanimity. i want to emphasize that the systems in the member states are of course different and that the decision on them is not a technical matter of secondary importance, so i fully understand that the member states are taking this matter seriously, but as i said, this is the situation at the moment.
question no 48 by robert evans (h-0443/08) subject: medical support across the eu can the commission clarify exactly what entitlements to medical support eu citizens have when travelling to another member state? does the support provided by the european health insurance card apply to all age-related illnesses? as the methods of financing health services vary from member state to member state, what procedures are in place to enable a fair and equitable system that provides proper support for all those in need? what arrangements are in place for those travelling to tax havens such as andorra, the channel islands, lichtenstein, etc., which are surrounded by the eu but are not themselves deemed eu territory?
member of the commission. − if you have mr president, madam member, ladies and gentlemen, the holder of a european health insurance card is considered to be insured under the legal system of the member state to which he has travelled. in accordance with article 22 of regulation no 1408/71, this card is valid for temporary residence for any purpose: tourism, employment or study. if the holder requires medical care during the stay, the card shall allow such care to be provided by medical professionals. the healthcare covered by the european health insurance card is 'essential healthcare'. this term, which depends on the patient's state of health and the expected duration of the stay, was defined by the administrative commission on social security for migrant workers in 2004. this is the treatment that must be provided to a person temporarily staying in the territory of another state in order not to put his life in danger and at the same time not to be forced to return prematurely to his country in order to provide the necessary medical assistance. in any case, these criteria must be used by the healthcare professionals depending on the patient's medical condition and the length of the patient's stay. the administrative commission on social security for migrant workers has also adopted guidelines to ensure that the term is interpreted in a uniform way by all stakeholders (healthcare providers, insurers and health insurance companies). these guidelines are available on the europa portal. a pensioner spending three months with his children or a student using the erasmus programme will thus have access not only to emergency healthcare but also to care that would be available to persons residing in the same situation in the member state concerned. the system of access to health care, as laid down in article 22 of regulation no 1408/71, provides for access to and payment for health care in accordance with the legislation of the state in which the patient is staying. it follows that persons who are temporarily resident in a state have access to healthcare in that state under the same conditions as persons who are part of the health insurance system of that state. article 22 of regulation no 1408/71 also applies to the states of the european economic area, including liechtenstein and switzerland. as regards andorra, the ongoing negotiations have not yet been successfully concluded.
member of the commission. - you have asked a number of questions which clearly require a comprehensive answer, but i would simply answer the first question as follows: this morning we discussed regulation 883, which will be a substantial amendment to regulation 1408 and will undoubtedly improve the situation for many people, particularly in terms of crossborder contact. if you've opened up the question of medical tourism, i think it's a term that is very open and it's so open that it's dangerous. it is necessary to clarify very carefully what this is, because it is a concept that can take on a special significance in our view, although in reality, in my opinion, genuine medical tourism is very limited, because in most cases, when people are really suffering, they try to be in their immediate environment and the systems of the various member states do not differ substantially in their basic level. it is clear, of course, that regulation 1408 and future regulation 883 deal mainly with the huge amount of cases which are related to tourism, but not to medical tourism, because they concern people who have gone primarily somewhere else and something happened to them on the way. that's hundreds of thousands and millions, maybe even about a million cases a year, and it's a thing that's being handled quite well and doesn't compromise the stability of health systems. as for the commission's will to improve matters in this area, that will is obvious and one of the proofs is also the amendments tabled by my colleague, mrs andrulla vassillia. i think this will be an opportunity to discuss in great detail the possibilities of crossborder care and the other aspects that are associated with it, but let me once again express a considerable distance from the concept of medical tourism or medical tourism, because in my opinion it is a very poorly defined concept that can provoke reactions that are not adequate to the situation.
i would like to inform you that the time limit for questions to be put to commissioner špidla has expired. the answers to questions 49 to 54 will be sent to the members in writing.
question no 55 by eoin ryan (h-0439/08) subject: reporting burden of small and medium enterprises i welcome the recent initiative taken by the commission to reduce the statistical reporting burden on businesses, especially small and medium enterprises. however smes still face large reporting burdens, such as vat reporting, that cost many man-hours and that put small businesses at a competitive disadvantage. does the commission have any proposals in the pipeline that will reduce red tape and the reporting burden for smes?
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, i have to say something. i am very grateful to you, mr president, for this question, because it deals with a problem which has been the subject of intense attention by the commission for many years: how can we avoid unnecessary bureaucratic burdens on small and mediumsized enterprises in europe? and i'm very happy to tell you that we have indeed made tremendous progress in this field, and that i firmly believe we are on the verge of a real breakthrough. we have identified bureaucratic costs for european companies as essentially those arising from reporting, documentation and information obligations. we are now in the midst of the largest action of this kind in history to actually measure these costs, to actually look at the costs of these regulations in the companies, so that we can identify where the costs are coming from and whether we can reduce them. so you can expect, mr president, that from about september this year onwards, the commission will be making a large number of proposals, based on the results of the measurements and the screening of all the existing rules. our expectation is that this will enable us to make so many proposals to you by the end of 2009 that the bureaucratic costs for european businesses will be reduced by 25% in 2012. we expect this to result in a growth spurt of between 1.4 and 1.5% of the total gross national product of europe. so you see, we're really talking about significant scales here. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. of the normal costs of bureaucracy, namely the burden imposed on small businesses in particular by tax requirements - you know that the european union's powers are extremely limited here - i can tell you that we know from all our research that the burden imposed by the requirements of the financial authorities is by far the most important and strongest for companies themselves, so that the member states are really called upon to simplify. we have only a very limited competence in the area of turnover taxes. the commission has, however, made a very important proposal which would be of great help to small and mediumsized enterprises, namely to raise more significantly the threshold above which vat pre-registration must be made. the threshold is currently set at eur 20 000, but we want to raise it to eur 100 000, so that almost all very small businesses, and above all newly created ones, will be relieved of this heavy burden. i regret to say that the member states have not been ready to accept this proposal. i hope that the small business act, which the commission has put forward a few days ago, when we have raised the subject again, will increase the pressure on those member states which are having difficulties here, and i am extremely grateful to the european parliament for the support which it has already signalled on this point on several occasions.
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, as i said, this is an official proposal which the commission adopted back in 2004. and since 2004 this proposal has not been adopted by the council. i have pointed out that we have now renewed the proposal in connection with the small business act, we are practically putting it back on the table now. this is not an announcement; the commission has already proposed this. she thinks it's necessary. mr špidla has already pointed out in another reply that unanimity is required on certain questions. we have the requirement of unanimity here too, and unfortunately it could not be achieved. but i do not need to tell you, as the representative of ireland, that for a number of member states taxation in the european union is a taboo.
i'm not going to let you do this. i have a favor to ask. if all these studies are done, what are the costs of doing business for small and medium-sized businesses? if you could look at this world bank report, which was about two years ago, that indicated these costs. it shows that poland, for example, has very low legal costs, which turns out not to be true. i have a request about that, because that's not a question. can you not look at what the officials are saying and officially look at the actual cost? all the stamps that have to be paid for, every letter that's filed. there's a lot of extra work to do.
vice-president of the commission. − the measurement project we are currently carrying out and which is about to be completed will give us precise information on which european regulations cause which costs. we will be able to say quite precisely: this specific european regulation is causing these and those costs for businesses. we already know a lot of things. we know, for example, that most of the costs come from a very small number of regulations. there are only about 42 directives, from which the vast majority of the regulations originate. we also know the area which is causing the greatest costs, namely european company law, and that is why we have already made the first proposals in this area. we also know that the costs vary greatly depending on the size of the companies. and we can assume as a rule of thumb that the smaller a company is, the greater the relative burden of bureaucratic costs. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the task of drawing up a report on the implementation of the directive. but we know all this already and it will be taken into account in the proposals. i would like to take this opportunity to ask parliament: the success of the whole operation will of course depend very much on parliament's swift consideration of the commission's proposals. there is a general political agreement on this, and i would just like to remind you that these are all amendments to existing legislation, which therefore require the agreement of the two co-legislators.
question no 56 by colm burke (h-0448/08) subject: price of fertiliser the price of fertiliser has gone up dramatically over the last 12 months. ammonia phosphate, for instance, has increased from eur 181 per tonne to eur 800 per tonne in wholesale markets. does the commission plan to take any action to counteract this price hike?
vice-president of the commission. - mr. deputy, i have to go. i share your concern about the development of fertiliser prices. these prices have indeed increased disproportionately. this is understandably causing great problems and great concern to european agriculture. the increase in fertiliser prices is due to a strong increase in demand, and this higher demand is associated with higher transport and energy costs. so there are three factors: higher demand due to rapid growth in other parts of the world, higher energy prices and higher transportation costs. the increase in demand is a worldwide phenomenon, as you know, affecting not only fertilisers but also a whole range of other goods, including crops and food. it's important to remember that. because it is true that european farmers have to spend more money on fertilisers. they do. but they also get higher prices for their crops. fao statistics for a comparable period show that food prices have increased by 37% over 12 months. the most significant increases were in milk products, 80 to 200%, and in cereals, 50 to 80%. the commission considers that compliance with the competition rules is crucial. as long as this is the case, the commission does not consider it appropriate to intervene in a market whose recent development is largely due to factors beyond the commission's control. once again, we have no influence on the three decisive factors which have led to price developments. with a view to longer-term developments, the commission also stresses the importance of promoting competition in the natural gas market. i see here an opportunity to relax a little. if the measures proposed by the commission are adopted under the third energy package, we should get cheaper prices on the gas market. and this could also lead to a fall in the prices of nitrogen fertilisers produced in the european union. but you know that all depends on the adoption of the energy package proposed by the commission.
vice-president of the commission. − as regards russia and ukraine as important suppliers, i must point out that we have trade protection instruments in place for both countries concerning the export of fertilisers from ukraine and russia. and quite simply, both of them can of course offer the fertiliser at a very low price because, as you know, the energy used in the production of this product is particularly high, and in ukraine and russia there are different prices for the energy exported and for the energy used in the country itself. this price difference leads to dumping. and because of this dumping, we have measures in place against russia and ukraine. the commission has little influence on the diversification of supplies. i can tell you from my experience that the major european producers and distributors are naturally seeking to diversify their raw material base. i am prepared to look at this question in particular again.
vice-president of the commission. - mrs fischer boel is here, so i will answer very carefully, because she is actually responsible for the question of the prices that european farmers can achieve. i have assumed from what the honourable member has reported to the commission so far that producer prices are indeed rising for all the major products in the european union. i do not, however, exclude the possibility that you are right in saying that the higher income does not in all cases fully compensate for the increased costs. this is a point which the commission will certainly look into. as regards the overall development of the food sector - we are not just talking about producer prices here, we are also concerned about what the consumer ends up paying in the store - we have just launched an initiative a few weeks ago and set up a high level group to look at the future of the european food industry, which, by the way, is not well known, but is the largest industry in europe. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. in this high level group we are dealing very specifically with price developments and will be able to complete the work by the end of the year and make recommendations accordingly.

vice-president of the commission. - madam president, i am very grateful for your support. i knew it. i knew i could count on you. you can count on me, too. as regards the question of network density, i must admit that we have not yet reached the density we want to achieve throughout europe. but in the final stage of expansion, which we will reach over the next five months, all regions in europe will be covered by these facilities. there will be contact points in all regions, so close to the enterprises that it will not be difficult for anyone to reach these contact points.

the commission is now debating the proposal for a council regulation establishing a temporary special measure to support the restructuring of the european union's fishing fleets affected by the economic crisis (commission fisheries) (com (2008) 0454 - c6-0270/2008 - 2008/0144 (cns)).
member of the commission. − mr president, thank you very much for all those interventions and for the number of questions that have been placed. i will try to respond to as many of them as i can given the fact that we did not have sufficient time as we usually have within the fisheries committee and in plenary to discuss proposals given the urgent nature of this proposal. on de minimis, as we said in the communication, we will be carrying out the necessary economic analyses in the coming weeks and months and we intend to come forward with a commission proposal, if appropriate, if the economic analysis shows that we can move forward in this direction and if wto rules allow, before the end of this year. the subsequent, quite lengthy procedure involving consultation of the advisory committee of member states and of stakeholders, and the final adoption by the commission will normally take around six months. so we are speaking of a time frame which is quite extensive, it is true. however, i need to underline that the de minimis is not the solution to the restructuring of the fleet which is needed. whether we like it or not we have a situation of significant over-capacity, and unless we address it effectively we are never going to find a permanent solution. it is no use, i have said it on a number of occasions, throwing money at the problem without trying to address the real cause of the problem, and this is what we are attempting to do. we are willing to give assistance immediately and in the medium term to fishers but we are also stressing that there needs to be effective restructuring. otherwise we will need to come back here, year in year out, to discuss the same issue. so i need to make this abundantly clear: the commission is not prepared simply to throw money at the problem. so any form of permanent operating gate to fishers is a non-starter. this is why i need to make it abundantly clear that we need to really address the problem. so that is my answer on de minimis, which we are looking into. concerning market measures, we will be providing more specifics and making the situation much clearer, because there are various fronts on which we intend to deliver on this. first of all we will be making more financing available for pos and other industry associations in order to elaborate fishing plans, marketing plans, quality initiatives, labelling initiatives and inter-branch initiatives. and, as shown in other countries, for example in norway, we can see how pos can work efficiently to assist the catching sector. as we indicated in our communication, these are not new tools or instruments. they are outlined extensively in both the cmo and in the eff. the problem is that, so far, industry and member states have not promoted them sufficiently. with regard to the price monitoring system, again, together with the industry and the member states we will use this additional knowledge to set up monitoring tools along the value chain to help the sector to anticipate price developments more effectively in the future. the commission has launched a study on this issue which will be completed in september. there is political momentum on this issue on a wider level. the recent european summit has supported wider initiatives of the commission for monitoring food prices and price development mechanisms. again, additional funding for a price monitoring system on fish prices will be made available by the budgetary authorities by september. we will start the work immediately, first through launching a pilot project on the scope and modalities of this exercise, and the full price monitoring system should then be defined and become operational before the end of 2009.concerning more control with respect to certification, labelling requirements and mitigating ieu, here again, the commission will give financial support to industry initiatives in the area of market monitoring, and in particular in relation to monitoring the sector’s compliance with legal requirements concerning certification, labelling etc. we plan to launch calls for proposals by the end of 2008 whereby we would invite sectoral organisations to elaborate concrete proposals, and implementation of these projects will start during 2009. then in 2009 we also have the full cmo review. so i will try to give some indicative time-frames with regard to the various market measures that we are envisaging. on the question of the reference period raised by both mrs fraga and mrs doyle, i can repeat again that the preliminary assessment of this suggestion indicates that we can take this on board. we realise that the fuel situation has changed considerably since 2007 and it does seem logical that current realities should be reflected in the aim of this package. we will nevertheless need to ensure that all economic data used for the reference period 2007 to 2008 are an accurate depiction of the economic situation for the fleet and vessels concerned. the mandatory 30% capacity reduction will still be maintained. the possible impact of using the 2008 figures could indirectly lead to more extensive application of the package. so i can confirm that we will be moving forward and taking on board this suggestion that came from the fisheries committee this morning. concerning the point as to whether the proposal attacks the causes of the problem, i would state my belief that in fact there are two primary objectives: tackling over-capacity, as i have just said, so that we can survive in a profitable way long into the future, and also trying to assist fishers to get a fair price for their catch. i have just outlined the measures that we are proposing in this regard. with regard to the question, raised by general morillon, concerning measures which should not be implemented to the detriment of those who have already undergone restructuring, and with regard to the point raised by mr allister and mrs attwooll and others, these are very relevant. i would like to say that in general terms, if there is further reduction of capacity by some member states, this will benefit other member states, because if there is a reduction of capacity with a consequent reduction of effort, there would be more resources and more market opportunities. however, more specifically let me say that the proposed ad hoc instrument to which i will come to soon will be designed in such a way as to set criteria that are needs-based and do not follow the eff so that, for example, the requirements of those who have already undertaken substantial restructurings are recognised and that those who have low eff allocations are also recognised. on the question of social aid, first of all we have to see how this measure will be defined in practice. to the extent that the measure only provides benefits to workers and not to companies, it might be that aid elements are not even involved. therefore that would mean that the process of adoption of this would be faster. if an amendment to the state aid guidelines is required, then we will prepare a commission decision, which normally takes two to three months. concerning the irish court ruling, we shall analyse how the definition of workers as self-employed potentially impacts on the application of this measure, and will seek a solution in order to address the specific problem concerning ireland. on the request that emergency temporary cessation should not be linked to restructuring (which was also raised by mrs doyle), restructuring is relatively loosely defined in our package so there should be ample opportunity for vessels in trouble to adapt to new realities. they can receive aid now, and then they have six months to adapt. this link to restructuring has to be maintained for the emergency package, however, to have the desired result. with regard to the question concerning the financial requirement which was raised by mrs mcguinness, the financial requirement solely for the temporary and permanent cessation of fishing activities is estimated at around eur 1.6 billion. the total financial requirement is estimated to be in the region of eur 2 billion. the current programming of the eff axis 1 for these measures is estimated to cover around eur 600 million with an estimated additional eur 250 million coming from national co-financing. the commission further estimates that eur 550 million will have to come from the programming of eff operational programmes. therefore this would leave a shortfall of eur 600 million. so there is additionality as well. we are not just making use of eff funds. there is an additionality of eur 600 million. a substantial part of this amount could be financed through the unallocated margin under heading 2 of the financial framework ceilings for the years 2009-2010, with the bulk coming in 2009. it is this additionality which could form the ad hoc instrument i referred to before. the ad hoc instrument should be needs-based, so it would not directly reflect the proportionate allocations under the eff but should target those segments of the fleet that need to restructure but which would not find assistance under the eff, either because the eff allocation to the member state concerned is very limited or because it relates to areas which are non-convergence and therefore which have very limited allocations of eff, or because there is enormous demand and therefore the eff falls short. so that is my response with regard to the financial allocations. i would also like to make the point, in regard to the question raised, that while in the short term we are not proposing any miracle solution, we are providing for immediate temporary cessation for three months effective from 1 july 2008 and, as i said, we will be taking a flexible view with regard to the definition of restructuring, whereas with regard to the further temporary cessation provisions, those have to be part and parcel of a fleet adaptation scheme. but with regard to the first three months, as long as there is restructuring in a general way then the entitlement would apply. on the point raised as to whether we can deliver within the time-frame because of conditionalities involved, my response is that most of the conditionalities relate to partial decommissioning which is a new instrument and which was very contentious even in reaching this stage. removing partial decommissioning would remove also most of the conditionalities attached to it. i am sure, however, that this is not what you would want. but i can assure you that the commission will urge member states and the industry to take up the fleet adaptation schemes and to ensure that these are properly monitored and properly implemented so that the time-frames envisaged and the conditionalities set will be adhered to and respected. again i would like to say that it is not true to say that all measures relate to decommissioning of vessels. it is true that there is a continuation of total decommissioning but there is the introduction of partial decommissioning, and partial decommissioning means that we will be removing older vessels and introducing new smaller ones, and in this sense therefore there will be introduction of new vessels with lower capacity in absolute terms. we will have a real effective reduction of capacity but at the same time we will also have properly addressed the fuel problems. there are also measures with regard to engine substitution and with regard to gear and equipment change, and there are the measures that i have outlined concerning the market measures and social aid. so i do not think it is correct to say that what we are proposing is simply a continuation of total decommissioning of vessels. there are various other instruments and i hope that member states will be able to pick from these the ones that would in the most appropriate way address the concerns and realities of the sector. with regard to the point made by mrs stihler concerning the fact that these could be harmful subsidies for new construction, i need to underline the fact that we will not be paying one cent for decommissioning for vessels whose capacity is maintained. what we will be paying is the scrapping aid for total decommissioning and we will be paying scrapping aid for the part that is decommissioned. we are not paying any state assistance for the capacity that remains. we are simply trying to find a solution whereby the necessary restructuring through reducing capacity, which we attempted by virtue of total decommissioning which has not proved too successful, might hopefully be more effectively addressed through this new instrument of partial decommissioning. the combination of partial decommissioning, total decommissioning, retaining vessels in operation with the possibility of engine substitutions, with the possibility of modernisation on board etc., all measures which already exist, and the whole package within a fleet adaptation scheme, could lead to a situation where we effectively bring about the needed reduction in capacity, which would translate to a reduction of effort to meet with the present state of affairs we have concerning the health of fish stocks. i just want to conclude with regard to the original intervention by mrs stihler that i can only repeat the well-known maxim that you are damned if you do and damned if you don’t.
i'm closing the debate. the vote will take place on thursday 10 july 2008. the competent authority shall inform the applicant of the reasons for the refusal of the application.

on behalf of the uen group. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: i want to draw attention to three points in this debate. first, it is estimated that tax losses due to vat and excise fraud amount to over 2% of the european union's gdp, amounting to eur 200-250 billion. these are huge sums, therefore, which reduce the revenues of national budgets, but also affect the structure of the revenues of the budget of the european union, increasing the share of own revenues based on gross national income. secondly, despite this diagnosis, the solutions proposed in the report for intra-community transactions, such as the reverse charge mechanism, whereby the tax is paid by the recipient rather than the supplier, the attempt to harmonise vat rates, which in effect means abolishing reduced rates, and finally the establishment of a clearing house to settle the tax between member states, are solutions which may do more harm than good. thirdly, it seems that, in order to reduce tax fraud, closer cooperation between the tax administrations of the member states is needed, consisting primarily in a more rapid exchange of information and perhaps even automatic access to certain vat and excise taxpayers' data.
mr. chairman, please! tax fraud has been a global problem for some time. the estimated losses correspond to 2-2.5% of gdp, or eur 200-250 billion at the european level. there is therefore a clear need for coordination at community level and for closer cooperation between member states. articles 10 and 280 of the treaty establishing the european community require the member states to take appropriate measures to fulfil their obligations under the treaty and to coordinate their action in order to protect the community's financial interests. however, it should be borne in mind that while the free movement of goods and services within the community market makes it difficult for individual member states to combat this type of fraud, the measures taken must not impede economic activity and impose unnecessary burdens on taxpayers.

member of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, two months ago the commission adopted a renewed social agenda. it is designed to help the union address the social challenges facing europe in the 21st century. it contains an ambitious and coherent set of social policy measures to enable europeans to seize the opportunities that lie ahead. as mentioned above, the renewed social agenda was discussed by the ministers for labour and social affairs at the informal meeting of the council in its social policy composition held in chantilly at the beginning of july. i was pleased to hear of the very positive reception of the renewed social agenda by the member states and look forward to the conclusions that the council should adopt later this year. i have already had the opportunity to present this package to the conference of presidents and the employment committee. so it's a good time for a deep debate here in parliament. i am convinced that today's exchange of views will help us to move closer to a consensus on the kind of social europe we want to build for european citizens. let me remind you of the developments so far. this comprehensive package is the result of two years of joint effort. the commission cooperated with all stakeholders social partners, civil society, member states and regional and local authorities. the package forms a coherent whole, emphasising links with other areas such as education, health, the environment, the information society and the economy, and making clear that economic and social objectives are two sides of the same coin and must work in close synergy for the benefit of people. it is an ambitious package that seeks to offer practical answers to people's concerns and improve their living conditions. it is also a very comprehensive package the largest ever adopted by the commission at one time 18 initiatives presented together with the communication. and more than 20 others covering a wide range of topics are under negotiation. today i will focus on two measures the draft anti-discrimination directive and the recast directive establishing a european works council. but first, let me say a few words about the basic principles of this package. the renewed social agenda is based on three main principles: opportunity, access and solidarity. we europeans value the value of individuals and want everyone to have an equal chance to develop their potential. it means removing the obstacles that people have to overcome and creating the conditions that allow everyone to seize the opportunities that are offered, while respecting europe's diversity and avoiding conflicts with one another. europeans' belief in equality is reflected in their shared sense of social solidarity. solidarity between generations, between regions, between those better off and those worse off, between richer and less wealthy member states. and also with our neighbours and friends in other continents, since solidarity is an integral part of the functioning of european society and of our relations with the rest of the world. ladies and gentlemen, you are aware that the extent of legal protection against discrimination currently varies across the eu depending on the grounds for discrimination. however, discrimination is not limited to one area. this is why we have proposed, as part of the package, a horizontal directive prohibiting discrimination on grounds of age, sexual orientation, religion and disability outside the field of employment. the horizontal directive will bring the greatest clarity and legal certainty to member states, economic operators and citizens. this proposal responds to repeated calls from parliament and fulfils the political commitment made by the commission when it took office. it is a flexible instrument, building on principles already adopted in the member states and enshrined in existing rules. i would like to emphasise that addressing all grounds of discrimination in the same way does not mean that uniform rules have to apply in all areas. for example, in insurance and banking, it will be possible to differentiate treatment on the basis of age or disability. however, these differences will have to be substantiated by convincing reasons and reliable statistical data. older people will continue to enjoy reduced fares on public transport and at cultural events. and it will continue to be possible to restrict access to certain goods for reasons of public health, for example when selling alcohol to minors. the directive covers all supplies of all goods and services and applies to both businesses and private persons, but only where the supply of goods and services is carried out for commercial purposes. the directive will also be proportionate in terms of the burden it imposes, in line with the concept of proportionate adaptation enshrined both in the existing anti-discrimination directives and in the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities, to which the member states and the european community are signatories. the proposed directive prohibits discrimination, but at the same time respects other fundamental rights and freedoms, including the protection of private and family life and acts carried out in that context, as well as freedom of religion and freedom of association. another issue i would like to highlight is discrimination against roma, which the commission has repeatedly condemned as incompatible with eu principles. the package includes a communication on our renewed commitment to equal opportunities and the fight against discrimination and a commission staff working document on community instruments and policies for roma inclusion. this is in response to a request from the european council in december 2007 for the commission to review existing policies and instruments and report to the council on progress made. according to the commission staff working document, the necessary legislative, financial and coordination instruments exist and are being used, but still not to the required extent. the renewed social agenda includes several initiatives aimed at enhancing the union's capacity to respond more effectively to change. we believe that the european social dialogue and the european works councils have a special role to play in this respect. the directive on the establishment of european works councils has been calling for an update for some time. there are currently 820 european works councils in the union, representing 15 million workers. however, recent cases show that they do not fulfil their role fully and that employees are often not well informed or consulted about the restructuring of enterprises. the initiative therefore aims to strengthen the role of social dialogue in enterprises at transnational level. it is a balanced proposal that should ensure that workers' representatives are adequately informed and consulted when making decisions on matters affecting them, while allowing businesses to adapt to globalisation. the commission would naturally prefer a solution negotiated in advance by the social partners. however, the fact that they were not able to be brought to the round table last june forced the commission to submit a proposal on its own initiative. i do, however, appreciate the joint letter from the social partners to the council and parliament in august. we appreciate the efforts both sides have made to reach agreement on this complex issue. and i am also pleased that they have decided to accept the commission's proposal as a basis from which to work further. i hope very much that when parliament goes to its first reading it will take account of the practical proposals of the social partners. i trust we'll come to a solution as soon as possible. the commission shall, within its powers, make every effort to facilitate access to it as far as possible. now a few words about the effects of globalization. restructuring of businesses is sometimes unavoidable, but its effects on employees and their families can be very painful. the european globalisation adjustment fund exists to help in such situations. so far, the fund has helped 7,250 employees find new jobs. we can be happy about that, but we must ensure that the fund's possibilities are available to all those who can benefit from its help. the report contained in the social agenda package states that only 4% of the €500 million available annually was used in 2007. it is therefore necessary to consider how to improve the performance of the fund. as regards the mobility of workers, i would point out that the 1996 posting of workers directive promotes the free movement of services, while at the same time offering protection against exploitation of workers and guaranteeing respect for their fundamental rights in the member states to which they are posted. recent judgments of the court of justice on this issue have raised a number of questions. the reactions to them are entirely legitimate and we must find answers to them together. i invite you to a forum on 9 october to discuss this complex issue with the political authorities, the social partners, representatives of the european institutions and experts in the fields of law and economics. the commission will of course continue to listen to all voices, but at this stage we do not see the need to amend the directive. in any event, we will ensure that there is no conflict between the fundamental freedoms enshrined in the treaty and the fundamental europeans in the social field. these values are social dialogue, solidarity between generations, the fight against poverty and discrimination, equality between men and women, social protection, occupational mobility, the importance of services of general interest in ensuring social cohesion and the social responsibility of enterprises. these values are the originality of the european social progress, quite the contrary. for me - and i'm not the only one - the two are inseparable. without social progress, the springs of economic progress will eventually run out. europe must therefore move in writing. – the criminal justice system serves to punish, deter and to rehabilitate the offender. in the same way sanctions broadly serve the same purposes. our criminal justice systems may punish, but how successful they are in deterring and rehabilitating is open to question. likewise, sanctions often have limited impact on deterring and rehabilitating nations which break international law and violate human rights. research based on the effectiveness of over 100 instances of economic sanctions since world war i has shown that they are most likely to be effective if: the change we demand is modest; large powerful nations or groups of nations act against a weaker nation; the target nation is truly dependent on trade with those imposing the sanctions; sanctions are imposed quickly and damage to the imposer of sanctions is limited. when the eu does impose sanctions they should be precise and well targeted. measures to consider include: freezing of financial assets, ban on transactions, investment restrictions; trade restrictions on particular goods; travel restrictions; diplomatic constraints and cultural and sports restrictions. it is vital that the eu reviews its sanctions policy, not only with the aim of achieving the desired changes in offending nations, but also to ensure its own credibility.
president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, like the european parliament, the council attaches great importance to the achievement of all the millennium development goals worldwide by 2015, in particular the one aimed at reducing the maternal mortality rate by three quarters between 1990 and 2015. the european union recalls in this regard that sustainable progress in this area requires respect for and promotion of the rights of women and girls by guaranteeing them access to health services, in particular sexual health services, and by protecting them against the aids virus. the three eu institutions have made clear their collective commitment to improving maternal health in developing countries, notably by signing the european consensus on development on 20 december 2005, which places maternal health among the priority objectives of the union's development policy. we have the financial instruments to achieve this, particularly in the framework of the partnership between the european union and africa on the millennium development goals. as you know, there are still considerable challenges to be met in the field of health. they were mentioned in the annual report of the united nations. 500,000 women still die each year from complications of pregnancy or childbirth that cannot be treated. these deaths cannot be prevented at this point if we do not make progress. the probability of a woman dying from these maternal causes is 1/16 in sub-saharan africa compared to 1/3800 in developed countries. so, in view of the scale of these challenges, in view of this totally unacceptable situation, the council has decided to accelerate and strengthen its action. in june it adopted an action plan. the agenda provides for the eu to urgently support efforts to achieve the 2005 target, including universal access to reproductive health, and the 2010 intermediate targets, which are - as you know - to save 4 million additional lives of children each year, including 2 million in africa, and to ensure that 35 million additional births are attended by qualified health workers each year, including 13 million in africa. if we are to reduce maternal mortality rates by three-quarters by 2015, that means that 21 million more births will need to be attended by trained health personnel every year by 2010. the union will support the achievement of its target of 50 million more women in africa having access to modern contraceptive methods by 2010 and, more generally, to family planning. the agenda implemented by the council also provides for the union to contribute to reducing the financing gap to achieve these objectives by 2010. i should like to point out that the world health organization estimates the current funding gap at over 13 billion euros. if the commissioner tells us that the european commission believes that to meet and close these financing gaps we need an increase in eu aid of €8 billion by 2010, of which €6 billion should be allocated to africa, it is essential that both partner and donor countries are involved in meeting the challenges ahead. so in this context, the presidency is convinced that strengthening health systems in developing countries remains a very important priority of the millennium development goals. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the health insurance system is not disrupted. the development ministers will meet at the informal meeting in bordeaux on 29 and 30 september, with a view to the conclusions of the november council and the forthcoming presidencies on universal access to care; finally, the council will examine the commission's report on the european union action plan against the shortage of health workers in developing countries. so, mr president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, you can be sure that the council will remain fully engaged and will do everything possible to ensure that the european union continues to play a leading role in improving maternal health in developing countries, particularly in africa.
member of the commission. − mr president, the right to health is probably the basic right with the most inequalities in the world today. those in greatest need, at greatest risk of ill health and premature death, have the worst access to health care – often zero access. this poses enormous challenges to the european union and to the world community as a whole. the european union is very committed to the implementation of the millennium development goals (mdgs), including mdg 5 on maternal health, which is the subject we are discussing today. we are aware of the fact that scaling up sexual and reproductive health and health funding in general requires a far more coherent and multi-sectoral approach, also involving other mdgs. health results cannot be achieved without adequate investment in the systems that deliver better health. health policy needs to be embedded in broader social and economic development planning. countries need long-term predictable aid from external donors. donors need to see a clear link between financing and results, and mechanisms to hold all partners accountable for their performance against international agreements are badly needed. poor people – women, men and children – living in developing countries encounter a wide range of interrelated sexual and reproductive health problems. these include hiv/aids, sexually transmitted diseases, unplanned or unwanted pregnancy, complications encountered in pregnancy and childbirth, genital mutilation or cutting, infertility, sexual abuse, unsafe abortion and cancer of the cervix, among others. together, these conditions are responsible for much suffering and many premature deaths. exacerbated by poverty and the secondary position of women in society they are basically due to the lack of access to appropriate health services, lack of information and inadequate availability of skilled professionals and supplies of reproductive health commodities. therefore, improving maternal health and reducing maternal mortality have been key concerns of the european commission’s work in health and development. however, despite our efforts and the mdg targets, mdg 5 is possibly the goal which is most off-track globally – especially, as has already been said, in africa. this is very serious, all the more so because most maternal deaths occur at home, far removed from the health services, and often go unrecorded. so the actual maternal mortality figure might even be much higher than the half million a year that we are aware of according to the statistics. from a political point of view, there is another issue which causes concern. this is the increasing tendency not to prioritise sexual and reproductive health and rights policies in programmes because of sensitivities to abortion. by doing so, we are forgetting about the unequal position of women in many of our partner countries who have no say about the number of children they want or are forced to have sexual relations, sometimes even with a partner who is likely to be hiv-infected. let us not forget about the many victims of rape, the young girls and women who, on top of their injuries and trauma, often get rejected by their relatives and communities. under the 10th european development fund and the commission budget, we are therefore programming direct support to health in 31 developing countries. many of these countries have very high maternal mortality rates and very weak health systems. in this regard, budget support linked to health outcomes becomes another important instrument to address maternal mortality. to make this aid more predictable, the commission is introducing in a number of partner countries a new financing modality called ‘mdg contracting’, under which budget support will be made over a longer term, linked with agreed outcomes which contribute towards the achievement of the mdgs. this will allow governments to support recurrent costs of health systems, such as the salaries of health workers. this is critical to increase access to basic healthcare, including safe deliveries and progress towards mdg 5. however, we know that what is being done in support of maternal health at the moment is not sufficient and that more efforts are needed to change the present situation. this is why on 24 june 2008 the council of the european union adopted the eu agenda for action on mdgs, whereby the commission and the member states commit themselves to increase their support to health by the additional eur 8 billion which has been mentioned, and eur 6 billion in africa, by 2010. regarding mdg 5, the agenda for action on mdgs mentioned two important targets by 2010: firstly, 21 million more births attended by skilled health workers and, secondly, 50 million more women to have access to modern contraceptives in africa. we the commission – but also the member states – will now have to make it happen together. we have made the commitment and we are determined to improve the situation of women in poor countries giving birth, which i think is the most natural thing in the world. i am glad that, as the commissioner for external relations today, in place of louis michel, i can say that, because, as a woman, i feel very much in solidarity. member of the commission. − mr president, i am grateful to the european parliament for this report. as it reflects, services account for the largest share of gdp in developed countries. the liberalisation of trade in services is therefore of key importance for our economic growth, as it is for developing countries, where services are not sufficiently advanced. i largely share the views that are expressed is this report. they are in line with our global europe strategy. it is built on an ambitious multilateral agenda and on a carefully crafted set of bilateral agreements. we are fully committed to the development dimension of the multilateral trade round and, as the report affirms, we see a multilateral deal on services as positive, both for the interests of the eu as well as for those of poorer countries. i welcome the encouragement of the report for an ambitious level of commitments in the ongoing and upcoming negotiations for bilateral and regional agreements. we take careful note of the recommendations of the report for the different ongoing negotiations that generally touch upon the sectors that our services industry considers of importance. allow me to make a general reflection on the negotiation of services agreements which is applicable to both bilateral and multilateral deals. there is no easy fix for negotiations in services, no simple formula that can apply across all service sectors and all countries. these negotiations involve addressing the complex and often detailed set of regulatory frameworks of countries in areas as diverse as those reflected in the last section of your report – from financial services to health care or education. we ought to do that in a non-intrusive way that preserves the right of third countries to regulate the different services sectors domestically as they wish, while opening them to external supply if competition is favoured. there should be no discrimination. we acknowledge that some services sectors account for a larger share of gdp than others and that, to this extent, the liberalisation of their trade may have a larger impact on our overall welfare. however, in prioritising any given sectors, we also have to take into consideration, amongst other factors, the relative specialisation of our eu countries and regions in different sectors. finally, let me offer a reflection on the multilateral process. your report welcomes the announcement of a signalling conference on services as part of the dda ministerial negotiations. we actually pushed very hard for this event, which took place in july in geneva. it was a relative success. we did not hear all the signals that we would have liked, but we heard enough to say that wto members and several of our target countries understood the importance that we attach to a satisfactory market access outcome in the services sector. i have no crystal ball to see where the multilateral talks in the dda will go from where we left them in july. we are in the situation where one issue – the special safeguard mechanism in agriculture for developing countries – has provided the proximate cause of breakdown, even if there are other issues that also need to be resolved. so support for the outline modalities deal as a whole is very fragile and not just a question of the us and india resolving their differences in agriculture. i feel as if we have a priceless, wafer-thin vase of great craftsmanship in our hands, but which now has to be carried from here over a very slippery floor. one false move and the whole thing could crash into many pieces. so we need to be careful of the moves we make. we cannot stand still but, equally, it is difficult to move forward. we stand ready to re-engage at whatever level is useful to make sure that we do not lose what we had achieved and which remains on the table. but there has to be genuine political commitment by others to participate in a negotiating process. in this context, the progress made at the services signalling conference will not be lost. the signals made threw some light on the flexibilities that our key trading partners have in the services field, and this is precious information. the best contribution that we can all make in the current circumstances of the breakdown in negotiations in geneva is to be realistically positive and explain how big an opportunity we may miss if we fail altogether. your report, therefore, is timely, for it sends a clear and balanced message on the importance that the liberalisation of trade in one of the key areas of a dda deal – services – would have, both for us and for our partners. i look forward to continuing my cooperation and dialogue with parliament, both in this area and other areas of trade policy.

in writing. computerised reservation systems (crs) are designed primarily to serve consumers. this is why it is so important to ensure transparency in the air ticket reservation market, especially where airlines may limit competition in the market through their participation in computerised reservation systems. of course, the situation on the airline market has changed significantly over the last few years and most airlines have divested their shares in ksr, which does not mean that this applies to all airlines. however, it is essential that, despite their participation in the reservation systems, airlines are not able to influence the operation of the systems in such a way as to favour their routes, which must be properly reflected in the definition of 'home carrier'. the simplification of the code of conduct will increase the possibility of negotiation between market participants (airlines and the ccc will be able to negotiate more freely the amount of the booking fee charged by the ccc). the current rules increase the cost of the cci and limit the flexibility of the cci in adapting its services to the specific needs of airlines and travel agencies, by not allowing the differentiation of the tariff offer for each cci. i hope that the changes will lead to more competition in the air ticket market, with the consumer himself benefiting, in particular, from the expansion of the existing offer and the lower final price of the air ticket.

2004-2010, which takes stock of the implementation of the action plan to date. i am glad that the european parliament has responded positively to this mid-term evaluation by attaching the same high importance as the commission to the interaction between the environment and health. and i am particularly pleased that the french presidency, today and with the minister on previous occasions, has awareness and encourage research on the environment and human health, in order to achieve a better understanding of the threats and risk factors to human health from the environment. this will enable political leaders at european and national level to develop more effective legislation and measures to protect the health of european citizens. the plan, which includes 13 specific actions for the period 2004-10, was drawn up following extensive consultation with experts and actors active in the fields of environment, health and research in europe. the action plan stresses that close cooperation between environmental, health and research services, both at national and european level, is vital to tackle the interactions between environment and health in the best possible way. four years after the adoption of the action plan, i am pleased to report that this close cooperation between the various services has now become established and is clearly a very positive development, in line with last year's mid-term evaluation. to give you a specific example: member states are now working together to develop a coordinated european approach to human biomonitoring involving the determining whether the exposure limit values set out in the council recommendation should be revised. the commission has recently asked its scientific committee on emerging and newly identified health risks to review its opinion in the light of the most recent data and reports. the relationship between climate change and health is clearly among the issues of growing importance, according to integration of the health dimension into european environmental policy. recent legislation such as the chemicals legislation, reach, and the new air quality directive enhance environmental and health in writing. mr president, respect for human rights, democracy and the rule of law is one of the priorities of the european union, which, if necessary, imposes restrictive measures called sanctions to enforce the above objectives. the use of sanctions should be considered in the event of a serious breach of security or civil rights or in the event of ineffective contractual or diplomatic action. the imposition of sanctions should also be justified at the moment of irreversible damage to the environment, as it becomes a threat to security and thus a serious violation of human rights. the application of 'double standards', i.e. lack of consistency and equality in the imposition and enforcement of sanctions, should be avoided. the most common sanctions in the european union are visa bans and arms embargoes. sanctions are also one of the instruments in the fight against terrorism. the blacklisting procedure for institutions and entities linked to terrorist activities is an important tool of the eu's counter-terrorism policy. and to make sanctions more effective, international coordination is needed. the union should continue to apply targeted, intelligent sanctions to address a specific problem and minimise the humanitarian consequences or adverse effects on those who are not targeted.

mr. chairman, please! although it has been almost a year since we adopted our position on the draft soil protection directive at first reading, the council has still not been able to reach an agreement. so far, several member states have used blocking minorities. now there is hope of reaching a compromise during the french presidency. from the statements of the french representative, it seems that this was the hope. we hear many voices of criticism accusing the project of adding bureaucracy or duplicating existing national and community legislation. i think it's the opposite. we need a directive because it will lead to the harmonisation of legislation in this area and will bring together efforts at eu level to protect the soil. to stop its degradation, we must act not only at local, regional but also at community level. the soil is our common property. there is therefore a need to define common principles and objectives and to take appropriate action. it is important that all citizens of the union are aware of the vital role it plays in the ecosystem, in our daily lives and in the economy. unfortunately, many member states still have dangerous substances, landfills and even chemical weapons left over from the soviet military presence. some countries will not be able to cope with these problems on their own. therefore, appropriate incentives and assistance to member states in the removal of these substances are necessary. appropriate regulations that allow the reuse of degraded land while limiting soil degradation and ensuring its sustainable use are urgently needed. this will undoubtedly be a step forward in environmental protection and in the preservation of the precious natural resource of soil. this directive will help us do that. we must therefore continue to legislate on it and seek the opinion of independent experts so that they can formulate views that we can take into account.

in writing. − the share of services in the european economy is over three quarters. the services sector is crucial to the competitiveness and innovation of europe's largely knowledge-based economy. an effective internal market for services in the european union is essential for the competitiveness of eu businesses in the global marketplace. timely and correct implementation and transposition of the directive on services in the internal market will be key to the functioning of the european market. trade in services is largely a transfer of expertise between countries. free trade in services therefore plays an important role in any development strategy, as it allows for the rapid and efficient transfer of know-how on a large scale. wider access to the services market is therefore an opportunity not only for developed countries but also for developing countries, which often lack access to know-how. in the case of services, market access is a difficult process in the context of the ongoing wto negotiations. however, it must not be forgotten that negotiations on trade in services must serve both the interests of the eu and the economic growth of the poorest countries. after all, it is the opening up of trade in services that could lead, through the opening up of foreign investment, to more and more sustainable production, as well as to the modernisation of infrastructure in all economies.
in writing. −the report on trade in services aims to highlight the role of trade in services as a sector that continuously creates new jobs and increases the well-being of citizens. these services now account for as much as 75% of the eu's gdp. the rapporteur calls for the opening up and liberalisation of the market for trade in services. of course, liberalization and increased competitiveness in the market are necessary, but i believe that opening up trade in services cannot mean privatisation. we must clearly distinguish the nature of commercial services from public services and, consequently, guarantee a firm distinction in the approach to opening up trade in public and commercial services.
in writing. - the 'services revolution' since the mid-20th century has made services the most important sector of the economy in most countries. technological progress, particularly in telecommunications and information technology, has fundamentally changed the way services are perceived and their ability to participate in international trade. the rapid expansion of this sector, combined with technological progress, has led to the development of international trade in services. poland's share in international trade in services, like that of other central and eastern european countries, has always been small. however, this was largely the result of the underdevelopment of the services sector in centrally planned economies. the sector was fundamentally transformed by the transition period, which was followed by the period of association with the european communities. as a result, the services sector is already undergoing major changes and poland's integration into the community and the associated process of adjusting the polish economy to ec requirements should increase the pace of development of the services sector and poland's ability to participate in international trade in services. i therefore believe that the eu should do its utmost to improve the quality of trade in services as a sector that creates wealth and jobs in all economies in the world and as a factor that accelerates development.

the global financial crisis means that the transparency of funds using alternative investment options should also be an important topic in the european parliament. increasing the transparency of companies through legal instruments, in particular with regard to the relationship between hedge funds and private equity funds and the companies in which they hold hold shares, is now a priority. the so-called codes of good practice developed so far may serve as a model, but they cannot replace legislative action in relation to instances of bad practice. the need to develop a code of best practice on how to rebalance the current corporate governance structure is essential. the new legislation should also require hedge funds and private equity funds to disclose and explain their investment policies and the associated risks to retail and institutional investors, insurance brokers and supervisory authorities.
madam president, such failure of financial markets has never happened until now. the main cause was the enormous increase in turnover, and the development of a new system of financial gain beyond the existing banking system without transparency, any effective evaluation or supervision. new investments and vehicles brought big profits, but also caused an increasing threat, even to the imf. although the proposal from mr rasmussen and his committee concerning transparency and supervision – particularly of the excessive debt leverage - are right and indispensable, we should also acknowledge as very dangerous the opinion of the committee on legal affairs which demands simply that it be left solely to participants in the market to assess the appropriate level of risk to take. the committee overlooked the fact that last year the average securities firm was leveraged 27 to 1, with no regulation or supervision. what is more, they regulated themselves completely on their own, and even the big lenders ignored the extent of the risk they were taking. the cost of this failure will be extremely high. the cost to americans, for example, has been terrible, at around usd 1 000 billion. it will have yet another additional effect: the actors on financial markets may not learn to be more cautious, because they will be accustomed to relying on help from taxpayers. we then have the choice of either protecting the almost full freedom of choice for financial actors in taking risks, or to impose distinct obligations and limitations insuring effectively against excessive shocks and guaranteeing a stabilising development of financial markets. the opinion of the commissioner gives some hope for the future, but i am afraid that the tasks facing the commission are extremely difficult and demand much more courage in finding new methods and new measures.
madam president! both events in recent years, and even months, and efforts by individual countries and regions, indicate the growing importance of transparency not only for individual companies but also for the development of individual countries' economies. the global nature of the hedge fund industry and the possibility of moving the fund's head office to another country to avoid being subject to national rules are obstacles to the direct regulation of the hedge fund industry. this is the main reason why all international institutions dealing with hedge funds seek to influence the activities of the funds through their relationships with regulated entities, in particular banks. the problems of transparency in the european union are mainly concentrated on the convergence and harmonisation of the laws of the member states. the areas of concern related to transparency aspects can be summarised as follows: the establishment of uniform standards for the disclosure of financial statements, the strengthening of the role of independent board members, standards for the establishment of committees within the board, the disclosure of information on remuneration of mountains are important areas of biodiversity, shelter for many animals, and home to unique plant species. they're often called water towers because they give rise to rivers. their landscape and ecological qualities are appreciated by tourists from all over the world. nevertheless, the lives of the people and the farming of these lands are not easy. in most mountain regions of the union we are witnessing processes of depopulation, a decline in the activity of the people living there, abandonment of agricultural activities. this is particularly true of less touristic and neglected rural areas. the problems are the great distance from cities, the difficult climatic conditions, the transportation difficulties, the higher production costs, the lack of access to all kinds of services, including even those such as education and health care. the regional disparities between the mountainous and the lowland areas are visible to the naked eye. therefore, there is an urgent need for special support for so-called mountain farmers who not only produce traditionally organic, healthy food, but also care about environmental protection, preservation of culture and tradition. the common agricultural policy should do more to support these regions and their people in meeting the challenges they face.

in writing. − the european internal market is one of the most important achievements of the european integration process. only a well-functioning internal market guarantees competitive conditions for business and promotes the development of the european economy. the internal market scoreboard is a tool to monitor the progress in the implementation, proper transposition and correct application of the internal market directives. analysis of the data in the internal market scoreboard provides very interesting information on the work of member states in implementing eu legislation. it is a typically political tool, but it should not be treated as a marginal one, and should serve as an incentive for those responsible to transpose more quickly and correctly. this is particularly true for new member states whose transposition deficits often exceed the target set by heads of state or government. the internal market scoreboard should also be used more frequently in discussions on the state of the internal market. it is therefore necessary to develop a more accessible form of the scoreboard which could also be used by citizens interested in internal market issues. the rapporteur pointed out that, due to the smooth functioning of the internal market, some directives, such as the services directive, are more important than others. i share the rapporteur's view on this and therefore believe that the european commission should take into account indicators that better reflect the direct relevance of directives to businesses and citizens.
in writing. - two reports are being voted on today which seem to complement each other: the doris pack report on the bologna process and the maria badia and cutchet report on improving the quality of teacher education. both initiatives aim to make european education more competitive and thus to increase the potential and competitiveness of the european union as a whole. putting education first is a great thing, but it's easy to neglect. in many countries, we have all the basic sins of the teacher education system. there is a lack of incentive and motivation for the best graduates to choose the teaching profession, the status of teachers (especially at primary and secondary level) is simply low, teachers are poorly paid and there is no investment in their development. the relationship between the quality of teacher education and the quality of teaching and, consequently, the level of knowledge of pupils is obvious. neglect in this area can have disastrous consequences, not only culturally but also economically. the recommendations made to the member states in the report seem to be sound: to recruit the best candidates, to improve the status, recognition and remuneration of teachers, to invest in training at all stages of the career, to exchange best practice between the 27 different education systems in the eu, to increase the empowerment of schools.
