in writing. - i voted in favour of the report by mrs doris pack on the bologna process and student mobility. it's a factual and good report. today, we still under-spend on research and academic education in the eu. the nine-year-old bologna idea (which now involves 46 countries) is to contribute to the creation of the european higher education area in 2010. the process is based on three priority areas of action. these are: the cycle of education (which comprises three stages: bachelor, master and doctorate), ensuring high quality of education and recognition of qualifications and periods of higher education. multi-faceted and coherent action is therefore needed in all member states, involving our universities. the ects credit systems should be clear, understandable and uniform. this will allow for the flexibility and mobility of young people in different academic centres and the much needed exchange of professors. although higher education is not a matter for the eu, we should seek close cooperation and coordination while preserving the independence of the member states in this area. we must also remember to ensure that all eu citizens have equal opportunities to access education at the highest possible level, which requires both organisational changes in the education system and the appropriate financial investment.
in writing. - ms doris pack deserves to be thanked for her contribution to the development and creative reflection on the bologna process, an initiative that allows european students to choose their own educational and career paths, regardless of national borders. this initiative, by strengthening the competitiveness of the european education system, enriches societies themselves through cultural and scientific penetration. of course, the content and quality of education at all levels is now the responsibility of the eu member states. much remains to be done in this regard. mobility and its promotion at european level, which is the main theme of mrs pack's report, is based, for example, in poland, on the outflow of valuable labour, which is often not recoverable. i agree with the report that the most important thing is student mobility, the creation of a system of incentives and facilities so that young people can take advantage of the offer of study wherever they want. however, it is particularly important to return to the country as a fully formed, educated person so that he can fulfil his potential in his country of origin. this is certainly a challenge for the new eu member states and i think that a prudent continuation of the bologna process is a step in that direction.
in writing. - a united europe is not just a common currency, the free movement of people, a common market for goods and services. it is also, or above all, the intellectual, cultural and social dimension of europe. the bologna process, an intergovernmental initiative launched less than a decade ago, is primarily designed to make it easier for students to choose the highest quality courses. one of the most important elements of the idea of creating a european higher education area is to increase student mobility and the quality of education, because it is these that create opportunities for personal, social and scientific development. i believe that action at both european level (the european parliament gives priority to mobility) and national level is important in order to improve the quality and attractiveness of education. it should be noted that higher education in the european union is not the responsibility of the commission of the european communities. the competence for the content and organisation of studies remains with the individual countries, which is why their role and that of the universities themselves is so important. they should emphasise the need to create european doctoral programmes, and seek to provide special support for students from disadvantaged social groups. dialogue and bilateral exchange of experience between enterprises and universities is also important, and higher education institutions should therefore strengthen cooperation with the private sector to find new effective mechanisms for co-financing student mobility.
in writing. − i am in favour of further protection of the economic interests in mineral water extraction sites, which have been guaranteed by the european parliament's directive on the extraction and marketing of natural mineral waters. the revenues generated by municipalities and enterprises, especially in the lesser poland voivodeship, make a significant contribution to the development of the region and its attractiveness as a health resort and tourist destination. it is worth noting that these are often agricultural areas with little income potential due to their mountainous and high-altitude location, but which conceal beneath their surface very valuable mineral waters and springs with medicinal properties.
in writing. − one of the main objectives of the european union's common policy on the area of freedom, security and justice is to ensure the security of 500 million citizens. to meet this challenge, the european union and its member states must confront modern terrorism. the most controversial point in the proposal to amend the council framework decision on combating terrorism is the requirement to introduce the concept of public incitement to commit terrorist offences. the line between free speech and breaking the law is very thin. we cannot allow a situation in which increased security leads to a reduction in the rights and freedoms of citizens. for this reason, i believe that it is essential to ensure the highest possible legal standard for the framework decision in question, in particular by clarifying the concept of public provocation to commit terrorist offences. the newly created instrument must be legally clear and harmonised so as to be an effective tool in the fight against terrorism, while ensuring a high level of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
in writing. - the attacks in madrid and london have shown us how serious a problem terrorism is for the eu. 2008 has reaped a huge harvest, from the february 1 attack on a funeral in baghdad that killed 30 people to the september 20 attack on the marriott hotel in islamabad that killed over 60 people and injured over 250. in all, 49 terrorist attacks took place in 2008. for comparison, this is the same number of attacks as between 2002 and 2007 (inclusive). one of the most effective ways to combat terrorism is to eliminate its causes. i therefore believe that the european union should do everything possible to combat terrorism on a global scale, with respect for human rights. the eu should make europe safer by enabling its citizens to enjoy freedom, security and justice, which will depend to a large extent on the will of the member states.
in writing. - i voted in favour of david hammerstein's report on the activities of the committee on petitions in the 2007 parliamentary year, as it clearly shows the positive effects of the committee's work. the committee itself, chaired by mr marcin libicki, has shown that it is very much needed. it provides union citizens with the opportunity to petition the member states for infringements of their civil rights by public authorities. the ep's rules of procedure (rule 191) state: 'every citizen of the eu ... or any person domiciled in a member state ... has the right to petition parliament, individually or jointly with other citizens or persons, on matters within the european union's sphere of activity which concern him or her directly'. i consider the availability of the epetition database to be a significant step forward in the work of this commission. this allows online access to all documents relating to each petition. it should also be noted that the number of petitions submitted electronically has increased significantly. last year, it was 42 percent. the committee on petitions cooperates well with the relevant commission departments and the european ombudsman, as well as with the relevant representatives of the member states and regional and local authorities, who provide the necessary clarifications. the fact that the commission visits the member states is very helpful in its work. the effectiveness of its work greatly enhances the good performance of secretariat staff.
madam president! we have mentioned examples of disasters known throughout europe. i come from poland, a country that recently celebrated the second anniversary of the death of dozens of people on the jan heweliusz ferry. safety is of the utmost importance. it's good that we're considering security in the package. it's a good package, it's good in numbers, it's got seven adjustments. the safety of people, ships, waters and, finally, the safety of trade should be and is reflected in this package. in this respect, i regard mr sterckx's report as particularly good, where i had the honour of being the substitute rapporteur. yes, we need to monitor the ships. mrs wortmann-kool is right that we must investigate the causes of potential disasters and prevent possible disasters. moreover, i think we should refer to the aviation situation in shipping, the study of near collision situations, because we can better understand the mechanisms and causes of hazards. i do not understand and cannot agree with the position of the member of parliament zīle, who spoke about special or specific treatment of small countries. after all, the size of a european union member state has little to do with the number of ships flying its flag.
on behalf of the ppe-de group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i'm not going to let you do this. wood is a valuable building material, it's healthy, it's practical, it's maybe not fire-resistant enough, but it's increasingly in demand. in short, it is a sought-after and attractive commodity, and often a major export product. tropical trees, confined to a narrow geographical band, are all the more attractive and are traded, often illegally, to the detriment of the tree and the entire ecosystem. so we have a dilemma: on the one hand, we need wood, we need building materials, and on the other hand, we need to protect the rainforests. if exploitation gets out of good, sensible control, it will end not only in ecological disaster, but also in demographic disaster. without forests, there will be no other vegetation, no animals, and no people. international agreements are needed, but the awareness of sound timber management is probably the most important thing. if that reasoning fails, we will destroy an important part of nature that cannot be replaced. we'll be destroyers instead of wise hosts. in general, i am in favour of extending the agreement (with the possibility of continuing to improve it), which will, at least in part, regulate the free and fair trade in this wood and may also serve as a model for the exploitation of wood from other regions. from siberia, commissioner, which is very quiet today, from the amazon, which is a little more, and from other sensitive regions of the world.
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i'm not going to let you do this. the conclusion of an international tropical timber agreement is certainly a very significant step towards the protection of tropical forests and the civilization of trade in certain timber species. let's not let procedural issues cloud our primary objectives. maybe it's important to establish a legal basis, maybe it's important whether it's a consultation procedure or an agreement, but will it protect the rainforests and more? every day, thousands of acres of forest, not just tropical, are lost forever. the land that remains after them is swamped or desertified. deforestation will not prevent replanting, at least not anytime soon. poor countries in africa, the americas, and asia have no means to control, prevent, or manage over-exploitation of forests. this includes the siberian forests. we don't protect trees and we don't respect wood. the poorer the countries, the more. during the cultural revolution, china lost many square miles of forest. wood is used as a primary energy source. so that's why the international tropical timber organization has a huge role to play. keep in mind that technological advances, modern logging machines, and logging have accelerated the process, and cheaper, illegally harvested timber has become attractive to traders. any trade seals, obstructions, certificates of origin and controls will be a success. i hope that this agreement will be fulfilled as soon as possible.
mr. chairman, please! the existing international agreements on tropical dendroflora are clearly not sufficient. the genetic resources of tropical forests are being depleted at an alarming rate because of human over-exploitation. there are two reasons. the most interesting tropical wood species are constantly finding markets in wealthy countries. they're being more efficiently searched and cut. however, the possibilities for growing them in the farmed forest are limited due to the lack of nursery methods to grow them. seeds are usually non-dormant, i.e. unsuitable for storage and transport. they hatch right after they fall out of the tree. special studies are therefore needed on the seed, vegetative propagation and nursery management of these endangered species. the traders of this wood should be taxed for this very research. the second reason is the over-exploitation of tropical trees, including shrubs, by the local population, who need them for fuel, for cooking food. he can't stop this devastation without arranging for another fuel supply for this population.
despite its commitment to environmental protection, the united states seems to be blind to the growing problem of the loss of primary forests, which is mainly caused by deforestation for the tropical timber trade. so far, nearly 80 percent of the total area of these forests has been deforested. the union must increase financial assistance to producer countries to prevent illegal logging and promote sustainable forest management. certainly it is also a good idea to introduce wood certification on the european market. the commission notes that the union industry is not only a major importer of wood but also a major importer of wood products. the fight to preserve the remaining primary forests is in fact a fight for the future of future generations.

in writing. − i voted in favour of adopting the report on the amendment of rule 121 of parliament's rules of procedure concerning the procedure before the european court of justice, as it is an expression of respect for the rule of law. the third paragraph of rule 121 provides that the president is to bring an action before the court of justice on parliament's behalf, as recommended by the committee responsible. that provision expressly relates only to actions brought before the court of justice. an extension of the scope of that provision, which would cover cases of a different kind pending before the court, cannot be applied in that case. it is only applied in the event of an action (for example, for the annulment of a legislative act) in the event of legal proceedings being initiated by parliament. in the interests of legal certainty and completeness, the rapporteur has rightly proposed that a new paragraph be added to rule 121 to confirm the established practice of the president of the european parliament submitting observations to the court of justice or appearing before it on the recommendation of the legal affairs committee. the proposed amendment establishes a procedure for dealing with disagreements between the chair and the committee responsible. this change will give the procedure in practice a democratic legal basis.
in writing. - i am disappointed that a matter as important to eu citizens as sis is being dealt with in a consultative manner, in which parliament is basically merely formulating its position, which is not binding on the council. the sis (schengen information system) is the symbol of 'a europe without borders' guaranteeing an area of freedom, security and justice within the eu. the sis has opened up the possibility of police and judicial cooperation in criminal matters in the old eu member states, allowing the creation of a unique european database on persons and objects. this is crucial for issuing visas and residence permits. the entry of the new twelve into the eu has created the need to include them in the sis. only sis ii, as a new generation system covering all eu member states and allowing for the full collection of data (including biometric data and information on european arrest warrants), meets this need. the union now faces the delicate task of transporting all data to the new sis ii. it's a very necessary and complicated operation. that's why i'm asking for your attention and consideration. the data stored in the old system cannot escape or otherwise fall into the wrong hands. they must be secure, because the security of eu citizens and member states also depends on them.
in writing. − the adopted report on universal service and the rights of users of telecommunications services will help to improve the position of consumers in the electronic services market. universal service should provide users with access to public telephone service at a competitive price, guaranteeing national, international and emergency calls. the user rights will be increased by the measures adopted. he will have the right to change telecommunications operator while keeping his current telephone number, and more importantly, the transfer time should not be longer than one day. the maximum duration of contracts that a telecommunications undertaking may conclude with subscribers will also be limited to 24 months, but the operator should also provide the user with the possibility of concluding a contract for a maximum period of 12 months covering all services and terminal equipment. the availability of the 112 emergency number should also be increased, which is particularly important in emergency situations. member states should ensure the full availability of publicly available telephone services in the event of a network failure resulting from a disaster or an act of force majeure. the emergency number for missing children, 116, which is currently operated on a voluntary basis in only seven european union countries, should also be disseminated.
in writing. - i very much welcomed the report on the amendments to the directives on telecommunications users' rights presented by mr malcolm harbour. it is a balanced document and aims to bring about a substantial improvement in the situation on the market for electronic services. it is good that the compromise amendments have been formulated and accepted by a large majority of members. despite the very large number of amendments, this allowed the whole report to be adopted. i believe that the changes in the directives represent a great opportunity to adapt the eu telecommunications legislation, which was established in the early 1990s, to the enormous changes in technology. it is also worth noting that we want to include mobile television and broadband internet as universal services. subscribers should be guaranteed the right to full information on any restrictions on access to lawful software. service providers must ensure network security, protect users' personal data and stem the tide of so-called spam. i think it is particularly important to recognise the needs of disabled people and older people who need to have easier access to telecommunications services. new equipment designs are also expected in this area. i am convinced that these measures will contribute to a significant reduction in the price of telecommunications services throughout the union. today, despite the schengen rules, we still face high costs of data transmission across the eu's internal borders.

in writing. i would like to draw your attention to the following points: the us government and the federal reserve have so far committed nearly a trillion dollars to combat the effects of the financial crisis, and the subsequent proposals in the so-called paulson package, estimated to cost another 700-800 billion dollars, show that it can be compared to the great depression of 1929. 2.the reactions of the ecb, which has mobilised some usd 750 billion and the bank of england, which has mobilised some usd 80 billion to improve liquidity, also confirmed that the situation in european financial markets is considered serious. 3. all these developments indicate that a strong and determined state interventionism is returning to favor, and even the most liberal economists recognize the need for crisis-prevention regulation and are willing to accept the involvement of governments and international financial institutions in these processes. 4. the scale and extent of this crisis will have a negative impact on the course of real economic processes, which in the us economy means recession and therefore negative economic growth, and in europe a significant slowdown in economic growth. 5.in this context, it is necessary to strengthen financial supervisory institutions in all countries, and in particular in the eu, which would have stronger oversight of the activities of the most important banks, investment funds and insurance institutions. only such enhanced supervision can improve financial security and ensure financial stability in the future.
president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after listening to the various questions that everyone is asking, let me make three or four remarks. the first point concerns the rather erratic nature of prices: $ 10, then $ 140, recently $ 100, now $ 100. there is indeed a disconnect between the appreciation of the product itself and the financial market that operates on that product. nevertheless, in the long term, i think it is quite clear that speculators will still be able to play a part if we have the feeling that our growing global energy needs are not being met by a new energy mix that is less dependent on hydrocarbons. i note that in jeddah at the end of june, when commissioner piebalgs and i visited and all the producing and consuming countries were present, the common message was quite clear in this area. there was a clear expectation that the major consuming countries would have to make it clear that they are changing their energy mix, that they are practicing energy efficiency and that they are less dependent on hydrocarbons. the producing countries themselves agreed. i think that's the whole point of the climate-energy package that's going to be presented, that the 500 million european consumers are saying: we're going to go to more local, more autonomous energy, with a more direct link between producers and consumers. that said, in the very short term, it is clear that there are a number of regulatory problems, particularly with regard to the knowledge of commercial stocks and not just strategic stocks. the united states does it, japan does it. the commission has been asked to consider this. i believe that the commission will be presenting a proposal for greater transparency in the very near future at the end of october or the beginning of november. but a genuine energy self-sufficiency strategy and a change in the mix seem to us to be the most appropriate response in the medium and long term.
member of the commission. − mr president, i think these are very timely questions and this is a very important debate. the commission is now finalising the second strategic energy review, which is also based on the debates in this house. i expect that this second strategic energy review will be adopted in november, and it will particularly cover the issues that we have been addressing today. definitely there is a limit to what we can propose in the strategic energy review due to the lisbon treaty ratification, because there is an energy article that would give much more opportunity to streamline the response. but still we can do quite a lot. the commission shares the opinion that oil prices are likely to remain high in the medium and long term. the justification for this type of prognosis is volatility in daily markets. even if now, the oil price is usd 106 or usd 110 per barrel, which is much lower than it was some time ago, at usd 145, the daily volatility still makes the situation relatively difficult to predict, and it is definitely making a major, wide-ranging impact and deserves a response. while there is clearly a need for short-term action by member states to mitigate the impact on the most vulnerable households, the main policy response should aim at facilitating our transition towards clearly more sustainable ways of producing and consuming energy. in other words, to pursue our aim of becoming a low-carbon and energy-efficient economy. in order to do so it will be vital to take forward the commission’s proposals on climate and energy policy, following up on the political commitments of the european council. on the structural reforms. it is important to underline that we are facing an energy price increase, not only for oil: it also goes for coal, it also goes for gas and, as a result, it also has an impact on electricity prices. links between these prices are related by pricing structure: for example, gas contracts often use oil price benchmarks; gas-fired electricity generation is increasingly marginal and thus price-setting. so i think it is very important to address not only issues about oil prices but all the sectors. the situation clearly reinforces the need for encouraging competition throughout the whole energy sector. that is why, again, i would like to underline the importance of swiftly reaching an agreement on the third internal energy market package. europe can and must develop its own strengths to deal with the fast-changing global energy economy. a well-functioning, fully interconnected and competitive eu-wide internal market is a response. this will diminish european vulnerability to energy-supply disruption and facilitate our cooperation with energy producer and transit countries. solidarity between member states in crises will be enabled by european networks. on european energy oil stocks, we have now prepared legislation that will clearly address two things: one, that these oil stocks will be always available at moments of crisis and can be easily used; and second, it is issues of precedence addressed, it is transparency and reporting on a weekly basis on commercial stocks. in this respect, even though we are not the biggest oil consumer in the world, we are able to influence transparency in the market and diminish volatility and the level of speculation in the market. speculation is definitely an issue. we have done an analysis. the available evidence suggests that supply and demand are the main drivers of oil prices, and that these fundamentals are set to underpin high prices in the future. but, at the same time, we will continue our work on analysing what impact speculation has at a particular moment and whether there is really the ability to diminish volatility and have more supervision in the energy market. in any case, it is very clear that transparency in oil markets, both in terms of contracts and related financial instruments and fundamentals, is a must. i would also like to say that both commission and national competition authorities are acting against anti-competitive behaviour. this is a way in which we can pass the changes in oil prices to the consumers, because consumers use refined products. the commission will make additional efforts in this respect – we are following this issue – and a lot of competition authorities in member countries have already started investigations into the issue of how soon and how fast the oil price changes are being passed to the consumers. at the same time it is very clear that there are differences between different member countries, because there are different sourcing strategies for the companies concerned. also, in some countries there are biofuel blends that also influence the velocity of the possibility to change prices according to the oil price. nevertheless, it should be very clearly in the focus of attention in all anti-trust authorities. energy efficiency, renewables and diversification: it is very clear that our main lines are in our energy and climate policy, and it will be prominent in our strategic energy review. there is already a substantial european legal framework in place. in addition, there are many actions being pursued under the current energy efficiency action plan, including also legislative initiatives and studies. and there are also support actions, for example under the intelligent energy europe programme. regarding existing eu legislation, it is implementation that is very essential. the ambitious 2020 target for energy savings cannot be met without adequate transposition by member states. the commission is vigorously pursuing infringement procedures to ensure that member countries are really implementing their existing eu legisaltion. this year the commission also will adopt an energy efficiency package. this will include a communication with a comprehensive overview of the commission’s ambitions for energy effciency, as well as legislative and policy initiatives – in particular, prominent proposals for an ambitious recast of the directive on the energy performance of buildings; also for a modification of the energy labelling directive, to ensure more effective and dynamic labelling. needless to say, continued high energy prices further support the need for action in this area. and also we get clear involvement of the european investment bank in this area. the european council, when analysing the appropriate responses to the high oil price situation, underlines the importance of a sustainable and adequate tax framework. there is considerable scope for the eu and its member states to make more systematic and effective use of taxation to encourage energy savings. the commission intends to present proposals and recommendations on the cost-effective use of taxation and specific tax incentives, including reduced vat, to promote the demand and supply of energy-efficient goods and services. furthermore, in its review of the energy tax directive, the commission will look at how it can better support the eu’s energy and climate policy, encouraging energy efficiency and emission reductions. more widespread and systematic use of road pricing, in line with the principles of the commission’s ‘greening transport’ communication, would also encourage a shift to more energy-efficient transparency rules. on financing alternative energy technologies and research, let me draw your attention to the fact that we are in the process of preparing a communication on financing low-carbon technologies as a follow-up to the european strategic energy technology plan. the communication will analyse the resource needs for long-term research and development, large-scale demonstration projects and the early-stage commercialisation phase. we are considering measures that best use public investment to leverage additional private investment, such as the creation of a specific facility for large-scale demonstration projects. this could be built on existing instruments such as the risk sharing financing facility, a joint initiative of the commission and the european investment bank. the commission also encourages member states to use national resources, for example potential resources that could be raised through the auctioning of co2 allowances in the revised ets schemes. on energy security and foreign policy aspects, i come back to the idea that europe can and must reinforce its own strengths to deal with the fast-changing global energy economy. internal and external policy in energy work together. the stronger a common european energy market is, the stronger it will be towards external energy suppliers. we are pursuing diversification with countries like azerbaijan, turkmenistan, egypt, iraq, nigeria, but it is clear that we also encourage predictable relations with current suppliers like russia, and definitely we are looking very much at the possibility that norway could increase supply to the market, because it is very clear that the eu market is attractive for suppliers, and we should not be afraid that we will run out of gas, but we should really work for competitive supplies to the european market and not be in a situation where we could be blackmailed on prices. regarding the issue of assistance to oil-importing developing countries. given the strong impact of access and price of energy on development and global climate change, energy cooperation is increasingly important throughout our development assistance activities. it was a central theme of my joint visit with commissioner michel to the african union and a number of african countries earlier this month. we invest substantial resources in supporting movement of these countries, not only to eliminate energy poverty, but to power themselves with clean and new energy sources. on macroeconomic and social aspects, the increase in oil price levels certainly put a strain on consumers and certain sectors of the economy which face difficult adjustment processes. more immediately, most member countries have undertaken – or are currently considering – short-term measures in response to the recent surge in energy prices. in line with the european council conclusions, most of these policies focus on vulnerable households. some member states have also implemented or discussed temporary measures targeted at specific sectors. as high energy prices are expected to prevail in the long term, it is essential that the policy measures aim at facilitating the structural shift to more sustainable patterns of production, transport and consumption. this also points to the significance of flexible product and labour markets and the lisbon agenda, and to the importance of the transition towards a low-carbon and highly energy-efficient economy. but i believe there is clearly not one answer to these issues. still, the framework that we propose with the energy and climate change package and the internal energy market package is a backbone, because, the sooner it is adopted, the stronger we will be, and also there will be more competition and lower prices for consumers. at the same time we should be open and honest and say to the people: do not expect oil prices to come back to usd 20 per barrel. that means each of us also should change our behaviour, because part of the issue is also our behaviour, and i believe that we should really pay true attention in our everyday lives.
on behalf of the ppe-de group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. there are two different problems. firstly, the prices of oil and gas, which are mainly imported by the union, and secondly, the prices of electricity. as regards the first point, oil and gas prices may fall if producers of these raw materials, and not only consumers, are subject to the market. this is a matter for our joint eu negotiations with countries such as opec, russia and the countries of north africa. we also need to make significant improvements in energy efficiency and energy conservation. this is our most important duty and priority, and we've been talking about it for a long time. of course, we have to develop renewable energy, because it's our own non-imported raw materials. but that's not enough for us. so that leaves our coal and our nuclear power. and we can't deny any of these sources unless we want to drive up prices drastically. and that brings us to the second punch line: electricity. the price of electricity can be reduced by the decisive establishment of a common european energy market. the third energy package needs to be implemented quickly. we can also control electricity prices by introducing a sensible, moderate energy-climate package. this is particularly important for the electricity sector, where it is necessary to consider, in the emissions trading system directive, benchmarking or phase-in principles for this sector. i thank the commission for its efforts in this direction and the authors of the resolution for raising this issue.

mr. chairman, please! the document on health issues related to nutrition, obesity and overweight contains a number of important observations. the alarming prevalence of obesity is a reason to pay particular attention to the promotion of organic food, physical activity from an early age, sports and the harmful effects of subconsciously stimulating eating advertising. the document also promotes breastfeeding, improves the nutritional standards of school meals, provides fruit, and prohibits the sale of foods and beverages containing high fat, salt and sugar in schools. but there are other causes of obesity, and psychological and traumatic factors play a major role. a variety of mental disorders lead to eating disorders that are unconscious, such as bulimia and anorexia. not just the personal retardation, but the lack of respect for values, the prevalence of depression, the neuroses, make the biological automatism perpetuated by the ubiquitous presence of fast food available at every turn more important than conscious action. the disregard for ethical and moral principles, the disregard for the importance of fasting, can even hinder personal growth by making a person dependent on blood sugar and taste and sight. and in the email discussions and the corrections that have been reported, it's a little surprising that the importance of saturated fat is being overlooked, and that's increasing. the problem of the different effects of artificial trans acids from the others seems to be solved, since in the form of natural trans acids they are present in few products, especially in a small percentage in milk.

mr. chairman, please! health issues related to nutrition, overweight and obesity are extremely topical and timely. not only europe, but the whole world is facing a huge challenge today, which is obesity and related diseases, directly and indirectly. the rate at which medical costs are rising is alarming. according to recent statistics, in the united states, where 60 percent of the population is overweight and one third is obese, health care costs more than 10 percent of the national budget, or $100 billion, each year. europe is slowly catching up with its neighbours in these unseemly rates. more and more children and adolescents are suffering from hypertension and diabetes, often as a result of poor diet and lack of physical activity. with the future of europe and its people in mind, we need to pay more attention to the problems raised in mr foglietti's report. only joint, decisive and rapid action can prevent the health catastrophe facing europe and the whole globalised world. the european parliament is currently dealing with a wide range of economic, social and environmental issues. but to be able to fully realize them, we must not forget that only healthy societies will be able to fully enjoy the goods that are given to them. it is necessary to take action not only to promote healthy lifestyles but also to introduce legislation which will oblige all member states to take more active action in the field of physical fitness, healthy eating and sport. it is, of course, up to the member states to take the specific measures and policies needed to combat this phenomenon.

acting president of the council. - mr president, madam commissioner, dear androula vassiliou, rapporteur, dear john bowis, co-rapporteurs, draftsmen of opinions, and honourable members, i thank the european parliament for agreeing to postpone our working session, which was originally scheduled for the beginning of this month. as you know, the french presidency attaches great importance to consultation and dialogue on legislative texts. i was very keen to have a first exchange of views with my fellow ministers at the informal meeting of ministers held on 8 and 9 september in angers, before coming to you to present, not the french position, of course, but the position of the council of 27 ministers of health. this first exchange of views, like the first work launched in the council's health group, will not allow me to answer all your questions on such a complex and rich subject, but certainly our meeting today will allow the commissioner responsible for health to explain the european commission's main choices and will allow me to share with you the first impressions of the council. the council welcomed the adoption of a directive on crossborder healthcare and patients' rights. it is not conceivable to let the law be constructed in this field by the case law of the court of justice of the european communities alone. in my mind, as in that of my colleagues, this reflection should not be interpreted as a criticism of the court, or even of the content of the judgments, which often bring great advances for patients. however, it is not desirable that the europe of health should not be built by the two co-legislators, that is, you and us, and through political dialogue and a democratic process. our common objective must be to build a legislative framework which can contribute to legal certainty. secondly, the delegations from the 27 countries were unanimous in angers in welcoming the quality of the work done in recent months and in acknowledging that they had been heard in the recent consultations. commissioner androula vassiliou was warmly thanked for this at the informal meeting of ministers. the slovenian presidency has certainly informed you of the council's serious reservations about the initial version of the text, the main outlines of which were presented to the epsco council on 19 december 2007. only a small minority of states had supported this version. this hostility was also widely echoed in your parliament, as was confirmed to me by the members of parliament whom i met during my preparatory consultations on the french presidency in strasbourg, brussels and paris. the political dialogue initiated by commissioner vassiliou on her arrival in office has undoubtedly provided a good basis for negotiation and the council welcomes this. thirdly, as regards the timetable, this proposal adopted by the college of commissioners on 2 july came too late for us to consider a first reading under our presidency, but we will push the negotiations in the council as far as possible, while engaging in a political dialogue with the european parliament. the public health group has already looked at the directive on several occasions. it meets again tomorrow to continue its article-by-article examination of the text. on this issue, as on our other political priorities, france will play the role of the presidential trio by working in good faith with the czech republic and sweden. i would remind you that the theme of a europe of health for the benefit of patients is a priority of our joint programme for the next 18 months. fourthly, as regards the scope of the draft directive, i know from having spoken to the members of the committee on the internal market when i was in paris last may that many of you regret the choice to limit this text to the mobility of patients alone and not to deal with the question of the mobility of professionals. as a member of the european parliament at the time of the vote on the report by evelyn gebhardt, and as someone who left parliament just a few days before the debate on the report by bernadette vergnaud, i can understand the logic of this demand. the exclusion of health services from the services directive in the internal market leaves a grey area which is not fully covered by the current proposal for a directive which only addresses patient mobility. it can even be said that the proposal for a directive has more to do with the desire to integrate and adapt the case law of the court of justice than with the exclusion of health services from the services directive and thus the demand made by some members in favour of a specific sectoral instrument on health services. the health ministers did not discuss this. however, everything on this subject is linked to the timetable and the choice of the european commission can be explained by the need to respond as quickly as possible to the challenges that arise in the already vast field of patient mobility. it is certain that a broader directive including the mobility of professionals would have had no chance of being adopted before the elections next june. fifthly, as regards the content of the text, we have not yet dealt with all the provisions of the draft. however, at this stage the presidency can say that the council considers that the issue of prior authorization for hospital care is central to the member states of the european union. it could even be called the fundamental concern of health ministers. at the working lunch on this subject held in angers on 9 september, the ministers who spoke felt that there was a need to strike a better balance between the individual rights of patients to mobility and the maintenance of national regulatory and planning capacities for the benefit of all. this improved balance is reflected in particular in the reintroduction of prior authorisation for hospital care. the question is not to challenge the case law of the court of justice, which has clarified how the principles of free movement laid down by the treaty apply to health, but to incorporate into positive law the balance which the court has already established in its case law between the principle of free movement and the piloting capacity of the member states. it distinguished between outpatient care, for which the affiliation system cannot require prior authorisation, and hospital care, for which the requirement of prior authorisation appears to be a necessary and reasonable measure. in a context of strong budgetary constraints ageing, technical progress , member states must be able to retain full control of their care, in particular hospital planning. in particular, as the court itself acknowledges, such planning pursues the objective of ensuring sufficient and permanent access to a balanced range of quality hospital care on a national territory. it also contributes to the desire to control costs and to avoid, as far as possible, any waste of human, financial or technical resources. i would also point out that the framework for prior authorization ensures that the benefit of crossborder care is granted when medically justified. the regulation on the coordination of social security schemes already recognises this: authorisation cannot be refused if the same treatment is not available within a reasonable period of time. the protection of patients is also a matter for consideration, as prior authorisation ensures that the care they receive in another member state will be covered. finally, while we are committed to what we believe to be the correct interpretation of the court's case law, the directive would nevertheless bring a great deal of added value by clarifying the rights of patients, providing them with the necessary information and ensuring a uniform interpretation and thus a universal and consistent application of the case law in all the member states of the european union. i thank you for your attention, ladies and gentlemen, and i shall return to the floor at the end of this debate to answer your questions.
member of the commission. − mr president, i have already had the opportunity to discuss this proposal at length with various stakeholders and players in the decision-making process. you may recall that i presented the proposal to the committee on the environment and public health upon its adoption by the college and had a fruitful exchange of views. and i have also had the chance to exchange views with various national parliaments and, of course, the member states in the context of the recent informal health council in angers. it now gives me great pleasure to have this discussion, and i am looking forward to it with you, the honourable members, in plenary. i take this opportunity to thank mrs bachelot-narquin for the support and the chance she gave me to discuss this issue at length with the ministers. i would like to put the proposal on patients’ rights into context. following the numerous discussions of the european court of justice on the question of the inherent right of european citizens under the treaty to seek health care in the member state of their choice and following the specific request by the european council and the european parliament alike to present a proposal to regulate the right after the health-care-related provisions had been taken out – and quite rightly so – of the services directive proposal, the commission adopted the proposal on patients’ rights in cross-border health care on 2 july. it is without doubt the most important initiative on health of this present commission. its aim is to provide patients with better opportunities and access to health care, regardless of their place of residence while fully respecting national responsibilities over health-care organisation. it has three main objectives: first, to clarify the conditions under which patients will be entitled to seek cross-border health care and be reimbursed and to make it effective, if this is the best solution for their particular situation; second, to ensure high-quality and safe cross-border health care throughout europe; and, third, to foster european cooperation between health-care systems. it is based, as i said, on the court of justice jurisprudence. it is fully in line with the treaty, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, with the competences of the member states for the organisation and delivery of health services and medical care. the proposal is structured around three main areas. first, it clarifies and reaffirms the common principles of all eu health systems: universality, equity, access to good-quality health care, and solidarity. it recalls the overarching principle underlined by the treaty and the court that the member state on whose territory the health care is provided is fully responsible for setting the rules and ensuring compliance with these common principles. to help the member states translate this principle in more transparent terms, we have proposed to better clarify the objectives in terms of quality and safety standards for health care provided on their territory to patients from other member states. we also introduced a provision so as to ensure that patients from other member states shall enjoy equal treatment with the nationals of the member state of treatment. second, the directive clarifies the entitlements of patients and related conditions to receive health care in another member state. for instance, for people in border regions, it may be easier to seek health care abroad rather than travelling long distances to the nearest relevant domestic health facility. the added value of cross-border health care is also evident for people seeking highly specialised treatment, which only a very limited number of practitioners in europe can provide. this might be the case, for example, for rare diseases. the reality, however, is that most patients are simply unaware that they have the right to seek health care in another eu country, and that they are entitled to reimbursement for such treatment. and, even if they are aware of this right, the rules and procedures are often far from clear. this is what we aim to clarify with this new directive: patients will all get the same clear information and guarantees on cross-border health care. in practice, as long as the treatment is covered under their national health-care system, patients will be allowed to receive that treatment abroad and be reimbursed up to the cost of the same or similar treatment at home. we are also clarifying that, under specified circumstances, member states are entitled to introduce limits on the reimbursement or payment of hospital health care obtained abroad through prior authorisation, if there is a clear risk – even potential – of undermining the national health system. in addition to this, the directive clarifies the definitions of hospital and non-hospital care and in that way simplifies the procedures and conditions to access cross-border health care. in such a context, i would like to stress that we have maintained the possibility to expand the concept of ‘hospital care’ to some health care which does not necessarily require hospitalisation, but which is by nature costly or needs a heavy infrastructure to be properly delivered. third, the directive establishes a new framework for european cooperation in areas that we have identified as key areas for the future and where we must act together at eu level to better meet the challenges ahead of us. this is done in line with the principles i mentioned earlier through streamlined and improved cooperation, through common technical guidance and through a systematic search for best practices. this framework will provide for developing enhanced future collaboration at european level in areas such as european reference networks, with a view to pooling together expertise, knowledge and medical skills, both for applied medical research and for diagnosis and treatment. in particular, this will be very important in the field of rare diseases, the provision of new therapies, as well as the rapid spread of new health technologies. the second area is health-technology assessment, whereby the most efficient therapies will be identified at eu level by the best experts from the member states, and spread in order to promote their use. indeed, as regards new therapies and their high costs, the resources available being limited, we must ensure that they will be chosen and used in the most efficient possible way. the third area is e-health, where it is time to promote technical requirements to ensure interoperability at all levels and help to establish – at least – e-health as an integral part of health-care services of tomorrow. fourthly, there is a need for a wider approach at eu level on the collection of health data related to cross-border health care in order to better monitor the effects of the proposed measures and enhance our epidemiological surveillance. finally, there is the facilitation of the recognition of medical prescriptions in all member states. however, we must note that prescriptions issued in another member state will be reimbursed by the patient’s country of origin, only if the medicine is approved and eligible for reimbursement in his country of origin. let us also be clear that this initiative is not about harmonising health-care systems. it is not about changing roles in the management of health care. member states are responsible for deciding how to organise their respective systems, what benefits they provide to their citizens and what treatments and medicines they will pay for. this will remain the case. for now and for the future, what we want with this draft legislation is to grant patients the opportunities and information to access the safest, best-quality and most suitable treatment wherever that treatment is available in europe. more cooperation between health systems will also create more solidarity and more health-care availability. the aim of the proposed legislation is, indeed, to pave the way for better health care across europe. the directive is already being discussed, as was said by mrs bachelot-narquin, in the council, and i hope that the discussions will proceed swiftly in parliament as well and that ultimately they will bear fruit. (applause)
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i wish we had had the opportunity to speak on this very subject at the last part-session when we discussed the two previous legislative proposals. but as the title of the american film says, "better late than never". we are glad that the commission's proposals are really moving in the direction of what the european parliament has been talking about, of putting a certain amount of pressure on the commission in this area. if europe is to be a europe without borders, it is certainly first and foremost in the field of health care. ensuring this for the citizens of our member states will be a real demonstration of what we are doing for european taxpayers and voters. because the average pole, but also the average hungarian, cypriot, englishman, italian is more interested than the lisbon treaty in whether he can be treated abroad during his holidays, or even go abroad specifically to use a highly specialized hospital. in conclusion, i believe that the measures we are discussing today can indeed increase the real health care for foreigners, but also increase the authority of the union as such, an authority that has been wasted recently on ideological debates and on imposing institutional solutions on citizens that they do not want.

mr. chairman, please! media pluralism is the diversity of content delivery and ownership of broadcasters. both of these aspects are at risk in the media market today. the increasing concentration of ownership of media companies competing in the market has led to a situation where information of social and cultural value is hard to find in the cluster of readily available and standardised news for everyone. it is difficult to predict what a deteriorating situation in this area may lead to, not just for an individual, but for society as a whole. the rapporteur rightly emphasised the role of the public media as a custodian of diversity of content with a mission to disseminate high-quality information. it also rightly postulates a model of coexistence of strong public media outside the competitive media market and private media companies whose aim is profit. the balance of these pillars should be unquestionable. the content of the report and, therefore, the intentions of the rapporteur appear to be clear and transparent. the compromise reached at the cultural affairs committee is a good one. in addition, the legal status of new content delivery options such as blogs or, more generally, messages created by officials should be clearly defined so that users who create them are aware of the rights and obligations arising from this and of any sanctions. the next item is the report by richard seeber, drawn up on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, on tackling water scarcity and drought in the european union (2008/2074 (ini)) (a6-0362/2008).
mr. chairman, please! the protection of water resources, aquatic ecosystems and drinking water is one of the foundations of environmental protection. coordinated action at european union level is therefore necessary to ensure the effective protection of this valuable resource. the three main challenges facing the european union in terms of water use are conservation, sustainability and efficiency. climate change is not the only challenge facing europe. despite the increasing demand for water resources, we still face an excessive, unsustainable and inefficient use of water that is growing at almost twice the rate of the world's population. in europe alone, at least 20% of resources are wasted because of inefficient management. demand-setting measures should therefore be preferred to simply increasing water supplies. supply management measures should only be considered after the possibilities of more efficient water management, better demand control and educational activities have been exhausted. regional cooperation and the use of the structural funds can also play a significant role.
member of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for the discussion which dealt with the issue of water management and the problems connected with water from many different perspectives, and i will not comment on each of the contributions. i would like to touch on a few points, however, which i believe are particularly important in the report. first, the report recognises the importance of the water framework directive. full implementation of this directive is a priority to help tackle water mismanagement. the report also recalls that demand-side approaches should be clarified and welcomes the fact that water saving is the commission's first priority to tackle this problem. there is a huge potential for water saving in europe: 33% in households and 43% in agriculture. the report also highlights the link between water scarcity, drought and climate change and the need to take account of water issues in other policies, such as land use planning, where in the past bad decisions have in some cases exacerbated the problem. the report also calls on regional and local authorities to take advantage of the opportunities offered by the structural funds and highlights the role played by environmental programmes under the second pillar of the common agricultural policy. this integration will be at the forefront of the shift towards water-saving habits. the report also recognises the importance of high-quality information and calls on the commission to support the launch of a european drought observatory. following the communication, the commission's joint research centre is currently developing a prototype. finally, the report stresses the need for precise measures and concrete timetables for their implementation. i can assure you that the commission is committed to further deepening the objectives of the communication and is working on a report assessing progress towards addressing the issues identified in the report. in addition, the commission is fully committed to continue addressing these issues at international level, in particular in the framework of the united nations convention to combat desertification and the united nations framework convention on climate change. in conclusion, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to say that water will continue to be at the heart of our political agenda and that your report is a very useful and timely contribution to the commission's ongoing efforts to adapt to climate change. ladies and gentlemen, i think that the debate has really shown that water management is a complex issue, and i think that it is necessary to underline your point that it must go through all policies transversally and that it also has its great importance and strong international aspect.
i'm closing the debate. the vote will take place on thursday 9 october 2008. the competent authority shall inform the applicant of the reasons for the refusal of the application.

the next item is the brief presentation of the report by mr alejandra cercas, drawn up on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the implementation of social legislation relating to road transport (2008/2062 (ini)) (a6-0357/2008).
member of the commission. ladies and gentlemen, the european parliament is today discussing the implementation and possible ways of further developing the directive on working time for mobile road workers. it is a specific part of the legislation governing working hours for road transport workers such as bus or lorry drivers. however, the directive does not apply to self-employed drivers. many members will recall that the directive was adopted in 2002 after a difficult conciliation procedure, which resulted in the adoption of a complex review clause. this clause provides that, as from 23 march 2009, the provisions of the directive will be extended to all self-employed drivers, provided that the commission submits a report on the impact of the current non-inclusion of self-employed drivers and a draft legislative provision to the council and the european parliament on self-employed drivers. the inclusion or non-inclusion of self-employed drivers in the scope of the directive is a real dilemma, but if you will, also a false problem. the main objective of the commission in presenting its legislative proposal on working conditions in road transport is to ensure a high level of social protection, a level playing field and, at the same time, to improve road safety. the commission therefore considered it necessary to introduce a special regime for mobile road workers by means of a special law for the general working time directive. however, since 2002, other provisions of the legislation applying to drivers have changed significantly for the better. with your support, and in particular with the help of mr markov, a set of new measures on driving times, rest periods and checks was adopted in 2005. while the working time directive adopted in 2002 was originally applicable only to employed drivers, the rules adopted in 2005 apply to all drivers, both employed and self-employed. the rules cover 80% of the working hours of all drivers. parliament's legitimate concerns in this respect were therefore correctly addressed during the conciliation procedure on the 2002 working time directive. as regards the revision of the 2002 working time directive, it is no secret that member states' positions on this issue differ widely and that this division of opinion exists both within member states and within sectors. the commission published its report on the implications of not including self-employed drivers in the scope of the directive in may 2007. the report reached two conclusions: firstly, that the advantages and disadvantages of the two options are rather mixed, and secondly, that the implementation of the directive has been hampered by the difficulties encountered by member states in enforcing it, in particular because of the pseudo-self-employed drivers, as those drivers are called in the industry who are formally self-employed but in fact dependent on one company and cannot organise their work activities as they would like. they are socially vulnerable and, as i said, the directive already applies to them, but enforcement needs to be significantly improved. the commission has closely monitored the transposition of the directive into national law and, where necessary, has initiated infringement proceedings. once member states have completed the transposition of the directive into national law, we have carried out a thorough quality control of this implementation. this has led to infringement proceedings being initiated in many cases. in addition, the commission is currently carrying out an impact assessment to establish a compact basis for a legislative proposal, which will be worked on later this year. it would therefore be premature for the commission to take a position on the issue of selfemployed drivers at this stage, if the question concerns only their inclusion or exclusion from the scope of the working time directive. i am pleased with mr cercas' report, and particularly with in writing. true, symbols represent emotional attachment to a favorite organization or state. when we see a flag, a motto, a national anthem, or even a coin, we associate it with a country or an organization. it is obvious that the european union also has such symbols, which allow for easy identification and emotional connection. the dark blue flag with twelve golden stars; 'ode to joy' from ludwig van beethoven's ninth symphony; 'europe day' on 9 may; the euro as the official currency of 15 member states; these are long-established, well-known and widely accepted symbols, first of the communities and now of the eu. if we add to this the motto of the union, 'united in diversity', we have a perfect description of the essence of the european project. as a member of the convention, i very much regret that the eu symbols described in the european constitution were never implemented. they were seen as 'quasi-state' elements and were therefore removed from the text of the lisbon treaty. however, i believe that they have not lost their attractiveness and character for eu citizens and continue to be the bearers of the values on which the european union is founded and the expression of the sense of community of its citizens. it is therefore good that the impetus for the use of european symbols comes from the european parliament itself.

in writing. - unregistered work in the eu has become commonplace. in denmark, for example, as many as 18 percent of the population are engaged in or have had contact with such work. very often, the employee is not at risk for this work. the employer is most often punished, and in the 'best case' the employee is only obliged to pay a fine which is lower than the fine paid by the employer. in theory, no one can be deported to their home country for unregistered work, although some countries (e.g. denmark and belgium) reserve the right to do so in 'certain cases' (such as 'persistent' and 'long-term' breaches of the law). the european union should do all it can to combat this phenomenon effectively. the most effective way is to reduce taxes and remove administrative barriers in the legal labour market so that unregistered work is no longer profitable for both parties.

although we live in a time when borders are disappearing, our citizens are free to move and marry, we have not yet been able to create facilities for those who have decided to separate. an example of the problems associated with the lack of uniformity of divorce law in europe is the case of polish-german marriages. since 1990, more than 100,000 such couples have been legalised. many of them have not stood the test of time. last year, poles who lost contact with their children because of the german office for children and youth were invited to the european parliament. allegations of kidnapping and the prohibition of the use of the polish language are just some of the humiliations faced by parents and their children. because the above-mentioned institution violates basic rights, even the polish association of parents against discrimination against children was founded in germany. if we were to introduce the proposed changes to the divorce law, we would help many of our citizens to end a certain stage of life in a civilized way and, above all, not to allow children to be separated from one of their parents.
it seems to me that there is no treaty competence anywhere to shape marriage and family law at eu, community level. i therefore believe that the commission's proposal is a typical example of a certain overactivity, which is completely unnecessary and which only confuses the real competences of the european union. i think it's a deliberate breakthrough in this area, to further work on marriage law and its harmonization. this is a completely unnecessary activity, because private international law, as it stands, is perfectly capable of dealing with the problems of marriage, as well as with divorce, which is carried out on an international scale.
