in writing. with the increasing mobility of the population, the number of international marriages and divorces is increasing. the problem often arises as to which law applies to couples from different eu countries or when one of them is from a member state and the other is not. there is therefore an urgent need to harmonise the rules on international marriages in order to prevent situations of discrimination during the divorce procedure. as regards the choice of court, it should be based on the access of both spouses to full information on the most important aspects of national and community law and of divorce and legal separation proceedings. the choice of court and the law applicable should not affect the rights and equal opportunities of either spouse. the choice of law must therefore be between the law of the place of the marriage, the law of the place where the spouses have resided for the last three years or the law of the country of origin. moreover, it seems appropriate to apply the 'law of the place of the court' where there is a risk of discrimination between one of the spouses. this is the case for women from third countries who do not recognise divorce and who, while living in an eu country, apply for divorce or separation. in such a situation, the interest of the individual in obtaining separation or divorce as an expression of personal autonomy should prevail over the application of national law.
the next item is the joint debate on the report by sophia in't veld, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the conclusion of an agreement between the european union and australia on the processing and transfer of european union-sourced passenger name record (pnr) data by air carriers to the australian customs service [2008/2187ini] (a6-0403/2008) and the oral question to the commission on the european union and pnr data by sophia in't veld, martin roure, philippa bradbour, sylvia-ivonne kaufmann, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (o100/2008 b6-047/2008).
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we have heard a strong indictment. i do not know if i will be able to answer all these questions, but first i would like to thank you, mrs int veld, for giving us the opportunity to talk first of all about the pnr agreement between australia and the european union, which was concluded on 30 june. the agreement is the result of negotiations which began in march this year and were conducted by the slovenian presidency, assisted by the commission. the agreement is valid for a period of seven years. it is intended to provide legal certainty for air carriers and reservation systems within the european union regarding the transfer of pnr data to australian customs, in accordance with union data protection law. the agreement contains important commitments to address data protection concerns, the right of individuals to access personal information stored under the agreement, the right of individuals, regardless of their nationality, to complain to the australian privacy commissioner about the way their data is processed. parliament has always favoured the transfer of pnr data on the basis of a 'push' system. after the transition period, pnr data will only be transferred to australian customs on the basis of the 'push' system. in other words, the australian customs service will not be allowed to access this data directly from the databases. the agreement also contains important safeguard clauses concerning the retention of pnr data, the transfer of such data to other agencies or to third countries and a clear reference to the purposes for which the data may be used. the draft recommendation states that the purpose of pnr data is not in line with article 8 of the european convention on human rights. i will answer that the agreement states that pnr data may be processed for three purposes. it specifies three objectives: the fight against terrorism and related offences, the fight against serious transnational crime, including organised crime, and, thirdly, to prevent persons from evading warrants and measures of provisional detention issued against them for the same offences. if you like, i think we can say in this case that the aims have been specified. the agreement also provides for the processing of pnr data on a case-by-case basis, where necessary for the protection of the vital interests of the data subject. for the sake of clarity, the agreement states that pnr data may be processed on a case-by-case basis where such processing is also required by a court order, for example where the processing would need to be carried out in order to verify that pnr data is processed in accordance with australian human rights law. i would like to say that in future i will be very attentive to the good involvement of parliament in such negotiations. i am well aware of the need to keep you well informed. however, it seems to me that a number of safeguards have been taken both as regards the purpose of the data, the use of the data and the retention of the data. i have tried to be objective, but i think that agreement was necessary. and since we have a partner who is attentive, who has an authority to ensure data protection, i still believe that we have reason to hope that this agreement will be implemented in full respect of data protection. i now come to the most important, if i may say so, oral question you have submitted, which of course raises the whole problem of the pnr. international terrorism and crime are a serious threat and it is true that the collection and analysis of pnr data has emerged as a useful tool in the fight against terrorism and crime. pnr data is indeed commercial information provided by the passenger to the carrier on a voluntary basis. this is information that is collected by carriers to implement their reservation systems. recently, some countries have begun to require carriers to provide them with pnr data for use in preventing and combating terrorism and serious crime, such as human trafficking and drug trafficking. these countries include the united states, canada, the united kingdom, australia, new zealand and south korea. this is the case for a number of third countries - not the uk - which have begun to require carriers to provide them with pnr data. some member states are initiating legislative processes along the same lines or are considering the possibility of initiating a legislative process france, denmark, sweden and belgium. several other countries have begun to consider the idea of using pnr data. but we're still in the early stages. it should be borne in mind that the pnr is simply a tool to be used by law enforcement authorities with other tools and information, because the question you have raised as to what the real utility of such use is, can only be assessed to the extent that the police authorities do not use the pnr alone but use the pnr with other instruments. of course, it is much more difficult to see exactly what the usefulness of pnr data is. nevertheless, some countries that have used pnr data seem to have really demonstrated that pnr is a useful tool in the fight against terrorism and crime. the pnr systems have been evaluated by the authorities of each country. the results of such evaluations are generally positive and confirm the effectiveness of the use of pnr systems. in preparing its proposal on the european pnr, the commission has been in close contact with the police authorities of the member states. and the commission has obviously been quite convinced by the evidence provided by the member states. most of the evidence is from confidential information and cannot be shared in an open setting. parliament held a hearing on the pnr during which four member states and three third countries presented their use of the pnr and reported on their success. but given the confidential and sensitive nature of this information, the hearing was held in camera. i would like to say a few words about automated methods of analysis because this is a real question. it is true that pnr is normally analysed automatically on the basis of risk indicators, but i would like to emphasise this point: the commission wants a guarantee that such an automated analysis will never lead to a decision which directly affects the individual. the result of the automated analysis must always be re-analysed manually by a specialised officer. the commission proposal suggests that pnr data be used to prevent and combat terrorism and organised crime, including - as you have acknowledged - drug trafficking, human trafficking. i would add that the pnr could be useful in the fight against other serious crimes, which do not fall under the category of organised crime. however, we have limited the proposal to organized crime for reasons of proportionality. some member states consider that pnr can generally be useful for combating illegal immigration, supporting public health and aviation safety. in the fight against illegal immigration, the pnr would be useful because it is true that it has data much faster than the advance passenger information data. in aviation security, pnr could be useful if the pnr system gives the possibility to refuse boarding to a potential terrorist or criminal, but the commission proposal does not give such powers. in public health matters, the pnr could be useful in the prevention of potentially epidemic diseases. if a passenger discovers that he or she has a potentially epidemic disease, the pnr can be used to communicate with other passengers on the same flight and advise them accordingly. but the commission proposal did not go as far as that because the proportionality was not demonstrated. i am sorry to disagree with you entirely, but it seems to me that the aims described in the proposal are sufficiently precise to provide an otherwise desirable legal certainty. you also mentioned subsidiarity and asked whether there was a need for an initiative by the european union. the commission considers this proposal of the european union to be necessary. three member states have already enacted national legislation on pnr, several other member states already use pnr in other ways. a comparison of the systems shows a great deal of divergence in terms of both the obligations imposed on the carriers and the purposes. such differences complicate the lives of passengers and of course cause problems for carriers. the proposal therefore aims to harmonise the obligations of carriers and to provide uniform rules for member states using pnr, and also, at the same time, to oblige them to respect our data protection mechanisms. the proposal will also allow for more effective cooperation between police forces. above all, the commission believes that international terrorism and crime are serious threats in our time, and that measures must be taken to deal with these problems, while respecting human rights and fundamental rights. you also mentioned the choice of a decentralised architecture for data collection, saying: "but, for once, by choosing a decentralised system, do we not lose a right of view?" the commission has examined the alternative between a centralised system and a decentralised architecture and, during the consultations with the member states, it has become clear that the processing of pnr requires the use of highly sensitive information from intelligence. so, of course, the member states did not feel ready to share such information with a central european pnr unit. it is true that a centralised system would be cheaper, would have some advantages, but we have chosen the alternative of a decentralised architecture out of political realism. from the data protection point of view, the decentralised option may also allow each member state to establish clear safeguards for access to and exchange of data. finally, mr president, i would like to conclude by apologizing for the length of the debate, which is important, on the question of democratic control by the european parliament and the national parliaments. the commission notes, of course, that its proposal will be adopted in accordance with a consultation procedure. the commission wants to be in close contact with you, with parliament. national parliaments will be heavily involved in the process as the proposal is or will be examined in most national parliaments. data protection authorities will be involved in the pnr system and will be responsible for the independent control of the systems. that is why, madam rapporteur, mrs sophie in 't veld, i recognize that your objections are serious. i tried to answer them honestly. i think, however, that this european framework is useful if we do not want each member state to embark on a totally different approach to pnr in this area, and certainly with the risk of not complying with a number of data protection rules. as regards the usefulness, it is true that we must specify the uses, we must be very careful about the proper use of this data, but it is true that in the fight against organized crime we need to be so much more efficient that i tend to think that an additional means is not worth neglecting. i will say this very simply in response to your questions, which i have listened to very carefully.
thank you very much for the comprehensive explanation and the rapporteur's introduction. i would like to inform the rapporteur that the agenda is decided by the european parliament, but that it is proposed by the conference of presidents. the decision on which item is to be placed shall also specify whether or not a representative of the council is to be present. there was no initiative at the conference of presidents to have this item on the agenda on any other day than monday, and as a rule on mondays the council representative does not take part in our discussions. so if you have any comments on this, please refer them to the chairman of your group, who could have initiated this matter, but did not. the council is therefore not present today, and this is not a sign of disrespect for the european parliament, but is due to procedural reasons.
thank you very much. thank you. i take note of your dissatisfaction, but please address it to the chairman of your group, who could have caused this item to be discussed when the council representative is present at the european parliament. i didn't ask the member anything, but i understand you've expressed your concern.
i'm not going to let you do this. i welcome this opportunity to discuss with you, although you are no longer transport commissioner, but i have a grateful memory of this period of cooperation. but speaking of data exchange, i also remember our discussions back then in the transport committee on such elements as passenger safety, protecting personal data from falling into the wrong hands. these are the key issues. therefore, the sharing of data, the circumstances and recipients of this collection, the sharing rules and the purposes, should, in my view, be central to this agreement. i'm not going to let you do this. we have subtleties in our cooperation with the united states, it's true, we know how important the united states is, but please know that we europeans often feel a certain discomfort at airports and we should bear that in mind. thank you, sir.

in writing. a programme to protect children using the internet and new technologies is one of the basic forms of child protection, both because of the spread of technology and the increase in computer literacy. children are therefore now exposed to risks related to illegal content and inappropriate behaviour such as harassment, child pornography, harassment, online seduction, etc. according to the data, more than 70% of young people aged 12 to 15 use the internet for about 3 hours a day and unfortunately most of them have come across pornographic images. also alarming is the increase in the number of internet sites containing pornographic material and the decline in the average age of children who are victims of this practice. increasing children's safety online can only be achieved through cooperation at many levels. children, their parents, schools, telecommunications operators, internet service providers and other institutions should be involved in this ambitious project. hotlines for the collection of reports on illegal content should play an important role in the fight against harmful behaviour online. children should be informed about how to avoid dangerous online behaviour and parents and teachers should be involved in a computer education campaign to reduce the generation gap in new technologies and effectively combat the threat.

the next item is the brief presentation of the report drawn up by ms joanna geringer de oedenberg on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights on the monitoring of the application of community law - 24th annual report of the commission (2008/2046 (ini)) (a6-0363/2008).
the rapporteur. - mr president! - what are you doing? the effectiveness of european union policies depends to a large extent on their implementation at national, regional and local level. therefore, compliance by member states with community law must be subject to strict control. the 24th annual report of the european parliament on this matter, which i have authored, showed that the number of infringement proceedings initiated by the commission in 2006 decreased slightly, but still exceeded the level of 2500 cases. it should also be noted that the number of non-compliance procedures in the enlarged union of 25 member states decreased by 16%, indicating better discipline in the notification of transposition measures by the member states. as in previous years, the complaints concerned mainly the poor functioning of the internal market, including the implementation of the principles of free movement of persons, services, goods and capital, and the violation of the rights conferred by european union citizenship, which in principle guarantees equal rights and opportunities for all citizens. the improvement of the existing working methods to improve the management of proceedings announced by the commission in its communication of 5 september 2007 was supported by a majority of the parliament. however, there is a concern that the new procedure for referring complaints received by the commission to the member state responsible in the first place for the incorrect application of community law may lead to a reduction in the commission's institutional responsibility as guardian of the treaties. it is therefore necessary that the commission submit to parliament a preliminary report on the results achieved in the first six months of the pilot project, which started on 15 april this year with the participation of 15 member states. moreover, the commission, often the ultimate institution to which citizens can report cases of misapplication of the law, should register as a complaint any correspondence potentially informing about cases of infringement of community law. as regards the current infringement procedure, the main problem is still the excessive length of time taken to deal with a complaint, on average 20.5 months. the commission should make every effort to reduce lengthy procedures and to find practical solutions by using, where possible, alternative methods such as solvit, which is still not sufficiently promoted. it is also concerned about the significant increase in cases of breaches resulting from non-compliance with the judgments of the european court of justice revised in 2006. this is often accompanied by a lack of cooperation between national courts and the court and by the non-use of the preliminary ruling mechanism under article 234 of the treaty, as a result of the still weak knowledge of community law in some member states. as regards interinstitutional cooperation, arrangements for monitoring the implementation of community law and close cooperation between the commission, the council, the european ombudsman and the competent committees of parliament should become the standard for ensuring effective intervention in all cases where a petitioner has lodged a well-founded complaint concerning an infringement of community law. given the continuing high annual rate of complaints lodged improperly, for example, with the committee on petitions or outside the remit of the institutions, which accounted for as much as 75% of the complaints received by the ombudsman in 2006, it is necessary to stress the urgent need to increase information activities to citizens in order to better direct complainants to the body with the best competence to deal with their cases, whether at national or european level. citizens' complaints are an indispensable source of information on their most pressing needs and should guide the commission in its legislative initiatives. in analysing the implementation of community law in 2006, i would particularly urge those countries which are most likely to benefit from the structural funds under the 2007-2013 financial framework to bring their national legislation into line with european standards, in particular in the field of environmental protection, in a timely and appropriate manner, in order to make effective use of the structural funds available and to accelerate the social and economic development of the regions. finally, i would like to express my regret that the ppe-de group in the legal affairs committee, in my report, has rejected important provisions concerning the lack of implementation of the directives on equal treatment for women and men in employment, education, promotion and social security, which still exists in many member states, in clear contradiction to the principle of equality, which should be a priority for all of us.
member of the commission. − mr president, the commission greatly welcomes the general support from parliament for the commission’s approach set out in its 2007 communication ‘a europe of results: applying community law’ and thanks mrs geringer for her informative report. the commission attributes high importance to the correct application of community law. it figures in the priorities of the barroso commission and the commission is vigilant in exercising its role as guardian of the treaty. this is why the commission has made a major effort to improve its working methods for the benefit of citizens and businesses, as explained in the 2007 communication. these improvements include the introduction this year of more frequent decision-taking on infringement cases to avoid delays in the advancement of cases, and the introduction of the eu pilot project in april this year. within 15 member states this pilot project will test an improved method for problem solving and information provision to ensure quicker and better results for citizens and businesses. up-to-date factual information on the functioning of this eu pilot project will be sent to the rapporteur, but a full report will only be possible, as already promised, after one year, when sufficient experience will have been obtained for first conclusions to be drawn. we are also testing the use of officials in some representation offices in member states to follow up on questions relating to the application of community law to see how this might improve efficiency. this reflects the reality that all questions concerning the application of community law involve actions taken by member states. this work, therefore, requires the commission to work closely with member state authorities to try to find correct member of the commission. - mr president, madam members, allow me to begin by apologising for the short delay, as i was unable to estimate the traffic situation in time. ladies and gentlemen, the recent judgments of the court of justice in the viking, laval and rüffert cases have triggered a wide debate at eu level and in the member states on the protection of workers' rights in the context of increased globalisation and labour mobility. for the european labour market to function well, appropriate rules need to be established. the posting of workers directive is a key instrument to achieve this. i would point out that the purpose of that directive is to harmonise, on the one hand, the appropriate protection of workers temporarily posted to another member state and, on the other, the free movement of services in the internal market. the commission intends to ensure that the fundamental freedoms of the treaty are not incompatible with the protection of fundamental rights. the commission expressed its wish to open a debate with all interested parties in order to analyse together the consequences of the court's judgments. this debate is of the utmost importance, as it must clarify the legal situation and finally enable member states to introduce appropriate legislation. on 9 october 2008, the commission organised a forum on this subject, which was attended by all interested parties. this forum should become the starting point for the debate we so desperately need. the commission agrees that the increased mobility of workers in europe has brought new challenges to the functioning of labour markets and the regulation of working conditions. the commission believes that the social partners are best placed to assess these challenges and to suggest possible improvements. the commission therefore invited the european social partners to focus on the implications of increased mobility in europe and the judgments of the european court of justice. i am pleased that the european social partners have taken up this challenge. the commission will support their work as necessary. the commission notes that the member states most affected by the court's judgments are currently implementing legislation that ensures compliance with the court's case-law. the commission cannot agree with the proposal that the posting of workers directive should also refer to freedom of movement. such an extension would necessarily lead to confusion as to the scope of the directive, since it would blur the distinction between two different categories of workers, namely posted workers and migrant workers. i emphasize posted workers and migrant workers, that's the difference, of course. the commission agrees with parliament on the need to improve the implementation and enforcement of the posting of workers directive. and in this context, let me recall that the commission adopted a recommendation on enhanced administrative cooperation in april 2008, calling on member states to remedy existing shortcomings. the commission will further promote increased cooperation by setting up a committee of experts from the member states in the future. the commission also believes that the proposed treaty of lisbon will bring about a very substantial strengthening of social rights, inter alia through a new social clause which should take social issues into account in all other european union policies, and also by introducing a legally binding reference to the charter of fundamental rights.
draftsman of the opinion of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection. - madam president! - what are you doing? the report we are debating today has made the current directive on the posting of workers a challenge to collective agreements. i, with this attitude, which i have always emphasized very strongly, cannot agree. i am aware that the ets rulings may have caused dissatisfaction in some member states, but they strike a balance between all the aims of the directive, namely freedom to provide services, respect for workers' rights and the observance of the principles of fair competition. i would like to stress that maintaining this balance is our top priority. we should not question the wording of the directive itself, but rather focus on the poor state of implementation by the member states, because this is the main problem in applying it correctly. this is why we need, first and foremost, a thorough analysis at member state level, which will allow us to assess the problems arising from the judgments and the possible challenges we face. i think that is why we must refrain at this stage from calling for a directive to be amended. let us not forget that the posting of workers is inextricably linked to the freedom to provide services, which is one of the fundamental principles of the european single market and should in no way be seen as a restriction on collective agreements.
author of the draft opinion of the legal affairs committee. - regardless of your beliefs, i consider it unacceptable to criticise the judgment of the european court of justice, which is an independent and impartial institution, crucial to the functioning of the european union. we may not like the law and of course we have the power to change it, but i find it hard to understand the criticism of the court, which rules on the basis of the law in force. i would like to emphasize two important aspects of the subject we are discussing today. first, the judgments of the court of justice do not in any way affect the content of the freedom to conclude collective agreements. second, according to the court's interpretation, member states may not introduce minimum standards in matters other than those listed in the posting of workers directive. the court expressly recognises the right to take collective action as a fundamental right which forms part of the general principles of community law. at the same time, the principles of the free movement of services, like the other freedoms of the internal market, are an equally important foundation of european integration. what is the consequence of this report? the rapporteur calls for a revision of the posting of workers directive, arguing that the court's interpretation is not in line with the intention of the legislator. i completely disagree with that position.
on behalf of the ppe-de group. - madam president! - i have to go. every year, around one million people in the european union are posted to work in a country other than the country of their employer. only a few cases in recent years have posed a problem in the interpretation of the provisions of the directive and the union law governing this issue, and these few cases have been the subject of interest to the european court of justice, which has ruled that, in general, the problem is not the content of the directive, but rather the lack of proper implementation of the directive in individual member states. what does that prove? well, it proves that the eu law that was created to regulate the issue of posting is correct, well-crafted. at most, there is a problem with its implementation in individual countries. of course, this does not mean that it is an ideal law. the current directive, however, protects the fundamental rights of workers by guaranteeing them a minimum level of both pay and occupational safety and health. secondly, and i want to emphasize this very clearly, it does not exclude the possibility of concluding collective agreements for more favourable working conditions than the minimum. at the same time, the directive strikes a very good balance between the freedom to provide services and the protection of the rights of workers who are posted to provide services in another country. that is why we agreed in the jan andersson report to invite the commission to look at the directive again. but we are absolutely opposed to the idea that this directive is wrong and that there is an urgent need for some radical change in european law on this issue.
on behalf of the uen group. - madam president! - i have to go. i regret to say, with reference in particular to the ets judgments in laval, viking and others, that too often economic rights are given priority over fundamental rights and freedoms. a clear hierarchy of these rights and respect for the fact that people are more important than money requires that these rights be clearly identified. the laws of economic liberty cannot block the right of people to associate and defend their rights together. in particular, workers have the right to organise and to negotiate collectively working conditions. collective bargaining systems and the collective agreements resulting from them deserve recognition and support, since the consent of the responsible social partners guarantees social peace and the chance to implement the agreements reached. this belief is reflected in the conventions of the international labour organisation. the main challenge facing us today in the area of collective agreements is to take account of the guarantee of equal rights for domestic, migrant and posted workers. i congratulate the rapporteur!

madam president! i would like to make two points in the debate on the conclusions of the european council. the first point concerns the financial crisis. it demonstrates beyond doubt that the regulatory framework for banking supervision requires substantial improvements. the main directions of these changes concern better asset risk assessment and the adaptation of prudential standards to new financial instruments. however, changes are also needed to eliminate the pro-cyclical nature of hypothetical loan decisions. the size of this loan increases with the increase in real estate prices and decreases with their decline. this is the mechanism that creates the bubble. the second point concerns the climate package. i welcome the council's decision to seek a compromise on the system of co2 allowance sales. in some member states, energy is based on 90% coal. to require these countries to buy 100% of the permits as early as 2013 would be an economic disaster. we need to introduce transitional periods. this is both the principle of equal treatment and common sense.
the brussels summit was also, thanks to the efforts of the polish president and prime minister, a voice of common sense when it came to the climate package. the summit's decisions, for which the leaders of the european union are to be thanked, have removed, though not entirely eliminated, the threat of such environmental stresses, which would have been a decidedly excessive economic burden, especially for the countries of the new union. the summit also addressed the financial crisis. the only strange thing is that a few days earlier, there was a small summit of the largest countries of the european union, like the political bureau of the communist party of the soviet union. it would be appropriate for the strongest members of the union not to impose their solutions on other countries. irritating, too, are the double standards that allow member states to finance banks but not polish shipyards. in this respect, the european union is like george orwell's animal farm: all animals are equal, but some are more equal.
one of the most important topics discussed at the summit was the global financial crisis combined with the climate change package. i'm glad the council has taken up the matter. however, it is worrying that key decisions were already taken earlier at a meeting of representatives from only four countries. this position was consolidated in the so-called euro group and only later in the european council. this raises a serious question: is the european council being taken seriously or is it just a forum for approving the decisions of a small group of leaders? is this the practical dimension of a three-speed europe? in the face of the global crisis, it is also worth revising previous decisions to reduce co2 emissions. their immediate implementation could further exacerbate the recession, especially in central and eastern european countries such as poland, and have a negative impact on the european economy. so we need to adopt a separate package for countries that are primarily coal-fired.

in writing. − apart from the positive effects of globalisation on growth and employment, it can also have negative effects on the most vulnerable and less skilled workers in some sectors. these negative effects may affect all member states, both large and small, long-standing and newly joined. the eu structural funds support the anticipation and management of change through activities such as lifelong learning with a long-term perspective. the european globalisation adjustment fund, on the other hand, provides one-off, time-limited individual assistance aimed at supporting workers affected by redundancies caused by market changes. the eu should pay particular attention to this fund.

in writing. − at today's sitting of parliament i voted in favour of the adoption of the legal affairs committee's annual report on monitoring the application of community law for 2006. the rapporteur, ms lidia geringer de oedenberg, made observations in the draft on the failure to meet the deadlines for transposing directives, the unsatisfactory cooperation between national judicial authorities and the european court of justice, and the methodology for dealing with complaints. the reluctance of the national courts of the member states to apply the principle of the primacy of community law and to use the preliminary ruling procedure is a very worrying phenomenon. the report also shows an increase in the number of infringements resulting from the failure to comply with the judgments of the court of justice and the late transposition of directives by the member states. in this context, there is an urgent need to strengthen cooperation between the european parliament and national parliaments and to strengthen the control of the application of community law at national and regional level. these actions are a condition for bringing the european union closer to its citizens and for strengthening its democratic legitimacy.
in writing. − erasmus mundus is a cooperation and mobility programme in higher education, aimed at promoting the european union worldwide as a centre of excellence in teaching. it extends the possibilities previously available under the erasmus programme by opening up educational cooperation to non-eu countries. education plays a key role in young people's lives. international experience is increasingly valued by students themselves and by prospective employers. knowledge of languages and cultures, country specificities and the ability to function in an international environment are just some of the many benefits of participating in the programme. the promotion of mobility is another element that is strongly emphasised in the programme's objectives. they are particularly important in the era of globalisation, when contacts with third countries are becoming more important. it is good that students from europe and from third countries will continue to have the opportunity to gain these experiences. i am pleased that the programme also proposes to solve the visa problem, which unnecessarily complicates the procedures for entry. the proposed facilitation should also cover the scope of the information available. students should be given all the information they need to prepare for their stay well in advance. in this respect, support from the european commission's existing delegations in third countries could be particularly beneficial.
in writing. − erasmus mundus has already played a major role in modern education for young people and adults. however, experience has shown that this issue should be approached with caution. too radical changes, for example in tuition fees, under the new conditions could undermine the market-verified education system and violate certain principles of academic autonomy. so we need to consider which is better whether to leave the decision to the erasmus mundus consortia or to set the conditions from the top. i believe that where there is a well-established practice and the possibility of decision-making by local communities, this should be respected and nothing should be introduced by decree, especially since we live in different regions, i.e. more developed or historically backward, with different traditions and different economic conditions. i would also like to point out that the european parliament continues to make use of documents which are not yet in force, such as the european constitution, which was rejected in the referendum, the treaty of lisbon and the charter of fundamental rights. law cannot be based on lawlessness.

in writing. − intrastat as a common and uniform system of eu member states aims to reduce unnecessary red tape and regulation. it is a flexible system that allows the specific needs and solutions of individual eu countries to be taken into account. at the same time, it is important to note that both intrastat and the international trade statistics system are based on the recommendations of the methodology for international trade statistics developed by the united nations department of statistics. this makes it possible to obtain complete, fully comparable information on international trade in goods. it is very important to receive up-to-date statistical data on important economic issues. member states should make every effort to modernise and improve this system.
in writing. − in the european union, we are seeing an increase in marriages where the spouses are from different countries, both within and outside the european union. this fact has led to the increasing problem of which law to apply and which court has jurisdiction in a given case. the european union needs effective conflict-of-law rules to decide on the jurisdiction of the law. with the increase in divorce, there is also discrimination in seeking divorce or separation. the better informed spouse first brings the case before the court of his choice in one of the spouses' home countries, thus deciding which law is more in his interest. in the case of marriages where one of the spouses lives outside the european union, attempts to obtain recognition of a divorce decree issued in a third country by a court prove difficult. the report put to the vote today aims to ensure that both spouses have access to reliable information on divorce and separation procedures and on the main issues of national and community law. rightly, the best interests of the child were considered paramount in each case.

building good relations with the russian federation is a major challenge for the european union. it is one of our most powerful partners politically, economically and militarily. recent events in georgia have seriously undermined trust in our eastern neighbor. russian foreign policy has revealed to us the kremlin's aspirations to rebuild a great world empire that does not properly respect accepted international agreements. moscow has clearly indicated where its sphere of influence is. this has put the union in a very difficult position, in which we have fortunately spoken with one voice, albeit a little muted. after the georgian experience, we should consider how to continue a coherent policy towards russia. the immediate issue for us is security. in writing. in the economy, this is reflected in russia's demand for eu investment and technology. the union needs russia's natural resources. in 2001, eu countries provided 79% of russian foreign investment, totalling almost usd 30 billion. in may 2004, the eu-25 accounted for more than half of russia's foreign trade (55%). the deterioration of relations with russia is not in the interests of the eu member states. the union needs diversification of oil and natural gas supplies. russia, with its political and economic potential, is a major partner for the eu. if the eu were to push for ideas different from the us on the international stage, gaining political support from russia could prove crucial to their implementation. an example was the entry into force of the kyoto protocol (thanks to russian ratification), in return for which the eu agreed to russia's accession to the wto.

president of the council. - mr president, i am very pleased to have the opportunity to reply to mrs doyle and mrs mcguinness at the same time. the french presidency has therefore decided to continue the complex and politically sensitive discussions on gmos which were initiated during the previous presidency with a view to reaching conclusions on this subject before the end of the year. the environment council, mrs doyle, mrs mcguinness, had an exchange of views on gmos yesterday following the informal meeting of environment ministers held at the celle saint-cloud, as you know, last july. this discussion will continue with a view to operational conclusions for the council in december, at the end of the french presidency. what are the guidelines being discussed at this stage? the first is to strengthen the procedures for environmental monitoring and assessment by harmonizing them at european level and, of course, i will report back on the results of this reflection in december. we must also, in the context of this reflection, take account of socioeconomic criteria in the management of risks relating to gmos, see how to improve the functioning of scientific expertise and establish harmonised labelling thresholds and finally take account of the fragility of certain territories which are sensitive or protected. so as you know, president barroso has set up a high-level group to look at this, and i think you should check with the commission as to where the work of this group is going. there was no report that was published at this stage. the group is concerned about the legislative framework, about trade-environment issues, about the rise in agricultural commodity prices and its impact on gmos. what is important - as i said - is what has emerged in the council, and the need to ensure that new guidelines on strengthening environmental assessment are adopted quickly in order to take into account the long-term environmental risk of gmos. that's what i wanted to point out.

member of the commission. − madam president, the commission is well aware of the historic importance of the polish shipyards, and that is why we have been working very hard to find a solution that will allow the restructuring of the sector in a way that provides a livelihood for the regions concerned. however, we depend on the cooperation of the polish authorities to arrive at a viable solution. to be quite clear, the state aid investigation in these cases has been pending for around four years. the investigation concerns a substantial amount of operating aid to the szczecin, gdynia and gdańsk shipyards. without even counting the state guarantees from 2002 until now, the gdynia shipyard received from the polish state – which means from the polish taxpayers – aid amounting to around eur 167 000 per worker. that is approximately eur 24 000 per worker per year, and that means that the subsidy to each shipyard worker is at least double the average annual income of polish workers. even without counting the state guarantees, the total aid received since 2002 by the gdynia and szczecin shipyards amount in nominal value to around eur 700 million and eur 1 billion respectively. despite all that money, the yards and the future of the workers remain vulnerable. that, i would stress, is what really scares me. i think that the future of the workers needs to be taken into account. they have avoided the painful but necessary restructuring that, for example, the german and the spanish shipyards have undertaken and which malta is also preparing for at this moment. at all times in those past four years the commission has had an open door for the successive polish governments. i have met quite a number of ministers and prime ministers of polish governments. we have tried again and again to reach an agreement and, unfortunately – and i say it with a sad heart – the polish authorities did not make use of those possibilities. in july of this year the commission came to the conclusion that the latest restructuring plans did not ensure the viability of the shipyards, but, again, conscious of the importance of the issue for the polish economy and for polish society, we, the commission, showed flexibility and offered two more months for new final plans to be presented by 12 september. during the summer, commission officials remained constantly available and gave feedback to the polish authorities on the draft submitted to them. i have now carefully assessed the restructuring plans submitted by the polish authorities on 12 september. unfortunately, i cannot see how to conclude that those revised final plans will ensure the viability of the yards. indeed, the plans require even more public money to be pumped in in future, including money for the day-to-day operating aid. it should also be underlined that the restructuring plans submitted on 12 september – and i am talking about the plans of the polish government – foresee job reductions of approximately 40%. however, these sacrifices would be made without giving any prospect of sustainable employment to the remaining workers, as the yards would very likely not become viable and would continue to need state support at the expense of the polish taxpayers. that is not an acceptable outcome. it is not acceptable from the eu competition law perspective, but also not acceptable for the future of the shipyards. not acceptable to their workers and more generally for the polish economy. therefore, as the situation currently stands, i do not see how to avoid the adoption of negative positions on the gdynia and szczecin shipyards. but the commission is not in the business of just saying ‘no’. we have been working actively to help the polish authorities come up with a solution that would ensure a viable commercial future for the economic centres of gdańsk, gdynia and szczecin and ensure sustainable jobs. according to this scenario, the assets of the gdynia and the szczecin shipyards would be sold on market terms in several bundles. the assets would be put into bundles following an open, unconditional and non-discriminatory tender; and the remaining shell company would use the proceeds from the sale of the assets to repay the aid received over the years and would be liquidated, and the buyers of the assets would then be able to speedily resume economic activities at the shipyard sites, without the burden of having to repay the large quantities of state aid received by the yards over the years. they may re-employ even more people than would be the case if the restructuring plans of 12 december were implemented. i can only assume that any investor willing to take on the yards – or at least some of their current liabilities – would be even happier to acquire the most important productive assets free of debts and develop them in a competitive and sustainable way. the final outcome would probably be positive in two respects: on the one hand, the number of workers left without a job would be lower than foreseen in the restructuring plan submitted by the polish authorities and, on the other hand, the workers re-employed by the purchasers of the yards’ assets would have much more stable working prospects within viable undertakings, because the burden of past debts would have been lifted. that solution, which would be in line with the recent precedent of olympic airways, would allow a fresh restart of economic activities at the shipyard sites, also benefiting the workers there. the commission has raised that possibility with the polish authorities. we have done that several times, and i sincerely hope that they will take advantage of our flexibility to bring us a concrete proposal. technical discussions on the possible implementation of the ‘olympic airways’ solution for the gdynia and the szczecin shipyards are being held between the polish authorities and commission officials. as for gdańsk, i think there is a good chance of reaching a positive outcome if there remains flexibility and good will on both sides. you will naturally ask me: why this approach for gdańsk? there are two reasons: firstly, gdańsk has already been sold to a private operator which injected fresh money into it and, secondly, this yard’s liabilities for past aid are far more limited compared to the gdynia and the szczecin shipyards. on the commissions side, we have already indicated to the polish authorities our position in assessing the compensatory measures needed to comply with ec state aid rules. because the yard has received less aid in the past, we can be less demanding in this respect. the quid pro quo for the openness on the commission’s part is that the polish authorities must now submit a draft restructuring plan for gdańsk in order to permit any outstanding issues to be discussed, and so far – and i regret this – we have not received such a plan, and it is essential that the polish authorities provide it quickly. moreover, the polish government can request support from the european globalisation adjustment fund – an application which is likely to be successful – and the size of the intervention would depend on the amount of co-funding the polish government is ready to invest, as the european globalisation adjustment fund co-finances a maximum of 50% of the cost. the european globalisation fund analysed by the commission to date the amount per person to be supported, ranged between eur 500 and eur 10 000 from the fund, to which must be added an equal amount to be funded by the member states. to conclude, i can say that the commission has been very forthcoming in assessing these cases and has shown a considerable amount of flexibility. we have done everything we can, and we will continue to work with the polish authorities to find an economically viable and socially sustainable solution which is in line with ec competition law and established commission precedents. now the ball is in the court of the polish authorities. the future of the shipyards and of their workers depends on the polish authorities’ willingness to cooperate with the commission to quickly find a positive solution in the framework i outlined earlier.

perspective of competition distortion and of safeguarding stable employment, the length of the restructuring process in poland is an aggravating factor. whereas the shipyards in germany were account. even during that period things were not working properly in a way comparable to the other shipyards. so if we take into account that the boom, with an assured inflow of orders and vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has already made a number of proposals. the debate has confirmed the broad consensus on the regulation on the authorization of variations. i do not want to go into that any further. we should put this into effect now and make sure that it is as effective as possible in practice. i think that beyond the day and overall more important are the other issues that have been raised here. let me make a few very basic remarks: my job is not to explain to you any technical rules, but my job is to tell you why we do certain things and why we don't do certain things. there is a conflict in our societies between the needs of the health bureaucracy on the one hand and the needs of patients on the other. that is absolutely clear and unambiguous. the proposals we are going to have to deal with in the future are in the middle of this conflict. the health bureaucracies in the member states are not interested in the informed patient. the informed patient does work, the informed patient does effort. he forces those who are supposed to be there to give him information. why am i not getting this medicine or why am i getting that medicine? why am i not getting this therapy and why should i have that therapy? man has a right to know that. i believe that the principle that will not change is that in a democratic society it is not the person who wants to give information to the people who has to justify himself, but the person who does not want to give information. it is the health bureaucrats in the member states who have to explain why they do not want the informed patient! i don't have to explain why i want the informed patient. i would like to make it absolutely clear that there will be a very intense, lively and controversial debate here, and i hope and wish that the european parliament will support the commission and me in that debate. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. this is about what civil liberties mean to us in health care. the second question, which concerns counterfeiting, i agree with all those who say that it is a criminal matter. where we are dealing with counterfeiting in the illegal distribution chain, the police are called in. illegal is illegal, there's not much more we can do. i think, however, that the proposals we can make will make it almost impossible to get counterfeit medicines into the legal distribution chain. that's what we can do. mrs roth-behrendt is absolutely right! it is, in my view, a rather unreasonable assumption to assume that this is really about restricting certain forms of distribution of pharmaceutical products for reasons of competition. i don't care about that. parallel trade is a legal activity within the european union. the european court of justice has clearly confirmed this. i do not think i want to go after the parallel trade, but i must say one thing: all those involved in the distribution of medicines must submit to the same strict safety requirements. i do not see why anyone should be exempted from safety requirements simply because he buys a medicine that is sold at a high price in one member state, which is sold at a lower price in another member state, buys it cheaply in that member state, brings it back to the more expensive country and sells it at a high price there. i don't know what you're talking about. those of you who know a little about food law will have wondered, as i have, why it is strictly forbidden in europe to open a pack of spaghetti on the way from the producer to the consumer - yes, it is strictly forbidden to open a pack of pasta on the way from the producer to the consumer - but medicines which, if taken incorrectly, can cause death can be opened on the way from the producer to the consumer. it's worth thinking about why we have this amazing difference, why it's banned for spaghetti, for example, but allowed for vital medicines. i'm having a hard time understanding this. we will find solutions which will enable everyone to continue to do his job, in the sense that mrs roth-behrendt has said: we must be a little creative, have a little brain and think, but the safety requirements apply to everyone. there are no exceptions! the next item is the report drawn up by toin mandersa on behalf of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council on consumer protection in relation to certain aspects of the occupancy of immovable property for a fixed period, long-term holiday products, exchanges and resales (com (2007) 303 - c6-0159/2007 - 2007/0113 (cod)) (a6-0159/2008).
on behalf of the uen group. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: the tourism industry plays an increasingly important role in the economies of the eu countries, including timeshare services, long-term holiday products, timeshare swaps and resales. in many cases, consumers were the victims of these transactions. the directive addresses these problems and creates the conditions for harmonising these services on the european union market by adopting a set of basic rules to increase transparency and protect consumers, inter alia by: establishing a uniform model for contracts, requiring contracts to be written in the consumer's language, ensuring better conditions for the consumer to make the right decision, establishing a cooling-off period within which the consumer can withdraw from a contract without giving reasons. the directive, together with its amendments, creates the conditions for the development of these services and increases consumer confidence in them. thank you, mr. mander, for your excellent report. the uen supports this directive.
member of the commission. − madam president, we need to ensure that consumers all over the eu are adequately protected against aggressive selling tactics by rogue traders operating in the timeshare and holiday product markets. the need for action at eu level is all the more crucial because of the cross-border nature of most timeshare contracts. furthermore, we need to ensure that consumers have enough confidence in the regulatory framework so that they do not refrain from purchasing timeshare abroad from legitimate traders. a healthy market in timeshare and similar holiday products will contribute to boosting growth and job creation in the european union. it is my firm belief that the compromise package that you will vote on today will make an important contribution to the achievement of these aims. the amendments put forward by the alde, ppe-de and pse groups – with which the council has agreed – are, in my view, fair and reasonable. the package is also in line with the commission’s original proposal. in my opinion, this package constitutes the best option in the interest of both consumers and traders. a vote for this package is a vote for consumer confidence in holiday products, for clear consumer information and for a competitive and responsible holiday industry. so i look to the members of this house to vote to support an agreement today on rules for timeshare and similar holiday products which will provide real added value for holidaymakers all over europe.
in writing. the use of real estate for a specified period is a form of holiday product. many consumers choose to purchase such services because of the attractiveness of the place they are going on holiday, which has unfortunately often been exploited by dishonest companies that do not provide comprehensive information on the service offered. the amendments introduced by the directive will increase the protection of the consumer against such practices. first of all, consumers will have a 14-day period to withdraw from their contracts without any consequences, which will help them to make an informed decision. the information that companies will be required to provide to potential service buyers will also be extended. the consumer will have the right to demand full information regardless of the member state in which he purchases the service. more importantly, this information should be provided in writing in the language of the member state of residence or nationality of the customer. if the consumer is not informed of the possibility of withdrawal within 14 days, the consumer shall have the right to withdraw from the contract for a period of one year and 14 days. all of these solutions are extremely beneficial to the consumer, especially at a time when international travel has become so common and consumers are therefore increasingly exposed to unfair practices by certain operators.

in writing. −the european parliament has approved the temporary staff directive after six years of negotiations. there are currently considerable differences between the national provisions of the member states on temporary employment. however, in all eu countries temporary work is becoming more important and the temporary work market is developing rapidly. it is estimated that there are about 3 million temporary workers in the european union, employed by some 20 000 enterprises. it is therefore necessary to define a more precise framework for this form of employment of workers. these regulations are particularly important for the workers themselves. temporary workers will receive guarantees that, while performing their tasks for their employer, the working conditions offered to them by that employer will be the same as if the undertaking using the services of a temporary worker had decided to employ him directly. moreover, these conditions must apply from the first day of employment. but the beneficiaries of the temporary workers' scheme will also be the temporary employment agencies themselves and the entrepreneur who uses this form of employment. temporary work allows companies to manage their staff flexibly, especially in seasonal situations where the company needs to increase the number of employees in order to cope with the market situation.
in writing. −temporary employment agencies employ 3 million workers across the european union. it is estimated that they provide services with a total value of around eur 75 billion. the draft directive on the working conditions of temporary agency workers aims to ensure a minimum level of protection for temporary agency workers while supporting the temporary agency sector. it is an example of legislation of a social nature in a time when the expectation of a social europe is widespread. the basic principle of this legislation is that workers employed by a temporary agency are not discriminated against in terms of pay, social and labour rights and the application of labour law. the prohibition of discrimination will apply to working hours, overtime, holidays and the protection of pregnant women. the protection of workers from the first day of work is a very important element of the directive. the social partners should always be consulted on any derogation from this principle. there is no doubt that there are huge differences in the working conditions and pay of temporary workers today. those differences should be corrected as soon as possible. in view of the above, i voted in favour of the adoption of legislation to protect these workers as soon as possible.
in writing. −as new technologies become more common, computer literacy and internet access are also increasing. one of the largest groups of internet users are children and young people. and while the internet brings with it access to information, it also brings with it risks. children and young people are one of the most vulnerable groups. research indicates that almost all children have been exposed to pornographic images. the trend of decreasing the age of child victims is also of great concern. i think that combating this phenomenon must be a priority. this requires a multi-level approach involving parents, schools, telecom operators, internet service providers, ngos and self-regulatory bodies. in particular, there is a need to improve knowledge and prevent harmful practices, an effective system for reporting abuses and to improve the sources used by the police for investigative purposes. i also believe that large-scale education campaigns should raise children's awareness of the types of risks associated with the use of new technologies. i therefore welcome the provision of €55 million for the years 2009-2013 under the 'safe internet' programme, which was part of the proposal voted. i believe that these funds will help achieve the objectives of the programme.
in writing. −to the eu citizen, an environmentally friendly and energy-efficient vehicle in public road transport seems to be a given. it's becoming a necessity for our cities and for our environment. we should also be mindful of integrating the use of clean cars into our actions in the context of the climate package. therefore, as a member of the committee on the environment, i support most of the actions proposed by the rapporteur (especially technical and organisational measures) which lead to the achievement of the basic objective of reducing pollution by investing in environmentally friendly vehicles with lower co2 emissions. this includes in particular commercial vehicles (e.g. special purpose trucks and buses for operational support, infrastructure maintenance, cleaning machines, etc.). on the other hand, i have some doubts about the proposal to make it compulsory to include co2 emission criteria in public procurement of public transport vehicles. i believe that it is better - at least in the first phase of the new regulation - to leave the contracting authorities in each member state (most often local authorities) the right to choose whether to include environmental criteria in the fleet ordered. i agree with the assessment that public procurement - as a very important part of the european market - should continue to be an instrument for promoting environmentally friendly vehicles, but it should not be done mechanically.
in writing. −in the absence of harmonisation at community level, changes concerning only national marketing authorisations are subject to national rules. in some member states, national requirements for national marketing authorisations only are consistent by analogy with the regulations on the amendment of authorisations. however, in most member states, this is not the case and this leads to divergences in the rules in force in the member states. this has negative consequences for public health, administrative burdens and the overall functioning of the internal market for pharmaceutical products. all medicinal products, irrespective of the authorisation procedure, should be subject to the same criteria for the assessment of the authorisation and the same administrative procedures for the amendment of the authorisations.

vice-president of the commission. − the lisbon treaty contains three main provisions of the amended treaty on the functioning of the european union which deal with administrative affairs: article 197 on administrative cooperation, article 298 on an open, efficient and independent european administration and article 336 on the staff regulations. article 197 provides for the union to take measures, excluding any harmonisation, to support the efforts of member states to improve their capacity to implement union law. article 336 is amended to change the procedure for adopting the institutions’ staff regulations to ordinary legislative procedure – that means normal codecision – currently, the council acts by qualified majority vote on a proposal from the commission, after consulting the other institution. the new article 298 requires the adoption of regulations ensuring an ‘open, efficient and independent european administration’, which is what we are already trying to do without waiting for the final entry into force of the lisbon treaty.

on behalf of the alde group. i'm not going to let you do that. the holodomor, the great famine in ukraine, was one of the most cruel crimes committed in europe in the 20th century. in order to prove the effectiveness of collective farming and destroy the source of the main threat to the communist soviet union - the independent ukrainian peasants - the stalinist regime created an artificial famine that led to the death of several million ukrainians. people were being deprived of all their food. the famine caused mass migration from the countryside to the cities, which the authorities blocked by introducing internal passports and banning rail travel. those who remained in the countryside were thus forced to forage illegally for food in the collective farms, for which they were imprisoned or even killed. they were not allowed to gather even a handful of grain for themselves. the five-barrel law was in effect at the time, and anyone who plucked more than five barrel barrels of grain was subject to the death penalty. in many countries of western europe, the holodomor, the great famine, is still a virtually unknown event. until recently, these historical facts were denied by the soviet union. any statements on this subject, until the fall of the soviet union, were classified as the crime of so-called anti-soviet propaganda. active disinformation measures were used against western journalists. only recently have census records been released that give the number of people who died in the great famine. the famine in ukraine has been recognized as genocide by the governments or parliaments of 26 countries, including my own country, poland. i am convinced that the european parliament will not remain silent on this matter either. we should recognize that the holodomor was a madam president! in 1932-1933, the soviet authorities seized agricultural products from collective farms in ukraine, using force to deprive their workers of food. the resulting famine, known in ukraine as the holodomor, killed millions of people in a country renowned for its fertility. since the target of this operation, for which stalin and his collaborators bear responsibility, were ukrainian peasants as a social and national group, the crime of the holodomor meets the definition of genocide in the un convention of 1948. the resolution we have drawn up on the occasion of the 75th anniversary of the holodomor is a compromise that largely captures the essence of this crime. the only thing missing is a clear indication that the holodomor was a genocide. it's the result of resistance from certain groups in this chamber. during the compromise negotiations, i learned that a group of socialists are opposed to discussing history at all. this is an interesting statement, considering that european socialists are always eager to condemn nazism and general franco, and equally emotionally refuse to do so in the case of the crimes of the soviet authorities or the spanish republicans. during these negotiations, i also heard that the memory of the victims requires respect, and that the avoidance of words like genocide. this kind of moralizing and selective memory shows that among european socialists, historical materialism is turning into hysterical relativism. i hope that this does not apply to all the members on the left of this house. i also heard that socialists are against the historical truth vote. that's right! the problem is that we're not talking about the truth about holodomor, we're voting the truth about ourselves. a resolution on history is always a declaration of values, and not taking a stand is also a stand. that means the voices are empty. how can you define your value system other than by evaluating past events? genocide is genocide, whether it was committed by hitler or stalin or how it is judged by the russian authorities today. to think that the victims of the holocaust deserve less attention than hitler's gas chambers today is to question one's own credibility. before the law and the truth, we are all equal!
madam president! the holocaust is a fact and a symbol of one of the most inhumane methods of killing. the ideology that was supposed to serve the common people, the workers, took on a form that is unimaginable today. and it was simple: no need for guns, no need for soldiers to kill, no need for gas ovens. all they had to do was take everything the land produced, and the so-called rebellious citizens disappeared from their villages because they didn't fit the system. they were pushing people towards a utopian vision, a vision that was terrible and expensive, and yet still appealing to many and defended by some of the colleagues on the left of this chamber. bolshevik ideology used methods of implementation that can not be justified. my phd student in ukraine has been studying the trauma of people who have managed to survive this socialist horror, although there are exceptions. well, interviews show that there was a famine that led to cannibalism, like a mother sending her 6-year-old son to the forest for the winter because in the countryside he wouldn't survive, he would be eaten. on one side, we have the 20th century, the 1930s, the so-called enlightened father and friend of the people, joseph stalin, who foretold the world revolution, and on the other side, millions of people with bloated bellies dying in the streets. it must have been a terrible picture, even for the political leaders in power. that's what happened in eastern ukraine. but 10 years later, something similar in quality to the tragedy of the poles in what was then eastern poland occurred, albeit on a smaller scale. the ukrainian upa's nationalist ideology, in collaboration with the nazi nazis, led to the ethnic cleansing of poles. the methods were equally cruel: burning alive, ripping open the bellies of pregnant women, beheading children with axes. men were at war then. to this day, this golgotha of the east, as survivors call it, is the subject of taboo and shameful silence. ironically, there are monuments to the leaders of the nationalists of that time. perhaps it is a good circumstance that while we are paying tribute to the victims of the holodomor, we also pay tribute to the memory of the poles and ukrainians who were brutally murdered and who did not agree with this ideology. it is not easy to admit such facts, but otherwise it is difficult to bring the nations closer together, to accept ukraine in the area of european values, which we are currently seeking here. i understand the russian protests against the union. if you talk about the holodomor, as they suggest, you have to talk about the extermination of the indians in the new world by the colonists. the holocaust deserves to be condemned in a special way. add to this the millions of people deported to siberia for forced labor or death camps during world war ii - ukrainians, poles, tatars. i'll just say for the information of this assembly that of the approximately 100,000 prisoners of the stalingrad paulist army deported to siberia, only 5,000 survived until 1955. for the sake of europe, its parliament cannot downplay these 20th century tragedies.
mao tse tung once said, when asked if it was worth risking nuclear war to overthrow capitalism, that it was worth sacrificing the lives of at least a hundred million people so that the rest of us could live happily under communism. joseph stalin reasoned with the same horrible, criminal logic. as resistance to collectivization grew in the countryside, he decided to physically eliminate those who lived in the most resistant regions. these were regions inhabited by ukrainians. their liquidation also solved the national problem, because as stalin said on another occasion, and i quote, "the national problem is basically the problem of the peasantry". and so, as a result of a criminal, planned action, millions of people starved to death in ukraine alone. suffice it to say that even according to official statistics, the population of ukraine in 1926 was well over 31 million, and in 1939, despite strong natural growth, ukraine had only 28 million inhabitants. not only did the people of soviet ukraine starve to death. administrative requisitions of all food, combined with the prohibition of its import from other regions, also caused starvation in the volga, kuban and the north caucasus. these lands were populated by ukrainians, but also by russians. today we are taking up the issue of hunger in ukraine to also give witness to our conviction that this is still too little known a part of the dramatic history of our common europe.
